Q01 Is existence definable?

What is being known when existence is said to be immediately intelligible, and what would a noncircular definition require?

A successful real definition explains a thing by prior and better-known constituents. But the proposed definitions of existence appeal to establishment, to an object about which one can make assertions, or to other notions that themselves presuppose something existent. The question is therefore not whether the word “existence” can be explained; it is whether the concept can be *resolved* into a more basic real definition. Ṭūsī also rejects defective proofs of the correct thesis: the conclusion must not be confused with the quality of every argument for it.

Ṭūsī’s precise target

The opening lemmata reject circular definitions, distinguish lexical explanation from real definition, and disallow certain arguments for indefinability. The rejection of an argument does not amount to a rejection of the conclusion.

A faulty demonstration can have a true conclusion

Al-Ḥillī identifies the circle

The attempted definition of the existent as what is established already embeds the very idea to be defined. A definition by the possibility of reporting something equally uses a demonstrative reference to something taken as established.

ALH01 — On the circularity of alleged definitions

al-Ḥillī · al-Ḥillī | Direct Tajrīd commentary | printed p. 29, edition with Ḥasan Zādeh Āmulī annotation. Arabic: https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/3439/29?lang=ar

وهذه الحدود كلها باطلة لاشتمالها على الدور، فإن الثابت مرادف للموجود، والمنفي للمعدوم.

All these definitions are invalid because they involve circularity: “established” is synonymous with “existent,” and “negated” with “nonexistent.”

The neighbouring modern editor’s metaphysical reflections must not be attributed to al-Ḥillī.

The operative objection is *prior intelligibility*, not a thesis about the independence of quiddity.

A rule for proper definition

Quṭb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī states the general requirement that the definiens be clearer than the definiendum. Ibn Taymiyya criticises the alleged necessity of a particular logical method; that broader criticism is registered as a distinct methodological challenge, not treated as support for Ṭūsī’s exact argument.

C31L04 — The alternative argument: whatever differs from existence is dependent

ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Lāhījī reporting an alternative interpretation · Shawāriq I, printed p.464 to opening of 465; PDF pages 465–466; electronic p.471

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

وقد يوجه بحيث لا يلزم القول بالانبساط، ومخالطته مع التعينات، لعدم إمكان عروض الوجود الذي هو الواجب القائم بذاته لشيء من الماهيات. والدليل على كون الوجود هو الواجب: أن كل مفهوم مغاير لحقيقة الوجود كالإنسان مثلا، فإنه ما لم ينضم إليه الوجود بوجه من الوجوه في نفس الأمر لم يكن موجودا فيها قطعا، وما لم يلاحظ العقل انضمام الوجود إليه لم يمكن له الحكم بكونه موجودا. فكل مفهوم مغاير للوجود، فهو في كونه موجودا في نفس الأمر محتاج إلى غيره الذي هو الوجود، وكل ما هو محتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره فهو ممكن، إذ لا معنى للممكن إلا ما يحتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره، سواء كان ذلك الغير موجدا له أو وجودا له، وكل مفهوم مغاير للوجود ممكن، ولا شيء من الممكن بواجب، فلا شيء من المفهومات المغايرة للوجود بواجب. وقد ثبت بالبرهان أن الواجب موجود، فهو لا يكون إلا الوجود الذي هو موجود بذاته، ويستغني في كونه موجودا عن غير ذاته، وإن كان المتبادر من لفظ الموجود بحسب اللغة ما قام به الوجود، فإن المتبع هو ما أدى إليه البرهان لا غير.

It may also be interpreted without entailing that existence spreads or mingles with determinations, since the existence which is the self-subsisting Necessary cannot be an accident of any quiddity. The argument that existence is the Necessary is this. Any concept different from the reality of existence, such as “human,” certainly does not exist in objective actuality unless existence is joined to it in some manner. Unless the intellect considers existence joined to it, it cannot judge it to exist. Every concept different from existence therefore depends, for its existence in objective actuality, on something other than itself, namely existence. Whatever depends on another for being existent is contingent: a contingent is precisely what needs another in order to exist, whether that other produces it or is its existence. Every concept different from existence is contingent; nothing contingent is necessary; hence no concept different from existence is necessary. It has been demonstrated that the Necessary exists. It must therefore be existence, which exists through itself and needs nothing other than its essence in order to exist. Even if the linguistic sense first suggested by “existent” is something in which existence subsists, what must be followed is the result of demonstration alone.

This is the argument under report, not Lāhījī’s final endorsement. Nafs al-amr means objective actuality here.

Interim judgment: The defensible result is modest: proposed explanations of the word are possible, but real definitions that contain existence implicitly are circular. Ṭūsī demands an examination of each purported proof. A common concept of being is an additional thesis, considered separately in Q02.

Boundary: No proof of the ontological unity of existence, of its numerical simplicity, or of the mental/external distinction follows from indefinability alone.

Remaining: Collate al-Ḥillī on the two rejected arguments in Kashf al-murād, al-Iṣfahānī at the opening of Tasdīd, the corresponding Qūshjī objections, and Sunni discussions of taṣawwur.

Q02 A common concept or graded realities?

Is wujūd predicated with one meaning of the Necessary and contingent beings, and what follows for the realities signified?

Three different claims are frequently conflated: the *meaning* of the predicate existence is common; the predicate is applied to things asymmetrically or analogically; and what exists outside the mind is a single reality. The first does not by itself prove the third. Here the issue is how one meaning can apply to the Necessary and the possible without making them members of a univocal species.

Ṭūsī and al-Ḥillī: retain existence while doubting the subject

The common-concept argument starts not from a mystical thesis but from the fact that one remains certain a cause exists even as one revises whether it is necessary or possible, substance or accident. This shows a stable intelligible predication.

المسألة الأولى: هل ثبت عندكم أنّ وجود واجب الوجود أمر زائد على حقيقته أم وجوده عين ماهيته وأن ليست له حقيقة وراء الوجود؟ وما البرهان الموضح تحقيق ذلك؟ فإنّ جميع ما ذكر في تقرير كل واحد من الأمرين غير تام ولا مقنع للّبيب، لأنه إن قيل بأنّ وجوده عين حقيقته اعتمادا ورضى بما ذكره جماعة في تقرير ذلك، فلقائل أن يقول: لا نسلّم أنّ وجود الحق عين حقيقته، ويدل على ذلك من وجوه. منها أنه من البيّن أنّ مفهوم الوجود من حيث تعيّنه في تعقّلنا مفهوم واحد. وهذا المفهوم من حيث إنه هو مع قطع النظر عن كل ما سواه إما أن يقتضي أن يكون عارضا لماهية شيء من الماهيات، أو يقتضي أن لا يكون عارضا لها، أو لا يقتضي واحدا من القسمين. فإن كان الأول، وجب أن يكون كل وجود عارضا لماهيته، أو له صلاحية ذلك. فوجود واجب الوجود يكون صفة لحقيقته. وإن كان الثاني، وجب أن لا يكون شيء من الوجودات المتعقّلة عارضا لشيء من الماهيات. فإما أن لا تكون هذه الماهيات الممكنة موجودة، أو تكون موجودة لكن وجودها نفس حقيقتها وحينئذ لا يكون مفهوم الوجود مفهوما واحدا. وقد فرضناه مفهوما واحدا. هذا خلف. وإن كان الثالث، فحينئذ لا يصير وجود واجب الوجود مجردا عن الماهية إلا لسبب منفصل، فيكون واجب الوجود لذاته واجب الوجود لغيره، هذا خلف.

First question. Has it been established, in your view, whether the existence of the Necessary Existent [واجب الوجود] is something additional [زائد] to His reality, or whether His existence is identical with His quiddity [ماهية], so that He has no reality beyond existence? What demonstration makes this clear? Everything advanced in support of either alternative seems incomplete and fails to satisfy a discerning mind. Suppose, following the arguments of certain thinkers, one says that His existence is identical with His reality. An objector may reply: We do not concede this. One reason is that the concept of existence [مفهوم الوجود], as determined in our understanding, is plainly one concept. Consider it solely as itself, disregarding everything else. Either it entails being an accident or concomitant of a quiddity, or entails not being so, or entails neither. On the first alternative, every instance of existence must belong to, or at least be capable of belonging to, a quiddity; hence the Necessary Existent’s existence would be an attribute of His reality. On the second, none of the conceived existences could belong to a quiddity: either possible quiddities do not exist, or their existence is identical with their respective realities. In that case, however, the concept of existence would not be one, contrary to our supposition. On the third, His existence would be independent of quiddity only through some distinct factor; He who is necessary through Himself would then be necessary through another. This too is contradictory.

READING NOTE Qūnawī’s argument depends upon a common conception being forced to have one uniform ontological consequence. Ṭūsī’s reply will deny precisely that inference by distinguishing univocal from graded predication. | Arabic source: https://www.ibnalarabi.com/qunawi/tusi.php?id=2

Ṭūsī on graded/shared predication

Ṭūsī allows a shared general concept predicated in different ways without conceding numerical unity of extra-mental existences. Yazdī’s three-case argument about gradation in what is essential separates varying individual intensity from intrinsic gradation of one defining concept.

al-Ṭūsī · Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī · Reply to Question 1 (two continuous response paragraphs)

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

أما البرهان الموضح تحقيق كون وجوده عين ماهيته وأن ليست له حقيقة وراء الوجود، فهو أنه لو كان له وجود وماهيته، لكان مبدأ الكل اثنين، وكل اثنين محتاج إلى واحد هو مبدأ الاثنين والمحتاج إلى مبدأ لا يكون مبدأ للكل. فإن قيل، الماهية موصوفة، والوجود صفة لها، والموصوف متقدم على الصفة القائمة بها، فالمبدأ الأول واحد وهو الماهية، قيل، الماهية على تقدير تقدمها على الوجود لا تكون موجودة ولا معدومة. وإذا يكون مبدأ الموجودات غير موجود، وهذا محال. فجوابه: أنّ الألفاظ التي لها مفهوم واحد مقول على كثيرين تنقسم إلى قسمين: أحدهما أن يكون ذلك المفهوم في آحاد تلك الكثيرين بالسواء وهو كالإنسان في زيد وعمرو، والفرس في هذا الفرس وذلك الفرس. وتسمّى تلك الألفاظ بالمتواطئة، ويكون حكمها فيما تقتضي تلك المفهومات حكما واحدا، كما ذكره. والقسم الآخر أن يكون ذلك المفهوم في تلك الكثرة لا على السواء، بل إما أن يكون في بعضها أقدم أو أولى أو أشد أو أكثر، وهو كالأبيض على الثلج والعاج، والموجود على الجوهر والعرض. وفي هذا القسم لا يجب أن تكون مقتضيات تلك المفهومات واحدة، بل ربّما تختلف، مثل اسم الضوء الواقع على ضوء الشمس وضوء القمر وضوء النار، وضوء الشمس يقتضي زوال العشيّ دون سائر الأضواء. والوجود من هذا القبيل، فإنه يكون في الواجب قائما بذاته من غير عروضه لماهيته، وفي غير الواجب يكون عارضا لماهيته.

As for the demonstration that His existence is identical with His quiddity and that He has no reality beyond existence: if He possessed both existence and a distinct quiddity, the principle of all things would be two. Any two depend upon a unity that is their principle; whatever depends on a principle cannot itself be the principle of everything. One might say that the quiddity is the qualified subject, and existence its qualification, so that the subject precedes its qualification and the first principle remains one—the quiddity. But if the quiddity precedes existence in this way, it is neither existent nor nonexistent; the principle of existents would therefore itself be nonexistent, which is impossible. [In answer to the argument from one concept of existence:] Terms predicated of many things with one concept divide into two classes. First, the concept can apply equally to its instances, as “human” applies to Zayd and ʿAmr, or “horse” to these two horses. These terms are called univocal [متواطئة], and the requirements of their concepts are uniform, as you suggest. Second, the concept may apply unequally—earlier or later, more properly or less properly, more intensely or less intensely. Examples include “white” as applied to snow and ivory, or “existent” as applied to substance and accident. Here the implications of the common concept need not be identical. “Light” is said of sunlight, moonlight, and firelight, yet sunlight dispels twilight in a way the others do not. Existence [الوجود] belongs to this latter class. In the Necessary it subsists through itself, without inhering in a quiddity; in what is not necessary it is additional to a quiddity.

READING NOTE Two points are different: the common mental concept and the real existence to which it refers. Ṭūsī uses graded or analogical predication [التشكيك]; he does not say that the Necessary and the possible are merely homonyms. | Arabic source: https://www.ibnalarabi.com/qunawi/tusi.php?id=2

A7 — Ṭūsī: common existence exists as a universal only in intellect

al-Ṭūsī · Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī · Reply to Question 3 (opening continuous paragraph)

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

الوجود العام المشترك لا يتحقق إلا في العقل، وكذلك في كل أمر عام مشترك. وذلك أنّ الشيء العيني لا يقع على أشياء متعددة. فإنه إن كان في كل واحد من تلك الأشياء، لم يكن شيئا بعينه، بل كان أشياء. وإن كان في الكلّ من حيث هو كلّ، والكلّ من تلك الحيثية شيء واحد، فلم يقع على أشياء. وإن كان في الكلّ بمعنى التفرّق في آحاده، كان في كل واحد جزء من ذلك الشيء، لا نفس ذلك الشيء. وإن لم يكن في شيء من الآحاد، ولا في الكل، لم يكن واقعا عليها. وبالجملة، وقوعه على غيره لا يكون إلا حمله على ذلك الغير. والحمل والوضع لا يكون إلا في العقل. والوجود العامّ المشترك لا يمكن أن يكون إلا عقليّا. وإذا كان كذلك، كان حصوله في العقل بسبب العقل، وكان ممكنا. ويكون له وجود آخر هو بذلك الوجود يكون ثابتا في العقل.

Common universal existence [الوجود العام المشترك] obtains only in the intellect; the same applies to every common universal. An extramental individual thing cannot be predicated of several things. If it were in each one, it would not be numerically the same thing but many things. If it were in the whole precisely as a whole, the whole in that respect would be one thing, and it would not be predicated of many. If it were in the whole in the sense of being distributed among its individuals, each individual would have only a part of it, not that very thing. And if it were in neither the individuals nor the whole, it would be predicated of neither. In sum, for something to apply to another is for it to be predicated of that other; predication and the assignment of a subject belong only to the intellect. Hence common universal existence can only be intellectual. As such, its obtaining in the intellect depends on an intellect and is possible; it has another existence through which it is established [ثابت] in the intellect.

READING NOTE Crucial distinction: Ṭūsī is not denying extramental existents. He denies that one numerical extramental existence is a universal literally distributed through many individuals. This challenges any simple identification of “the common concept of existence” with a single extramental existent. | Arabic source: https://www.ibnalarabi.com/qunawi/tusi.php?id=4

A8 — Ṭūsī: necessary existence is not the common mental universal

al-Ṭūsī · Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī · Conclusion of Reply to Question 3 (complete final paragraph)

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

الفرق هو أنّ وجود الحق عيني، ليس له وجود عارض له، والوجود العام عقلي، لا يتحقق في غير العقل، ويكون له وجود آخر عارض له، إذا اعتبر كونه في العقل. والحق الذي لا مرية فيه أنّ واجب الوجود لذاته لا يمكن أن يكون إلا شيء عينيّ وجوده عين ذاته، ولا يمكن أن يكون الموصوف بهذه الصفة إلا واحدا من كل جهة واجبا من كلّ اعتبار.

The difference is that the existence of the Real is extramental [عيني]: no further existence inheres in it. Universal existence is intellectual [عقلي]; it obtains only in the intellect, and when considered as being in the intellect it has a further existence inhering in it. The indubitable truth is that what is necessary in existence through itself [واجب الوجود لذاته] can only be an extramental reality whose existence is identical with its essence [ذات]. Only one can have this characteristic: one in every respect, necessary from every consideration.

READING NOTE Ṭūsī’s distinction between a mental universal and an extramental reality is not, without further argument, a complete reply to the Akbarī account of the one reality of existence, which need not treat “existence” as a universal genus. | Arabic source: https://www.ibnalarabi.com/qunawi/tusi.php?id=4

WIT05 — Trilemma against gradation of what is essential

Mullā ʿAbd Allāh al-Yazdī (al-Bahābādī) · Yazdī, Ḥāshiya ʿalā ḥāshiyat Sharḥ al-Tajrīd (gloss on Dawwānī’s old gloss), published PDF printed p.15; PDF image 14

Arabic visually transcribed from published PDF page image; quotation is Yazdī’s explanation

والحاصل أنه على تقدير وقوع التشكيك بالشدة أو الزيادة في الذاتي ثلاث احتمالات: الأول: أن لا يشتمل الأشد والأزيد على أمر ليس في الأضعف والأنقص. وهذا يستلزم أن لا يكون هاهنا تشكيك أصلا لا في الذاتي ولا في غيره. الثاني: أن يتحقق ذلك الأمر ويكون داخلا في مفهوم المشكك؛ وهذا يستلزم عدم اشتراكهما ضرورة انتفاء جزئه في الأضعف. الثالث: أن يتحقق ويكون خارجا عن مفهومه. هذا وإن لم يستلزم انتفاء التشكيك مطلقا، لكنه يستلزم انتفاء التشكيك في الذاتي.

In sum, if gradation by intensity or increase is supposed to occur in what belongs to a thing essentially, three alternatives arise. First, the more intense or greater contains nothing that the weaker or lesser lacks; in that case there is no gradation, whether essential or otherwise. Second, it contains something of this kind included within the concept shared by the gradated cases; then the weaker cannot share that concept, since it lacks part of it. Third, it contains such a difference outside the concept. This does not exclude gradation altogether, but it does exclude gradation in what is essential.

The disagreement distinguishes essential definition from differentiation in extrinsic determinations or predicates; not yet a source for full Dawwānī–Dashtakī exchange. | Bounded passage, not the whole work; do not infer an exhaustive manuscript collation.

WIT06 — Gradation of individuals and application of a derivative predicate

Mullā ʿAbd Allāh al-Yazdī (al-Bahābādī) · Yazdī, Ḥāshiya ʿalā ḥāshiyat Sharḥ al-Tajrīd, published PDF printed p.17; PDF image 16

Arabic visually transcribed from published PDF page image; bounded quotation

وبالجملة: فالكلي الذي تتفاوت أفراده بالشدة والزيادة لا يكون مشككا، إذ التفاوت بين أفراده بالذات لا في صدق هذا الكلي عليها. نعم، التفاوت الواقع بين أفراده بالذات يوجب تفاوت صدق المشتق من هذا الكلي على معروضات تلك الأفراد.

In short, a universal whose individuals differ in intensity and increase is not, on that account, itself predicated gradationally, because the differentiation occurs among its individuals in themselves rather than in the truth of the universal of them. Admittedly, the difference among the individuals can yield a differential application of the derivative predicate formed from that universal to the subjects possessing those individuals.

Prevents reading distinct intensities of blackness as though the definition of blackness were numerically different in each predicate application. | Bounded passage, not the whole work; do not infer an exhaustive manuscript collation.

The predicate of a derivative may exhibit graded application even when the universal itself has a stable essential meaning; this distinction becomes relevant to Lāhījī’s later Sufi interpretation but does not decide it.

Sunni comparison and logical boundary

Al-Taftāzānī separates semantic univocity, conceptual addition, and divine simplicity; the historical attribution to al-Ashʿarī requires comparison with his own texts.

TAF01 — al-Taftāzānī: the common concept of existence and the competing ontologies

Saʿd al-Dīn al-Taftāzānī · al-Taftāzānī, Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid, digital numbered p. 61 (Usul.ai, 1981 edition metadata), existence as shared concept vs real ontology.

Usul.ai page 61 checked 2026-10-29; printed-page/MS collation pending

قال: البحث الثاني: المنقول عن الشيخ أبي الحسن الأشعري أن وجود كل شيء عين ذاته، وليس للفظ الوجود مفهوم واحد مشترك بين الوجودات، بل الاشتراك لفظي. والجمهور على أن له مفهوما واحدا مشتركا بين الوجودات، إلا أنه عند المتكلمين حقيقة واحدة تختلف بالقيود والإضافات، حتى أن وجود الواجب هو كونه في الأعيان على ما يعقل من كون الإنسان، وإنما الاختلاف في الماهية، فالوجود معنى زائد على الماهية في الواجب والممكن جميعا. وعند الفلاسفة وجود الواجب مخالف لوجود الممكن في الحقيقة، واشتراكهما في مفهوم الكون اشتراك معروضين في لازم خارجي غير مقوم، وهو في الممكن زائد على الماهية عقلا، وفي الواجب نفس الماهية، بمعنى أنه لا ماهية للواجب سوى الوجود الخاص المجرد عن مقارنة الماهية، بخلاف الإنسان فإن له ماهية هو الحيوان الناطق ووجودا هو الكون في الأعيان. فوقع البحث في ثلاث مقامات: أنه مشترك معنى، وأنه زائد ذهنا، وأنه في الواجب زائد أيضا. والإنصاف أن الأولين بديهيان، والمذكور في معرض الاستدلال تنبيهات. فعلى الأول وجوه: الأول أنا إذا نظرنا في الحادث جزمنا بأن له مؤثرا مع التردد في كونه واجبا أو ممكنا، عرضا أو جوهرا، متحيزا وغير متحيز، ومع تبدل اعتقاد كونه ممكنا إلى اعتقاد كونه واجبا إلى غير ذلك من الخصوصيات، فبالضرورة يكون الأمر المقطوع به الباقي مع التردد في الخصوصيات وتبدل الاعتقادات مشتركا بين الكل.

[The section introduces a reported position:] The view transmitted from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī is that the existence of each thing is identical with that thing's essence and that 'existence' has no one concept shared by existents; the word is common only by homonymy. The majority maintain that it has one concept common to existents. According to the theologians, however, it is one reality differentiated by qualifications and relations, such that the Necessary's existence is His being in the external world, just as one understands a human being's existence. The difference lies in quiddity: existence is additional to the quiddity of the Necessary and of the possible alike. According to the philosophers, the Necessary's existence differs in reality from possible existence; their shared concept of 'being' pertains to subjects possessing a non-constitutive concomitant. In possibles, existence is intellectually additional to quiddity; in the Necessary it is His very essence, meaning He has no quiddity beyond His specific existence, unmixed with any other quiddity. A human being, by contrast, has the quiddity 'rational animal' and existence as being in the external world. Three questions arise: whether existence has one meaning; whether it is additional in intellect; and whether it is also additional in the Necessary. Fairness demands that the first two are self-evident; the arguments advanced are reminders. The first reminder for shared meaning is that, upon considering a newly arisen thing, we are certain that it has an agent while remaining undecided whether that agent is necessary or possible, accident or substance, spatial or non-spatial; our opinion of these particularities may change. Necessarily, then, what remains certain throughout these doubts and changes is common to all the alternatives.

SOURCE AND VOICE: “al-manqūl ʿan al-Shaykh Abī al-Ḥasan” explicitly attributes the first view to al-Ashʿarī as reported by al-Taftāzānī; it is NOT a direct quotation from al-Ashʿarī. The “majority,” “theologians” and “philosophers” are a doxographical map offered by al-Taftāzānī, not uniformly accepted self-descriptions. The first reminder supports a shared concept/predicable and does NOT by itself prove the identity of extramental realities. The following printed page explicitly warns that none of these proofs demonstrates that real existences are ontically identical. The final two reminders, further objection/reply and printed edition collation remain to be incorporated in full. Digital page 61 identified on Usul.ai, edition metadata first edition 1401/1981; printed pagination has not been independently checked against facsimile.

Question Q03 asks the status of the predicated concept relative to a quiddity.

The gap from common concept to one existence

Lāhījī entertains a Sufi reading where the universal concept of existence is only intellectual while the externally real ground would be absolute existence. This is presented as a possibility to be tested, not a deduction from concept sharing.

C31Y01 — Priority and intensity are not interchangeable

Mullā ʿAbd Allāh al-Yazdī · Yazdī, printed p.12 (= PDF page 12), paragraphs on aqdamiyya and ashaddiyya

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

وأما التشكيك بالأقدمية فهو أن يكون صدق الكلي على بعض أفراده متقدما على صدقه على بعض آخر بالذات والعلية لا بالزمان. فإن تقدم صدق الإنسان على الأب على صدقه على الابن لا يسمى تشكيكا. وأما الأشدية فقد يفسر بأكثرية ظهور آثار الكلي في بعض الأفراد. وزيفه السيد السند بأنه يستلزم كون كثير من الذاتيات كالإنسان مثلا مقولا بالشدة والضعف لاختلاف أفرادها في استتباع الآثار؛ ثم اختار تفسيرها بما استفاده من كلام بهمنيار فهو ازدياد طبيعة العام فيها في بعض الأفراد دون بعض كالطويل بالقياس إلى الذراع والذراعين، والأسود بالقياس إلى الفحم والقير.

Gradation by precedence means that the universal's being true of some of its instances precedes its being true of others essentially and causally, rather than temporally. The prior application of “human” to the father rather than the son is not called gradation. Intensity has sometimes been explained as the more abundant manifestation of the universal's effects in certain instances. Al-Sayyid al-Sanad rejected this because it would entail that many essential predicates, such as “human,” are said with intensity and weakness, since their instances differ in the effects that follow from them. He instead chose an explanation drawn from Bahmanyār: an increase of the common nature in some instances rather than others, as with “long” in relation to one cubit and two cubits, and “black” in relation to charcoal and pitch.

Printed footnote 6 identifies al-Sayyid al-Sanad as Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Dashtakī; footnote 8 separately identifies al-Muḥaqqiq al-Sharīf as Jurjānī. Reported position, not an independently collated Dashtakī text. | The p.12 text continues after the endpoint selected here.

C31L01 — A charitable interpretation in terms of manifestations

ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Lāhījī · Shawāriq I, scan printed p.462; PDF page 463; electronic p.468

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

اعلم: أن ما نقلنا من بعضهم سابقا في توجيه كلام الصوفية في وحدة الوجود مما يناسب مذهب الحكماء على ما حققنا من تحقق الحقائق المختلفة للوجود، فإنه إذا كان للوجود حقائق مختلفة متحققة ويمكن أن يتفطن بكون تلك الحقائق غير مختلفة بتمام الحقيقة، بل بالشدة والضعف، فيكون الوجود حقيقة واحدة متفاوتة في المظاهر التي هي الماهيات بحسب الشدة والضعف، والكمال والنقص. ولما كانت الوجودات المتفاوتة قائمة بالماهيات متعينة بتعيناتها، لم يلزم أن يكون اختلافها في نفس حقيقة الوجود، ليلزم التشكيك في الذاتي، بل في تعيناتها التابعة للماهيات المختلفة. وهذا في الحقيقة اختلاف في ظهور آثار الوجود قلة وكثرة، بل لما كان اختلاف الوجودات كما عرفت تبعا لاختلاف الماهيات، فمع قطع النظر عن الماهيات؛ لا اختلاف في حقيقة الوجود من حيث هي أصلا.

Know that the explanation of the Sufis' doctrine of the unity of existence which we previously transmitted from one of them accords with the philosophers' position, given what we established about distinct realities of existence. If existence has distinct realized realities, one may recognize that they differ not in their entire reality but in intensity and weakness. Existence would then be a single reality varying in its manifestations, namely the quiddities, according to intensity and weakness, perfection and deficiency. Since the varying existences subsist in quiddities and are determined by their determinations, their difference need not concern the very reality of existence, which would entail gradation in an essential constituent. It concerns instead their determinations, which follow the different quiddities. This is in reality a difference in the manifestation of existence's effects, in fewer or greater numbers. Indeed, since the difference between existences follows the difference between quiddities, as you have learned, setting the quiddities aside leaves no difference at all in the reality of existence considered as such.

Complete opening argument, spanning the end of printed 462 and first line of 463. Replaces reliance on the short WIT01 extract without deleting it.

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

فيكون الفرق بين هذا المذهب، ومذهب الحكماء: أنهم يخصون الواجبية بمرتبة واحدة؛ هي تلك الحقيقة بشرط أن لا يتعين بشيء من الماهيات. والصوفية يجعلون الواجبية لتلك الحقيقة؛ لا بشرط أن يتعين بشيء من الماهيات، فيكون كل حقيقة وجودية واجبة، إذا اعتبرت من حيث هي هي، مقطوعة النظر عن التعين، وممكنة باعتبار أخذها بشرط التعين، فيكون الممكنات في الحقيقة هي التعينات، والواجب هو الحقيقة المطلقة، فلا يلزم تعدد وتكثر فيما هو واجب، ولا كون شيء من الممكنات فردا للواجب، ولا حاجة إلى أن يقال: إن تلك الحقيقة غير متعينة في حد ذاتها؛ كالكلي الطبيعي، أو أنها متعينة بتعين؛ لا ينافي شيئا من التعينات، كما ارتكبوه ليرد عليه ما أشرنا إليه سابقا، بل هي متعينة بنفس ذاتها. وهذا التعين ينافي جميع التعينات، حيث يمتنع أن يؤثر فيها شيء من التعينات، ويقارنها مقارنة تأثير؛ كمقارنة العوارض المشخصة للماهيات، وإنما المقارنة التي للتعينات معها هي مقارنة تأثر وانفعال؛ منها كمقارنة المعلول للعلة.

The difference between this position and that of the philosophers would therefore be that the philosophers restrict necessity to one rank: that reality on condition that it is not determined by any quiddity. The Sufis ascribe necessity to that reality without stipulating its determination by any quiddity. Every existential reality, considered just as it is and apart from determination, would thus be necessary, while it would be contingent when taken under the condition of determination. The contingent things would in reality be the determinations, and the Necessary would be the unrestricted reality. Neither plurality in what is necessary nor any contingent thing's being an instance of the Necessary follows. There is no need to say that this reality is intrinsically undetermined, like the natural universal, or that it has a determination compatible with all determinations, as its interpreters proposed, thereby inviting our earlier objection. Rather, it is determined through its very essence. This determination excludes all [such other] determinations in the sense that none can affect it or accompany it as an affecting factor, as individuating accidents accompany quiddities. The determinations accompany it instead as things affected by it and receptive to it, as an effect accompanies its cause.

The restrictive clause explains ينافي: causal invulnerability, not an unqualified denial of any relation to determinations. | lā bi-sharṭ is being taken without a condition; bi-sharṭ lā imposes a negative condition.

C31L05 — Existence as a real particular; existent as a universal predicate

Lāhījī reporting al-Muḥaqqiq al-Sharīf and Dawwānī · Shawāriq I, printed p.465; PDF page 466; electronic p.472

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

ولما وجب كون الواجب جزئيا حقيقيا متعينا بنفس ذاته، فإنما بذاته وجب أن يكون الوجود أيضا لكونه هو الواجب كذلك، فلا يكون الوجود مفهوما كليا ليمكن له أفراد، فهو جزئي حقيقي ليس فيه إمكان تعدد ولا انقسام، وقائم بذاته منزه عن كونه عارضا لغيره، فيكون الواجب هو الوجود المطلق؛ أي المعرى عن التقيد بغيره والانضمام إليه. وعلى هذا لا يتصور عروض الوجود للماهيات الممكنة، فليس معنى كونها موجودة إلا أن لها نسبة مخصوصة إلى حضرة الوجود القائم بذاته، وتلك النسبة على وجوه مختلفة وأنحاء شتى يتعذر الاطلاع على ماهياتها، فالموجود كلي وإن كان الوجود جزئيا حقيقيا. كذا ذكره المحقق الشريف ملخصا لما ذكره بعض محققي مشايخهم، وأنه قال: ولا يعلمه إلا الراسخون في العلم، وتبعه المحقق الدواني في اختيار هذا التوجيه، ونسبه إلى ذوق المتألهين. وهو إنما يناسب مذهب المتكلمين النافين لكون الوجود ذا أفراد حقيقية كما لا يخفى.

Since the Necessary must be a real particular determined through its own essence, existence too, because it is the Necessary, must be so. Existence would not be a universal concept capable of having instances, but a real particular incapable of multiplicity or division, subsisting through itself and exempt from being an accident of another. The Necessary would thus be unrestricted existence: existence stripped of restriction by, or conjunction with, anything else. On this account existence cannot be an accident of contingent quiddities. Their being existent means only that they have a specific relation to the presence of self-subsisting existence. This relation takes different forms and diverse modes whose quiddities cannot be apprehended. Thus “existent” is universal although “existence” is a real particular. Al-Muḥaqqiq al-Sharīf stated this as a summary of what one of their accomplished masters had said, adding that only those firmly rooted in knowledge know it. Al-Muḥaqqiq al-Dawwānī followed him in choosing this interpretation and attributed it to the “taste of the theosophers” [dhawq al-mutaʾallihīn]. This, however, accords only with the theologians' position denying that existence has real instances, as is evident.

Here al-Muḥaqqiq al-Sharīf is the reported source conventionally identified as Jurjānī; do not confuse with the distinct title al-Sayyid al-Sanad in Yazdī. | A mediated account of Dawwānī’s adoption; not a transcript of any of the five original glosses.

By my life, this interpretation neither nourishes nor relieves hunger. That existence exists through itself and needs nothing other than its essence in order to exist is conceded only of self-subsisting existence, which cannot subsist in a quiddity. There is no doubt that this is necessarily existent. But how does it follow that there cannot be an existence other than it, subsisting in contingent quiddities, or that every existential reality must subsist through itself? The requirement that existence be a real particular concerns only a self-subsisting existential reality. How does it follow that the concept of existence, namely being in concrete reality, is not universal and does not have real instances, some self-subsisting and others subsisting in contingent quiddities? If this conclusion is based on the objections supporting the theologians' position, you have already learned their answers. Moreover, our present question concerns this transmitted argument: how does it establish that conclusion? We have treated this question at such unavoidable length because it is among the most important foundations of knowledge and the greatest questions concerning divine unity.

Completes the Ishāra ʿirfāniyya main text; printed p.467 opens a new numbered question. Does not establish the completeness of the whole Shawāriq.

Q03 The addition of existence to quiddity

Is existence distinct from essence in intellect, in reality, or as a really inhering accident?

If an essence can be grasped without judging it to exist, existence is not included in that essence’s definition. But what sort of distinction is this? An accidental form inhering in an already existent subject would seem to demand the existence of that subject before existence arrives; a purely verbal distinction would not account for informative existential predication. The central issue is to identify the respect in which existence is said to be “added.”

First: common existence is not the essence of every thing

Al-Ḥillī argues: if shared existence were identical to every distinct essence, all essences would collapse into one; if it were an internal generic component, every differentiating feature would also require existence, threatening an infinite complexity.

TAF02 — al-Taftāzānī: the alleged regress of existence and the intellectual mode of addition

Saʿd al-Dīn al-Taftāzānī · al-Taftāzānī, Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid, digital numbered p. 69, response to existence/quiddity regress (Usul.ai, metadata first ed. 1401/1981).

Usul.ai page 69 checked 2026-10-29; printed-page/MS collation pending

وأما تفصيلا فعن الأول أن قيامه بالماهية من حيث هي هي، لا بالماهية المعدومة ليلزم التناقض، ولا بالماهية الموجودة ليلزم الدور أو التسلسل. فإن قيل: إن أريد بالماهية من حيث هي هي ما لا يكون الوجود أو العدم نفسها ولا جزءا منها على ما قيل فغير مفيد، لأن العروض كاف في لزوم المحالات؛ وإن أريد ما لا يكون موجودا ولا معدوما لا بالعروض ولا بغيره فالتناقض فيه أظهر، لأن اللاوجود نقيض الوجود بلا نزاع ولا اشتباه. قلنا: المراد ما لا يعتبر فيه الوجود ولا العدم، وإن كان لا ينفك عن أحدهما في الخارج. فإن قيل: عدم الانفكاك عن أحدهما كاف في لزوم المحال، لأنه إن قارن العدم فيناقض أو الوجود فيدور أو يتسلسل. قلنا: قيام الوجود بالماهية أمر عقلي، ليس كقيام البياض بالجسم ليلزم تقدمها عليه بالوجود تقدما ذاتيا أو زمانيا فتلزم المحالات، بل غاية الأمر أنه يلزم تقدمها عليه بالوجود العقلي ولا استحالة فيه، لجواز أن تلاحظ وحدها من غير ملاحظة وجود خارجي أو ذهني، ويكون لها وجود ذهني لا بملاحظة العقل؛ فإن عدم الاعتبار غير اعتبار العدم. وإن اعتبر العقل وجودها الذهني لم يلزم التسلسل، بل ينقطع بانقطاع الاعتبار. وعن الثاني أنا نختار أن الوجود موجود ولا نسلم لزوم التسلسل؛ وإنما يلزم لو كان وجوده أيضا زائدا عليه وليس كذلك، بل وجوده عينه وإنما النزاع في غيره، والأدلة إنما قامت عليه. وتحقيق ذلك أنه لما كان تحقق كل شيء بالوجود فبالضرورة يكون تحققه بنفسه من غير احتياج إلى وجود آخر يقوم به، كما أنه لما كان التقدم والتأخر فيما بين الأشياء بالزمان كانا فيما بين أجزائه بالذات من غير افتقار إلى زمان آخر. فإن قيل فيكون كل وجود واجبا إذ لا معنى له سوى ما يكون تحققه بنفسه. قلنا ممنوع، فإن معنى وجود الواجب بنفسه أنه مقتضى ذاته من غير احتياج إلى فاعل، ومعنى تحقق الوجود بنفسه أنه إذا حصل للشيء إما من ذاته كما في الواجب أو من غيره كما في الممكن لم يفتقر تحققه إلى وجود آخر يقوم به.

In reply to the first objection, the inherence of existence pertains to the quiddity as such: not to a nonexistent quiddity (which would be contradictory), nor to an already existent one (which would cause a circle or an infinite regress). An objector presses: If 'quiddity as such' only means that neither existence nor nonexistence is identical with it or part of it, that does not solve the paradox; and if it means a quiddity neither existent nor nonexistent in any sense, that is yet more contradictory. We answer that neither existence nor nonexistence is being taken into consideration, although in external reality the thing cannot be without one or the other. The objector replies that this inseparability is enough to restore the paradox: if nonexistence accompanies it, there is contradiction; if existence does, there is circularity or regress. We answer: existence's 'inherence' in quiddity is an affair of intellect, not like whiteness's inherence in a body, which would entail that the substrate has priority of existence, whether essentially or temporally. At most the quiddity has priority in intellectual consideration, and there is nothing impossible about this. The intellect may consider it alone, without considering its external or mental existence, even while it has mental existence independently of that particular act of considering. For *not considering* something is different from *considering its absence*. And if the intellect considers its mental existence in turn, this does not force a real infinite regress: it ends when the act of considering ends. As to the second objection, we can affirm that existence itself exists without conceding a regress. The regress would follow only if its existence too were additional to it, which it is not; its existence is identical with itself. The disagreement concerns other things, to which the proofs pertain. Since all things are actual through existence, existence necessarily is actual through itself without requiring another existence inhering in it—just as, although priority and posteriority among things are by time, those relations among time's own parts are by time's very essence, without requiring a further time. If one then objects that each existence would be necessary because each is actual through itself, we reject the inference. For the Necessary to exist through itself is for existence to be demanded by its essence without need of an agent. For existence itself to be actual through itself merely means that, whether it comes to a thing from its essence (as with the Necessary) or from another (as with a possible), its actuality needs no second existence inhering in it.

STRUCTURE: direct response to two opposite attempts to treat the existential addition like a real accident in a previously actual subject. Taftāzānī makes the unconsidered/nonexistent distinction precise: ʿadam al-iʿtibār ≠ iʿtibār al-ʿadam. He also sharply differentiates (i) being self-actualizing in the sense of existence's not needing another 'existence' and (ii) the Necessary's causal independence. These are central checks on loose analogies between vertical preservation, participation and formal mediation. Digital Arabic source p. 69 has an unpunctuated transcription; punctuation and paragraphing here are editorial. The surrounding objections are on p. 68, and a further continuation follows the selected excerpt on p. 69; neither should be treated as included in this bounded unit.

وقد يوجه بحيث لا يلزم القول بالانبساط، ومخالطته مع التعينات، لعدم إمكان عروض الوجود الذي هو الواجب القائم بذاته لشيء من الماهيات. والدليل على كون الوجود هو الواجب: أن كل مفهوم مغاير لحقيقة الوجود كالإنسان مثلا، فإنه ما لم ينضم إليه الوجود بوجه من الوجوه في نفس الأمر لم يكن موجودا فيها قطعا، وما لم يلاحظ العقل انضمام الوجود إليه لم يمكن له الحكم بكونه موجودا. فكل مفهوم مغاير للوجود، فهو في كونه موجودا في نفس الأمر محتاج إلى غيره الذي هو الوجود، وكل ما هو محتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره فهو ممكن، إذ لا معنى للممكن إلا ما يحتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره، سواء كان ذلك الغير موجدا له أو وجودا له، وكل مفهوم مغاير للوجود ممكن، ولا شيء من الممكن بواجب، فلا شيء من المفهومات المغايرة للوجود بواجب. وقد ثبت بالبرهان أن الواجب موجود، فهو لا يكون إلا الوجود الذي هو موجود بذاته، ويستغني في كونه موجودا عن غير ذاته، وإن كان المتبادر من لفظ الموجود بحسب اللغة ما قام به الوجود، فإن المتبع هو ما أدى إليه البرهان لا غير.

It may also be interpreted without entailing that existence spreads or mingles with determinations, since the existence which is the self-subsisting Necessary cannot be an accident of any quiddity. The argument that existence is the Necessary is this. Any concept different from the reality of existence, such as “human,” certainly does not exist in objective actuality unless existence is joined to it in some manner. Unless the intellect considers existence joined to it, it cannot judge it to exist. Every concept different from existence therefore depends, for its existence in objective actuality, on something other than itself, namely existence. Whatever depends on another for being existent is contingent: a contingent is precisely what needs another in order to exist, whether that other produces it or is its existence. Every concept different from existence is contingent; nothing contingent is necessary; hence no concept different from existence is necessary. It has been demonstrated that the Necessary exists. It must therefore be existence, which exists through itself and needs nothing other than its essence in order to exist. Even if the linguistic sense first suggested by “existent” is something in which existence subsists, what must be followed is the result of demonstration alone.

This is the argument under report, not Lāhījī’s final endorsement. Nafs al-amr means objective actuality here.

C31L05 — Existence as a real particular; existent as a universal predicate

Lāhījī reporting al-Muḥaqqiq al-Sharīf and Dawwānī · Shawāriq I, printed p.465; PDF page 466; electronic p.472

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

ولما وجب كون الواجب جزئيا حقيقيا متعينا بنفس ذاته، فإنما بذاته وجب أن يكون الوجود أيضا لكونه هو الواجب كذلك، فلا يكون الوجود مفهوما كليا ليمكن له أفراد، فهو جزئي حقيقي ليس فيه إمكان تعدد ولا انقسام، وقائم بذاته منزه عن كونه عارضا لغيره، فيكون الواجب هو الوجود المطلق؛ أي المعرى عن التقيد بغيره والانضمام إليه. وعلى هذا لا يتصور عروض الوجود للماهيات الممكنة، فليس معنى كونها موجودة إلا أن لها نسبة مخصوصة إلى حضرة الوجود القائم بذاته، وتلك النسبة على وجوه مختلفة وأنحاء شتى يتعذر الاطلاع على ماهياتها، فالموجود كلي وإن كان الوجود جزئيا حقيقيا. كذا ذكره المحقق الشريف ملخصا لما ذكره بعض محققي مشايخهم، وأنه قال: ولا يعلمه إلا الراسخون في العلم، وتبعه المحقق الدواني في اختيار هذا التوجيه، ونسبه إلى ذوق المتألهين. وهو إنما يناسب مذهب المتكلمين النافين لكون الوجود ذا أفراد حقيقية كما لا يخفى.

Since the Necessary must be a real particular determined through its own essence, existence too, because it is the Necessary, must be so. Existence would not be a universal concept capable of having instances, but a real particular incapable of multiplicity or division, subsisting through itself and exempt from being an accident of another. The Necessary would thus be unrestricted existence: existence stripped of restriction by, or conjunction with, anything else. On this account existence cannot be an accident of contingent quiddities. Their being existent means only that they have a specific relation to the presence of self-subsisting existence. This relation takes different forms and diverse modes whose quiddities cannot be apprehended. Thus “existent” is universal although “existence” is a real particular. Al-Muḥaqqiq al-Sharīf stated this as a summary of what one of their accomplished masters had said, adding that only those firmly rooted in knowledge know it. Al-Muḥaqqiq al-Dawwānī followed him in choosing this interpretation and attributed it to the “taste of the theosophers” [dhawq al-mutaʾallihīn]. This, however, accords only with the theologians' position denying that existence has real instances, as is evident.

Here al-Muḥaqqiq al-Sharīf is the reported source conventionally identified as Jurjānī; do not confuse with the distinct title al-Sayyid al-Sanad in Yazdī. | A mediated account of Dawwānī’s adoption; not a transcript of any of the five original glosses.

Interim judgment: The sources converge on the necessity of distinguishing concept from external instantiation, while differing over how far this distinction goes in the Necessary. The core answer is not “there are two external things, essence and its existence,” but that existential attribution is intellectually informative without being an independently inhering external property.

Boundary: The ontology of *distinct external existences* remains contested; the anti-regress distinction alone does not settle it.

Remaining: Obtain the full al-Iṣfahānī base passage underlying Jurjānī’s three mystical glosses; compare al-Ḥillī, Qūshjī, Lāhījī and Sunni accounts word-for-word.

Q04 Quiddity in itself and the three considerations

What is meant by māhiyya min ḥaythu hiya, bi-sharṭ lā, and lā bi-sharṭ, and do any imply a freestanding essence?

Quiddity considered “in itself” is neither an actually existing external universal nor a third ontic realm. It is a rule for what belongs to the intelligible content *precisely qua* that content. This allows one to say that humanity as such is not intrinsically characterised by existence or nonexistence, while avoiding the logical absurdity of asserting that a thing lacks both members of a contradiction absolutely.

Ṭūsī distinguishes the considerations

The lemmata distinguish quiddity as itself, quiddity with accompanying restrictions, quiddity with other things excluded, and quiddity without condition. The natural, logical, and intellectual universals must not be collapsed.

Ṭūsī’s lemma “Considered just as it is, it is nothing but itself.” The meaning of this statement is that quiddity, insofar as it is quiddity—that is, insofar as it is at its own level, with nothing else considered alongside it—has nothing predicated of it except itself, not even its essential constituents or its concomitants. For the respect in which it is itself differs from the respect in which something else is considered, even if that other thing is essential to it or concomitant with it. Its essential constituents and concomitants may indeed be considered as enfolded and subsumed within it, but not in a differentiated manner. Thus the human, for example, considered just as it is, is human and nothing else—even ‘animal’ is not [predicated of it in this consideration]. For predicating ‘animal’ of it requires taking it out of the purity of itself and its own level, and introducing the consideration of a respect that warrants predicating ‘animal’ of it: namely, that it is a whole with an intellectual part, animal. Hence, if something other than the quiddity itself is to be predicated of it, something other than itself must be considered alongside it, to warrant and ground the predication of that thing. The statement does not mean that, considered just as it is—that is, at its own level—nothing is identical with it or a part of it except itself, as appears from the formulations of some eminent authorities. This is because of the exception: an exception affirms of what follows it what it denies of what precedes it, and conversely. Thus, in respect of what follows the exception, the meaning would become that the quiddity, at its own level, is identical with itself and is a part of itself. This is self-evidently false, since at its own level it is not a part of itself: the part is prior to the quiddity in respect of quiddity, just as a concomitant of quiddity—possibility, for example—is posterior to the quiddity in respect of quiddity. [Two short textual and grammatical notes omitted.] Al-Ḥillī’s lemma “A, nor any of the things …” That is, it is neither A, nor anything other than A, nor their opposites. Thus the human, for example, considered just as it is, is neither A nor its opposite; neither one nor its opposite; neither universal nor its opposite; neither existent nor its opposite; neither animal nor its opposite; and so on until every item has been enumerated. Rather, it is human only. If you object, ‘Is this anything other than the exclusion of both contradictories? How, then, have they allowed it here?’ I reply: this is not the exclusion of both contradictories, for its meaning is that neither contradictory is the quiddity itself. Certainly, if we said that the human, at the level of itself, is neither human nor nonhuman, that would be the exclusion of both contradictories. But we say that the human, at the level of itself, is human and nothing else. To put it another way, in its capacity as subject, the human is human and nothing else; but when we consider the predicates, it is either existent or nonexistent, either universal or nonuniversal, and so on. The exclusion or conjunction of contradictories concerns the predicates. Understand this.

This explains why the expression is legitimate without inventing a neutral state between existence and nonexistence.

Ṭūsī replies to Qūnawī’s making question

The correspondence asks whether possible quiddities are made. Ṭūsī distinguishes what belongs to them as abstracted quiddities from their mental and extra-mental existence, each of which has an appropriate account of causation.

Second question. Are possible quiddities [الماهيات الممكنة] made [مجعولة], or are they not made? Whichever answer is given, are they—considered simply as quiddities—existential realities possessing some manner of existence, or are they nonexistential? If they are unmade, they cannot be existential realities. For that would put them on the same footing as the Necessary in intrinsic necessity of existence [وجوب الوجود الذاتي] and in the sheer unity of essence. They would no longer be possible, but necessary, since they would lack the possibility and poverty entailed by receiving existence from another.

بل الحقّ أنّ جميع الماهيات والموجودات مجعولة، جاعلها اللّه سبحانه وتعالى. وإذا قلنا: الماهيات الممكنة صارت منسوبة إلى الوجود، فإنّ الإمكان لا يمكن أن توصف به الماهية من حيث هي ماهية فقط، إنما يمكن أن توصف به إذا قيست إلى الوجود أو إلى العدم. وأما قوله: «هل هي من كونها ماهيات فقط أمور وجودية؟». فالجواب: لا، فإنّ الماهية من حيث هي ماهية فقط لا يمكن أن تكون شيئا غير الماهية. وأما إذا فسّره بقوله: «هل لها ضرب من الوجود؟». فالجواب: نعم، فإنّ الماهية إذا تصوّرت، حدث لها وجود عقلي. وإذا فرضت في الأعيان، كان لها وجود عيني. والوجود العيني لا يكون إلّا من موجدها، والوجود العقلي يكون ممن تعقّلها. وكلا الوجودين ممكن له. وإذا قالوا: للماهية وجود قبلها، أرادوا به تعقّلها الذي يكون سببا لوجودها العيني. وهو العلم الفعلي. وإذا قالوا: لها وجود معها، أرادوا به الوجود العيني. وإذا قالوا: لها وجود بعدها، أرادوا به تعقّلها بعد وجودها، يعني العلم الانفعالي. وإذا نظر إلى الماهية فقط، لم يكن في القصد العقلي إلا الماهية، ولم يكن الوجود ولا العدم داخلين في ذلك النظر. ولذلك قالوا: إنها ليست بموجودة ولا معدومة.

Rather, the truth is that all quiddities and existents are made: God—glorified and exalted—is their maker. When we say that possible quiddities are related to existence, possibility [الإمكان] is not attributable to quiddity precisely insofar as it is quiddity alone. It can be attributed when quiddity is compared with existence or nonexistence. As for the question, “Are quiddities, simply as quiddities, existential realities?” the answer is no. Quiddity, precisely insofar as it is quiddity, can be nothing other than quiddity. But if the question means, “Do they have some manner of existence?” the answer is yes. When a quiddity is conceived, it acquires intellectual existence [وجود عقلي]; when it is posited among extramental individuals, it has extramental existence [وجود عيني]. Extramental existence comes only from its producer; intellectual existence arises through whoever conceives it. Both modes of existence are possible for it. When they say that a quiddity has an existence before itself, they mean the conception of it that causes its extramental existence: this is productive knowledge [العلم الفعلي]. When they say it has existence accompanying it, they mean extramental existence. When they say it has an existence after itself, they mean its being conceived after its extramental existence—receptive knowledge [العلم الانفعالي]. If quiddity alone is considered, nothing is intended by the intellect except quiddity itself; neither existence nor nonexistence enters into that consideration. Hence it is said that quiddity is neither existent nor nonexistent.

Q05 Thingness, establishment, and the nonexistent

Can a possible-but-nonexistent quiddity be an extramentally established thing, and in which precise sense is this denied?

The dispute over “the nonexistent is a thing” concerns *which kind of establishment* is affirmed, not whether humans can think of something absent. The strong contested position says a possible quiddity has determinate establishment outside the mind without existential actuality. Other positions accept knowability or specificity while denying that external ontic status.

Ṭūsī’s direct denial, interpreted by Iṣfahānī

Iṣfahānī presents the thesis that thingness is coextensive with existence, and narrows the disputed Muʿtazilī claim to possible, not impossible, nonexistent quiddities.

Ṭūsī says: “Existence is coextensive with thingness [الشيئية]; thingness is not realized without it, and anyone who disputes this defies what his own intellect requires.” I say: Whoever holds that existence [الوجود] is identical with quiddity [الماهية] cannot say that the nonexistent is a thing in the sense that a quiddity can be established outside the mind while separated from existence. Otherwise, the two contradictories—existence and nonexistence—would obtain together. Those who hold that existence is additional to quiddity disagree among themselves. Some maintain that a quiddity can be established extramentally while separated from existence. This is what they mean by “the nonexistent is a thing” [المعدوم شيء]. Others deny it. The former is the position of the Muʿtazila; the latter, that of the remaining theologians and philosophers. On this interpretation, they agree that what is absolutely excluded [المنفي] is not a thing: by this they mean quiddities whose extramental existence is impossible. The real dispute therefore concerns nonexistent quiddities that are possible of existence. Ṭūsī's statement that existence is coextensive with thingness means that whatever exists is a thing, and whatever does not exist is not a thing. Thus something nonexistent outside the mind—whether its existence is possible or impossible—is not an extramental thing.

TRANSLATOR’S NOTE The dispute is narrower than whether the intellect can conceive or speak about the nonexistent. The opposed claim is an extramental establishment [تقرر في الخارج] of a possible quiddity without existence. “Coextensive” [مساوق] does not mean that the concepts are synonymous.

A refutation that merely shows inexistents lack *effects* would not refute the opponent’s more limited conception of thubūt.

Jurjānī challenges an equivocation

Jurjānī distinguishes establishment qua intrinsic determinacy from actual effect-bearing existence. His point is methodological: a criticism must strike the first sense when that is the one asserted by the opponent.

T2 — Two senses of establishment in the Muʿtazilī thesis

al-Jurjānī · Al-Sayyid al-Sharīf al-Jurjānī | Ḥāshiya in the İSAM edition of Tasdīd, vol. II, printed p. 100, marginal commentary (selected beginning). | Arabic source: https://archive.org/download/tsdidqawaed/tqat2.pdf

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

مذهب المعتزلة أن التقرر على ضربين: تقرر الماهية في حد ذاتها، وتقررها بحيث يترتب عليها آثارها، كإحراق النار وترطيب الماء؛ فالأول يسمونه ثبوتًا ومقابله نفيًا، والثاني يسمونه وجودًا ومقابله عدمًا. وقد يطلقون العدم على النفي أيضًا، ويجوزون اجتماع الثبوت مع كل واحد من الوجود والعدم المقابل له. فإن أراد بقوله «المعدوم لا تقرر له» المعنى الأول فهو ممنوع، ودعوى المكابرة مكابرة؛ وإن أراد المعنى الثاني فهو مسلم، وإنما النزاع في المعنى الأول.

The Muʿtazilī position is that establishment [التقرر] has two kinds. The first is a quiddity's establishment in itself [في حد ذاتها]; the second is its establishment in such a way that its effects follow from it, as burning follows from fire and moistening from water. They call the first “establishment” [الثبوت], opposed to exclusion or negation [النفي], and the second “existence” [الوجود], opposed to nonexistence [العدم]. They sometimes use “nonexistence” for “exclusion” as well. They permit establishment to accompany either existence or its opposite, nonexistence. If “the nonexistent has no establishment” means the first kind, it is denied—and alleging that the opponent is defying reason is itself unwarranted. If it means the second kind, it is granted. But the disagreement concerns the first.

TRANSLATOR’S NOTE Jurjānī's gloss is methodological: one cannot refute the opponent by shifting from the disputed sense of thubūt to the conceded sense of effect-bearing wujūd. The translated passage is confined to the clear initial argument of the gloss, not its complete subsequent treatment.

Sunni classification

Al-Taftāzānī reports the debate over whether the nonexistent is a thing and whether states constitute a separate category. These questions are not simply settled by the everyday meaningfulness of fictional or future descriptions.

Q06 Second intelligibles, states, and logical predication

Do logical and metaphysical predicates disclose extra-mental constituents, or can they be objectively applicable without extra-mental instances?

“Thingness,” “universality,” “possibility,” and certain relations can truly be predicated without constituting independent extramental forms. But there are two different problems: identifying a second intelligible and deciding whether its objective basis is merely logical, founded in real properties, or the subject of a distinct dispute about states (aḥwāl).

The claim about thingness

Al-Ḥillī identifies thingness and similar predicates as second intelligibles attaching to first intelligibles. Their being attributable to things is not the same as an independently subsisting “thingness” existing alongside them.

T3 — Thingness as a second intelligible

al-Ḥillī · Al-ʿAllāma al-Ḥillī | Kashf al-murād, chapter on thingness, displayed in the Rafed transcription (corresponding to the Āmulī edition discussion around pp. 62–63). | Arabic source: https://lib.rafed.net/view.php?b_id=3486&page=56&type=c_fbook

Arabic digital transcription checked 2026-10-29; printed-edition and MS collation pending

قال: والشيئية من المعقولات الثانية وليست متأصلة في الوجود، فلا شيء مطلقًا ثابت بل هي تعرض لخصوصيات الماهيات. أقول: قال أبو علي بن سينا: الوجود إما ذهني وإما خارجي، والمشترك بينهما هو الشيئية. فإن أراد حمل الشيئية على القدر المشترك وصدقها عليه فهو صواب، وإلا فهو ممنوع. إذا عرفت هذا فنقول: الشيئية والذاتية والجزئية وأشباهها من المعقولات الثانية التي تعرض للمعقولات الأولى؛ لأنها لا تعقل إلا عارضة لغيرها من الماهيات، وليست متأصلة في الوجود كتأصل الحيوانية والإنسانية فيه، بل هي تابعة لغيرها في الوجود. وليس يمكن وجود شيئية مطلقة؛ فلا شيء مطلقًا ثابت، إنما الثبوت يعرض للماهيات المخصوصة الشخصية.

Ṭūsī says: “Thingness [الشيئية] belongs to the second intelligibles [المعقولات الثانية]. It does not have an independent foundation in existence. No thingness taken absolutely is established; rather, it attaches to particular quiddities.” I say: Abū ʿAlī Ibn Sīnā said that existence is either mental or extramental, and that thingness is common to both. If he meant that thingness can be predicated of what is common to them and applies to it, this is correct. If he meant something else, it is not conceded. Thingness, essentiality [الذاتية], particularity [الجزئية], and similar notions are second intelligibles attaching to first intelligibles. They cannot be conceived except as belonging to other quiddities. They do not have an independent foundation in existence in the way animality and humanity do; rather, they depend upon something else for their existence. There can be no thingness existing absolutely. It is not thingness as such that is established; establishment belongs to specifically determined quiddities.

TRANSLATOR’S NOTE The sense of “second intelligible” here is metaphysical and must not be silently identified with the narrower logical sense. The modern Āmulī footnote develops the distinction at length; that later explanation is not part of al-Ḥillī's medieval text.

C31Y02 — The counter-objection to an account in terms of union

Yazdī reporting al-Sayyid al-Sanad and responding · Yazdī, printed p.33 (= PDF page 33), complete paragraph beginning ثم أقول

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

ثم أقول: قد اختار السيد السند ـ قدس سره ـ أن المحكي عنه هو اتحاد الموضوع مع مفهوم المحمول في الخارج. فنقول: إن كانت تلك الحكاية صادقة لزم وجود الاتحاد في الخارج، وأنه يستلزم إليه؛ وإن كانت كاذبة لم يعتبر. فإن اختار أن الاتحاد في الخارج لا أنه موجود في الخارج، فقد صار إلى ما ذكرناه سواء بسواء.

Then I say: al-Sayyid al-Sanad chose the view that what is represented is the subject's union with the concept of the predicate in the external order. We therefore say: if that representation is true, the existence of the union in the external order follows, and it entails [a regress: the printed text reads “to it”]; if it is false, it is disregarded. If he chooses to say that the union is in the external order, without saying that it exists in the external order, he has arrived at precisely what we stated.

The printed phrase وأنه يستلزم إليه is awkward; the contextual supplement “a regress” is interpretive and must not be silently substituted into Arabic. | Probable Dashtakī report by contextual title usage; p.33 has no independent identifying footnote. | The reply does not establish that predication is arbitrary. It distinguishes an externally grounded union from an added externally existing relational entity.

C31Y03 — External qualification and the status of negative predicates

Mullā ʿAbd Allāh al-Yazdī · Yazdī p.33, sequence from فهو من حيث أنه ليس في الخارج through الذاتيات

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

قوله: «فهو من حيث أنه ليس في الخارج». أي لا يوجد فيه، وإلا فالاتصاف أيضا في الخارج. قوله: «ومن حيث إنه يستدعي ملاحظة أمر خارج عن الموضوع». لا وجوده، وإلا كان من قبيل حمل الإضافات من غير فوق. قوله: «فظهر أن مطابق الحكم الحملي قد يكون ذات الموضوع فقط كما في الذاتيات». وكذا العدميات، فإنها وإن استدعت ملاحظة أمر زائد لا يستدعي وجود أمر سوى ذات الموضوع. فإن الموجود في الخارج المحكي عنه هو الذات فحسب.

His words, “insofar as it is not in the external order”: that is, it does not exist there; otherwise qualification too is in the external order. His words, “insofar as it requires considering something outside the subject”: [considering it], rather than its existence; otherwise it would be like predicating relations without an “above.” His words, “It thus becomes clear that what corresponds to a predicative judgment may be the subject's essence alone, as in essential predicates”: the same applies to negative predicates. Although these require considering something additional, they do not require anything to exist besides the subject's essence. The externally existing thing that is represented is the essence alone.

Lemmata introduced by قوله belong to the annotated text as segmented by the editor; explanatory sentences belong to the gloss under that segmentation. | The peculiar printed phrase من غير فوق is retained rather than conjecturally repaired.

C31Q06 — The earlier interpretation reported before Qūshjī’s objections

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī, reporting an earlier commentary · Sharḥ Tajrīd al-ʿaqāʾid, ed. al-Zāriʿī al-Riḍāʾī, I p.173 (PDF p.173), from وقد قيل في شرحه to عدما مطلقا

Independently transcribed and translated from the specified printed page images; edition apparatus not exhaustively collated

وقد قيل في شرحه: «قد يجتمع الوجود المطلق والعدم المطلق، وذلك لأن العدم المطلق قد يتصور، فيعرض له كون في الذهن، فيعرض له الكون المطلق ـ أعني: الوجود المطلق ـ ضرورة استلزام عروض المقيد للشيء عروض المطلق له، لكن باعتبار التقابل غير اعتبار الاجتماع؛ وذلك لأن العدم المطلق من حيث إنه سلب للوجود المطلق مقابل له، ومن حيث إن الوجود المطلق عارض له يجتمع معه، وكل واحد من الاعتبارين مغاير للآخر؛ فإن اعتبار كونه سلب الوجود غير اعتبار كونه معروضه، فباعتبار أنه سلب له لا يجتمع معه، بل يقابله، وباعتبار أنه معروض له لا يقابله، بل يجتمع معه. وقوله: يعقلان معا؛ أي: الوجود المطلق والعدم المطلق، ردا لما يزعم من أن العدم المطلق لا يمكن أن يتصور، إذ لا تميز له في نفسه أصلا. وتقريره: أنه كما يمكن أن يتصور الوجود المطلق، يمكن أن يتصور رفعه قطعا، وهو العدم المضاف إلى الوجود المطلق، وذلك لا ينافي كونه عدما مطلقا».

It has been said in commenting on it: “Unqualified existence and unqualified nonexistence may occur together. Unqualified nonexistence may be conceived, so that being in the mind belongs to it. Unqualified being—that is, unqualified existence—therefore belongs to it, since the belonging of a qualified instance to something necessarily entails the belonging of the unqualified. But the respect of opposition differs from the respect of conjunction. Insofar as unqualified nonexistence negates unqualified existence, it is opposed to it; insofar as unqualified existence belongs to nonexistence, they occur together. These considerations differ: considering nonexistence as the negation of existence differs from considering it as the subject to which existence belongs. As negation, it does not occur together with existence but opposes it; as a subject of existence, it does not oppose it but occurs together with it. His words ‘the two are conceived together’ mean unqualified existence and unqualified nonexistence, rejecting the allegation that unqualified nonexistence cannot be conceived because it has no distinction whatsoever in itself. The explanation is that, just as unqualified existence may be conceived, its removal certainly may be conceived. That is nonexistence related to unqualified existence; this does not prevent its being unqualified nonexistence.”

The printed Qūshjī text introduces the reported view impersonally. Attribution to the old commentator is mediated by Lāhījī and is not silently inserted into the Arabic. | The quotation ends before أقول: فيه نظر, which marks Qūshjī’s criticism.

C31Q05 — Qūshjī’s complete three objections, directly checked

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī · Sharḥ Tajrīd al-ʿaqāʾid, ed. al-Zāriʿī al-Riḍāʾī, I pp.173–174 (PDF pp.173–174), أقول: فيه نظر through لغوا محضا

Independently transcribed and translated from the specified printed page images; edition apparatus not exhaustively collated

أقول: فيه نظر، أما أولا: فلأن اجتماع المتقابلين بعروض أحدهما للآخر ليس مستحيلا حتى يحتاج إلى الاعتذار بتغاير الجهة؛ إنما يستحيل اجتماعهما بعروضهما لمحل واحد. وأما ثانيا: فلأنه لو اجتمع الوجود والعدم في محل بأن يكون موجودا ومعدوما معا، يمكن إجراء هذا العذر فيه؛ بأن نقول: العدم من حيث إنه سلب للوجود مقابل له، ومن حيث إن الوجود عارض لمحله مجتمع معه، وكل واحد من الاعتبارين مغاير للآخر؛ فإن اعتبار كونه سلب الوجود غير اعتبار كونه عارضا لمحله، فباعتبار أنه سلب له لا يجتمع معه، بل يقابله، وباعتبار أنه عارض لمحله لا يقابله، بل يجتمع معه. وأما ثالثا: فلأنه لو كان معنى قوله: يعقلان معا، ما ذكر، لكان لفظة «معا» لغوا محضا.

I say: this is open to objection. First, two opposites occurring together through one’s belonging to the other is not impossible, so no defence based on differing respects is required. What is impossible is their occurring together by both belonging to one subject. Second, if existence and nonexistence occurred together in one subject, making it both existent and nonexistent, this same defence could be applied. We could say: insofar as nonexistence negates existence, it opposes it; insofar as existence belongs to nonexistence’s subject, they occur together. Each consideration differs from the other: considering it as the negation of existence differs from considering it as belonging to existence’s subject. As negation it does not occur together with existence but opposes it; as belonging to its subject it does not oppose it but occurs together with it. Third, if ‘the two are conceived together’ meant what was stated, the word ‘together’ would be entirely redundant.

Direct witness for the argument previously available as WIT14 through Lāhījī. The second objection is substantially fuller here. | Compared with the inherited WIT14 transcription: this edition reads المتقابلين (not المقابلين), سلب للوجود (not سلب الموجود), and لغوا محضا (not لغوا); it also lacks وقد before يعقلان معا in the third objection. These are differences between the present edition and the inherited mediated transcription, not a manuscript stemma or a fresh inspection of the Lāhījī page.

Interim judgment: The historical core is the move from conceptual predicability to, or away from, ontic multiplication. A correct argument must establish why a predicate demands a distinct external bearer; merely employing the predicate is insufficient. The polemic about aḥwāl is not therefore a quarrel about whether predicates have meanings.

Boundary: No general doctrine of “all second intelligibles are merely subjective” follows: their objective grounding must be considered case by case.

Remaining: The second collation supplies the bounded passages linked above. Obtain original Jurjānī and Dawwānī/Dashtakī gloss witnesses for the copula debate, then compare Yazdī’s quoted readings to those originals. Qūshjī’s source remains a scanned edition with poor OCR: use the facsimile, not OCR, for a critical text. Consult the current critical report for locally closed gaps and remaining whole-work and multi-witness work.

Q07 Mental existence and the known object

When a subject knows heat or a horse, is the quiddity or a cognitive form present, and which properties are thereby predicated?

When I know fire, my mind does not burn. Yet the thought of fire is genuinely an occurrence in my mind and can make “fire is hot” intelligible. The puzzle is to separate the object represented, the intentional content, and the particular psychic act of representing it. Treating them as one item generates false contradictions between substance and accident, universal and particular, hot and non-hot.

What the proof of mental existence must establish

The intended result is not that a material object literally moves into the soul. The claim is that the quiddity or objective content is cognized in a mode of being different from the original thing’s external existence. Al-Ḥillī tests this through cases where the external instance is absent or impossible.

T4 — Predication of the nonexistent and the objection from heat

al-Ḥillī · Al-ʿAllāma al-Ḥillī | Kashf al-murād, discussion of mental existence; al-Zanjānī recension, p. 19 (also Āmulī ed. around pp. 39–40). | Arabic source: https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/3438/19?lang=ar

Arabic digital page 19 checked 2026-10-29; printed-edition and MS collation pending

قال: وهو ينقسم إلى الذهني والخارجي وإلا لبطلت الحقيقية. أقول: اختلف العقلاء هاهنا؛ فجماعة منهم نفوا الوجود الذهني وحصروا الوجود في الخارجي، والمحققون منهم أثبتوه وقسموا الوجود إلى الخارجي والذهني قسمة حقيقية. واستدل المصنف بأن القضية الحقيقية صادقة قطعًا؛ لأنا نحكم بالأحكام الإيجابية على موضوعات معدومة في الأعيان، وتحقق الصفة يستدعي تحقق الموصوف، وإذ ليس ثابتًا في الأعيان فهو متحقق في الذهن. قال: والموجود في الذهن إنما هو الصورة المخالفة في كثير من اللوازم. أقول: هذا جواب عن استدلال من نفى الوجود الذهني، وتقرير استدلالهم أنه لو حلت الماهية في الأذهان لزم أن يكون الذهن حارًا باردًا أسود أبيض، فيلزم مع اتصاف الذهن بهذه الأشياء المنفية عنه اجتماع الضدين. والجواب أن الحاصل في الذهن ليس هو ماهية الحرارة والسواد بل صورتهما ومثالهما المخالفة للماهية في لوازمها وأحكامها، فالحرارة الخارجية تستلزم السخونة وصورتها لا تستلزمها، والتضاد إنما هو بين الماهيات لا بين صورها وأمثلتها.

Ṭūsī says: “Existence is divided into mental [الذهني] and extramental [الخارجي]; otherwise, the real or universally quantified proposition [القضية الحقيقية] would fail.” I say: Rational inquirers differ on this question. One group denies mental existence [الوجود الذهني] and confines existence to what is extramental; the investigators affirm it and recognize a genuine division into extramental and mental existence. Ṭūsī argues that a real proposition is certainly true, since we affirm predicates of subjects that have no existence among extramental individuals. A property's obtaining requires its subject to obtain. Since such a subject is not established extramentally, it is realized mentally. Ṭūsī says: “What exists in the mind is only the form [الصورة], which differs from the thing in many of its concomitants.” This answers the argument of those who deny mental existence. They argue: if a quiddity came to be in the mind, the mind would have to be hot and cold, black and white; the mind would then possess incompatible attributes, and contradictories would be combined. The answer is that what occurs in the mind is not heat and blackness as extramental realities, but their forms or representations, which differ from the quiddities in their consequences and properties. Extramental heat entails hotness; its mental form does not. Opposition belongs to the realities, not to their forms and representations.

TRANSLATOR’S NOTE The phrase qaḍiyya ḥaqīqiyya is a technical term of the logic of propositions, not a vague “true statement.” The argument from positive predication needs separate scrutiny: it may rely on a controversial principle concerning the existence of the subject. This is an al-Ḥillī translation, not proof that all later accounts endorse “likenesses” rather than presence of quiddities.

The objection from heat and other material qualities demands a distinction between the object represented and the representing occurrence.

Qūshjī: the form as a psychic quality

Qūshjī locates the cognitive form in the soul and takes its existence in the soul as a psychical quality. This does not erase its object-reference: what is known through it can still be described according to the original quiddity.

T5 — Knowledge as a psychic quality; the known as a universal

al-Qūshjī · ʿAlī al-Qūshjī | Sharḥ al-Tajrīd, ed. al-Zāriʿī al-Riḍāʾī, vol. I, printed p. 132, final substantive paragraph of the page. | Arabic source: https://archive.org/details/charhTajridKochaji

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

وعلى تحقيقنا هذا نقول: إن مفهوم الحيوان مثلًا إذا حصل في الذهن، فحيث يقوم بالذهن كيفية نفسانية هو العلم بهذا المفهوم، وهو عرض وجزئي لكونه قائمًا بنفس شخصي، ومشخصًا بشخصيات ذهنية، وهو الموجود في الخارج. وأما الموجود في الذهن فهو مفهوم الحيوان الحاصل في الذهن، وهو كلي وجوهر ومعلوم.

On the basis of our analysis, we say this: when the concept of animal [مفهوم الحيوان], for example, occurs in the mind, then insofar as it inheres in the mind as a psychic quality [كيفية نفسانية], it is knowledge [العلم] of that concept. In that respect it is an accident [عرض] and a particular [جزئي], because it inheres in an individual soul and is individuated by mental individuating features; in that respect it is something extramentally existent. What is mentally existent, however, is the concept of animal as occurring in the mind. This is a universal [كلي], a substance [جوهر], and an object known [معلوم].

TRANSLATOR’S NOTE Qūshjī distinguishes the intentional or predicative status of what is known from the ontological status of the act/quality of knowing. The case presses the problem of how one cognitive occurrence can support categorial descriptions that seem incompatible. The text has been checked against the scanned Arabic page; the printed edition's surrounding glosses must not be conflated with his main text.

The next question is whether the form itself is something externally real, though not externally identical with the thing represented.

Lāhījī: a representation in two different respects

The written word Zayd is the written existence of what it signifies, yet its inked inscription is independently a real external fact. Analogously a scientific form is the mental representation of the known object and itself an actual accident of a real knower. These two predications must not be collapsed.

T6 — Three objections to mental existence, and the distinction that answers them

al-Lāhījī · ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Lāhījī | Shawāriq al-ilhām, older Iṣfahān edition, vol. I, p. 48 (one argument unit; the discussion continues). | Arabic source: https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/9309/48?lang=ar
