والموجود في الذهن إنما هو الصورة المخالفة في كثير من اللوازم، إشارة إلى الجواب عن متمسكات النافين للوجود الذهني، وهم جمهور المتكلمين، فإن بعضهم قائلون به. ولما كان مبنى الوجود الذهني على استلزام التعقل إياه وقيام الموجود الذهني بالذهن اقتصر المانعون على نفيه بوجوه. الأول: لو كان تصور الشيء مستلزمًا لحصوله في العقل، لزم من تصور الحرارة والبرودة والاستقامة والاعوجاج أن يكون الذهن حارًا باردًا مستقيمًا معوجًا، وهو محال لما فيه من اجتماع الضدين واتصاف الذهن بما هو من خواص الأجسام. الثاني: أنه يلزم أن تحصل السماوات مثلًا بعظمها في العقل عند تعقلها، وفي الخيال عند تخيلها، وهو باطل بالضرورة. الثالث: أنه يلزم من تعقلنا للمعدومات وجودها في الخارج، لكونها موجودة في العقل الموجود في الخارج، مع القطع بأن الموجود في الموجود في الشيء موجود في ذلك الشيء، كالماء الموجود في الكوز الموجود في البيت. والجواب عن الكل أنه مبني على عدم التفرقة بين الوجود المتأصل الذي به الهوية العينية، وغير المتأصل الذي به الصورة العقلية. فإن المتصف بالحرارة مثلًا ما يقوم به هوية الحرارة لا صورتها، والتضاد إنما هو بين هويتي الحرارة والبرودة لا بين صورتيهما.

Ṭūsī's statement that what exists in the mind is a form differing in many of its concomitants points to the answer to the arguments of those who deny mental existence [الوجود الذهني]. They constitute the majority of the theologians, although some theologians affirm it. Because the thesis depends on thought entailing mental existence and on the mentally existent inhering in the mind, its opponents concentrate their objections on these claims. First: if conceiving a thing entailed its occurrence in the intellect, then conceiving heat and cold, straightness and curvature, would make the mind hot and cold, straight and curved. This is impossible: it would combine opposites and attribute to the mind properties belonging to bodies. Second: it would follow that the heavens, with their immense size, would occur in the intellect when understood and in imagination when imagined. This is necessarily false. Third: it would follow from thinking about nonexistent things that they exist outside the mind, because they exist in an intellect which itself exists outside the mind. Whatever exists in something that exists in a place also exists in that place—as water in a jug located in a house is in the house. All three objections rest on failing to distinguish independently realized existence [الوجود المتأصل], through which an individual extramental reality subsists, from non-independent existence, through which there is an intellectual form. What possesses heat is that in which the extramental reality of heat subsists, not that in which its form occurs. Opposition holds between the extramental realities of heat and cold, not between their intellectual forms.

TRANSLATOR’S NOTE Lāhījī here gives the objections considerable force, then restricts the supposed transfer of extramental properties to mental representations. Later pages introduce further difficulties involving categories, the object of knowledge, and Dawwānī's alternative. Those continuations require their own translation and are not silently included here.

Dawwānī and the dispute over literal categorical quality

Lāhījī explicitly rejects a characterization attributed to Dawwānī in which categorization as a quality is merely figurative. His own assertion that the cognitive form is genuinely a quality is not directly Dawwānī’s position.

Lāhījī explicitly distinguishes his ontology of the knowing form from Dawwānī’s reported figurative interpretation. This is a real disagreement over the ontology of cognition, not a disagreement about whether one may think of something absent.

Sunni kalām and later commentary as controls

Al-Taftāzānī’s selected passage tests the difference between original external existence and a non-original mental manner of being. Ṭihrānī articulates how the same object can be considered under different modes of existence. They supply comparison, not automatic agreement with Lāhījī.

Ṭūsī’s lemma “And it is divided …” This division is made with reference to the existent itself. Thus, for example, when an individual instance of the human exists externally, the human is said to exist with external existence; when an individual instance is represented in the imagination, or its quiddity is impressed upon the soul, it is said to exist with mental existence. The claim is therefore established by appeal to affirmative real propositions, which require the existence of their subject: the establishment of something for something presupposes the establishment of that for which it is established. Since a real proposition need not have all its instances—or many of them—existing [externally], they must have existence in the mind. Al-Ḥillī’s lemma “A genuine division” A genuine division is one whose two alternatives cannot both apply and cannot both fail to apply. A proposition containing such a division is called a strict disjunctive proposition, as when we say: ‘A number is either even or odd.’ The present case is similar: existence is either external or mental; existence can neither lack both nor combine both. ‘Genuine division’ may also be applied to a disjunction in which neither alternative can change into the other, even if combination or exclusion is possible. Consider: ‘An existent is either eternal in itself or eternal through another.’ An existent can fall under neither alternative and instead originate in time. But what is eternal in itself—the Necessary Existent—cannot change into what is eternal through another—the world, according to the philosophers—or vice versa. This differs from ‘A human is either at rest or in motion’: a human at rest can become one in motion, and vice versa, although combination and exclusion are impossible. The commentator may intend this second meaning by ‘genuine division.’ Al-Ḥillī’s lemma “Know that the term ‘proposition’ is used …” Propositions have four classifications, according to subject, predicate, modality, and copula. According to the subject, they divide into mental propositions, whose subject is in the mind—that is, its qualification by the predicate is in respect of the mind, as in ‘Animal is a genus’ and ‘A genus is either higher or lower.’ Natural propositions are among mental propositions: in these, the judgment does not take individuals into account but concerns the nature itself, as in ‘Animal is a part of human.’ The other division is external propositions, whose subject is external. These are external propositions in the broad sense, and they have three subdivisions: real propositions, external propositions in the narrower sense, and singular propositions. Examples are, respectively, ‘Body is finite,’ ‘Those in the army were killed,’ and ‘Zayd is standing.’ Real propositions divide into universal, particular, and unquantified propositions. All this is explained in logic. Al-Ḥillī’s lemma “And this is an unsound doctrine …” The pronoun refers, as is apparent, to his statement ‘its subject is taken with reference to external reality.’ His meaning is that taking the subject with reference to external reality in scientific investigations is an unsound doctrine. For the subject of a proposition in the sciences must be universal, encompassing all the instances actually realized or supposed in the way things are in themselves [nafs al-amr], as has been explained in the demonstrative part of logic—even though external propositions are current in ordinary conversation. Al-Ḥillī’s lemma “It would therefore follow, with the mind’s being qualified …” That is: although we know that these properties are absent from the mind, the supposition that it is qualified by them would entail the conjunction of contraries, because we conceive these properties together. Al-Ḥillī’s lemma “It is not the quiddity of heat …” That is, what is in the mind is not the reality of heat and blackness, but their form, abstracted from external matter by intellectual abstraction, which differs from that reality in many concomitants. The commentator—God have mercy on him—has used ‘quiddity’ to express ‘reality.’ The substance of the answer is that the quiddity is one in external reality and in the mind, whereas the two existences differ. Since many concomitants and effects depend upon external existence, the quiddity existing with mental existence does not have those effects.

Only after this distinction is secured may the text argue that the knowing soul is immaterial (Q20); the argument does not follow from mental existence alone.

31 October: independently inspected continuation

Lāhījī’s alternative interpretations precede his objection; Qūshjī’s reported answer precedes his criticism and decisive reply; İSAM separates Iṣfahānī’s base text from Jurjānī’s gloss. C31I01 — Genus and differentia: the objection and both answers

Shams al-Dīn al-Iṣfahānī · Tasdīd, İSAM II, printed pp.108–109 (= PDF pages 110–111), base text only from الحجة الثانية to قيام العرض بالعرض

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

الحجة الثانية: أن السواد يشارك البياض في اللونية ويخالفه في فصله المختص به، فإن وجد كل من الجنس والفصل، فلا بد وأن يقوم أحدهما بالآخر، وإلا امتنع أن تلتئم منهما حقيقة واحدة، فيلزم قيام العرض بالعرض. وإن عدما أو أحدهما لزم تركب الموجود عن المعدوم، وهو محال، فيكون كل منهما ليس بموجود ولا معدوم، وهما وصفان قائمان بالسواد الموجود، فيكونان حالين. أجاب عنه: بأن كل واحد منهما كلي، والكلي ثابت في الذهن، فلا ترد عليه هذه القسمة بحسب الخارج؛ إذ لا يقبلها، وبحسب الذهن يكون موجودا في الذهن، فلا يكون قائما بالموجود في الخارج، فلا يكون حالا. وأيضا: على تقدير أن يكون كل واحد منهما موجودا، أحدهما قائما بالآخر، لم يلزم منه محال؛ إذ يجوز قيام العرض بالعرض.

The second argument: blackness shares being a colour with whiteness and differs from it by its distinctive differentia. If both genus and differentia exist, one must inhere in the other; otherwise a single reality could not be composed of them. This entails an accident's inhering in an accident. If neither exists, or one does not exist, an existent would be composed from what does not exist, which is impossible. Each must therefore be neither existent nor nonexistent. As two attributes subsisting in existent blackness, they would be two states [aḥwāl]. The answer is that each is universal, and the universal is established in the mind. This external division therefore does not apply to it, since it does not admit it. Considered mentally, it exists in the mind; it does not subsist in an external existent and so is not a state. Furthermore, even if both existed and one inhered in the other, no impossibility would follow, since an accident may inhere in an accident.

Transcribes only the upper base-text register; the separate Jurjānī register and lower minhu notes are not merged into Iṣfahānī’s voice. | Aḥwāl are the disputed intermediate states, neither existent nor nonexistent, not merely ordinary conditions.

C31I02 — Jurjānī corrects the account of universals and composition

al-Sayyid al-Sharīf al-Jurjānī · Ḥāshiyat al-Tajrīd in İSAM Tasdīd II, printed p.109 (= PDF page 111), complete gloss [17.5]

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

قوله: «الكلي ثابت في الذهن، فلا ترد عليه هذه القسمة بحسب الخارج؛ إذ لا يقبلها» فيه ضعف ظاهر؛ لأن الكلي الثابت في الذهن فقط إذا نسب إلى الخارج كان معدوما فيه، فيكون قابلا قطعا للترديد بين الموجود في الخارج والمعدوم فيه. والصواب: أن يحمل قوله «والكلي ثابت ذهنا» على أن الكليات إذا كانت أجزاء لماهية الجزئيات كانت أجزاء عقلية لها ثابتة في الذهن، ويكون حاصل الكلام أن الجنس والفصل جزءان عقليان للسواد موجودان متمايزان عنه في الذهن. وأما في الخارج فهما عين السواد، ولا محذور فيه؛ لأن جزء الموجود إنما يكون متقدما عليه بالوجود حيثما كان جزءا له، إن ذهنا فذهنا، وإن خارجا فخارجا. وتلخيصه: أن السواد في الخارج بسيط، وفي الذهن مركب من أجزاء متميزة بالماهية وبالوجود هناك فقط، كما تقرر في تركيب الماهية من الأجزاء المحمولة.

His words, “The universal is established in the mind, so this external division does not apply to it, since it does not admit it”: there is an evident weakness here. A universal established only in the mind, when referred to the external order, is nonexistent there. It therefore certainly admits division into what exists externally and what does not. The correct course is to interpret “the universal is mentally established” as meaning that universals, when parts of the quiddity of particulars, are intellectual parts established in the mind. The argument would then be that genus and differentia are two intellectual parts of blackness, existent and distinguished from it in the mind, whereas externally they are identical with blackness. No difficulty follows. A part of an existent precedes that existent in existence only in the domain in which it is a part: mentally if mentally, externally if externally. In brief, blackness is externally simple but mentally composed of parts distinguished in quiddity and existence only there, as established concerning the composition of quiddity from predicable parts.

Complete numbered gloss [17.5], excluding the editor’s apparatus and minhu annotations. An independent printed witness to Jurjānī, not a Yazdī attribution.

Continuous witnesses and critical qualifications · second collation

C31Q06 — The earlier interpretation reported before Qūshjī’s objections

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī, reporting an earlier commentary · Sharḥ Tajrīd al-ʿaqāʾid, ed. al-Zāriʿī al-Riḍāʾī, I p.173 (PDF p.173), from وقد قيل في شرحه to عدما مطلقا

Independently transcribed and translated from the specified printed page images; edition apparatus not exhaustively collated

وقد قيل في شرحه: «قد يجتمع الوجود المطلق والعدم المطلق، وذلك لأن العدم المطلق قد يتصور، فيعرض له كون في الذهن، فيعرض له الكون المطلق ـ أعني: الوجود المطلق ـ ضرورة استلزام عروض المقيد للشيء عروض المطلق له، لكن باعتبار التقابل غير اعتبار الاجتماع؛ وذلك لأن العدم المطلق من حيث إنه سلب للوجود المطلق مقابل له، ومن حيث إن الوجود المطلق عارض له يجتمع معه، وكل واحد من الاعتبارين مغاير للآخر؛ فإن اعتبار كونه سلب الوجود غير اعتبار كونه معروضه، فباعتبار أنه سلب له لا يجتمع معه، بل يقابله، وباعتبار أنه معروض له لا يقابله، بل يجتمع معه. وقوله: يعقلان معا؛ أي: الوجود المطلق والعدم المطلق، ردا لما يزعم من أن العدم المطلق لا يمكن أن يتصور، إذ لا تميز له في نفسه أصلا. وتقريره: أنه كما يمكن أن يتصور الوجود المطلق، يمكن أن يتصور رفعه قطعا، وهو العدم المضاف إلى الوجود المطلق، وذلك لا ينافي كونه عدما مطلقا».

It has been said in commenting on it: “Unqualified existence and unqualified nonexistence may occur together. Unqualified nonexistence may be conceived, so that being in the mind belongs to it. Unqualified being—that is, unqualified existence—therefore belongs to it, since the belonging of a qualified instance to something necessarily entails the belonging of the unqualified. But the respect of opposition differs from the respect of conjunction. Insofar as unqualified nonexistence negates unqualified existence, it is opposed to it; insofar as unqualified existence belongs to nonexistence, they occur together. These considerations differ: considering nonexistence as the negation of existence differs from considering it as the subject to which existence belongs. As negation, it does not occur together with existence but opposes it; as a subject of existence, it does not oppose it but occurs together with it. His words ‘the two are conceived together’ mean unqualified existence and unqualified nonexistence, rejecting the allegation that unqualified nonexistence cannot be conceived because it has no distinction whatsoever in itself. The explanation is that, just as unqualified existence may be conceived, its removal certainly may be conceived. That is nonexistence related to unqualified existence; this does not prevent its being unqualified nonexistence.”

The printed Qūshjī text introduces the reported view impersonally. Attribution to the old commentator is mediated by Lāhījī and is not silently inserted into the Arabic. | The quotation ends before أقول: فيه نظر, which marks Qūshjī’s criticism.

C31Q05 — Qūshjī’s complete three objections, directly checked

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī · Sharḥ Tajrīd al-ʿaqāʾid, ed. al-Zāriʿī al-Riḍāʾī, I pp.173–174 (PDF pp.173–174), أقول: فيه نظر through لغوا محضا

Independently transcribed and translated from the specified printed page images; edition apparatus not exhaustively collated

أقول: فيه نظر، أما أولا: فلأن اجتماع المتقابلين بعروض أحدهما للآخر ليس مستحيلا حتى يحتاج إلى الاعتذار بتغاير الجهة؛ إنما يستحيل اجتماعهما بعروضهما لمحل واحد. وأما ثانيا: فلأنه لو اجتمع الوجود والعدم في محل بأن يكون موجودا ومعدوما معا، يمكن إجراء هذا العذر فيه؛ بأن نقول: العدم من حيث إنه سلب للوجود مقابل له، ومن حيث إن الوجود عارض لمحله مجتمع معه، وكل واحد من الاعتبارين مغاير للآخر؛ فإن اعتبار كونه سلب الوجود غير اعتبار كونه عارضا لمحله، فباعتبار أنه سلب له لا يجتمع معه، بل يقابله، وباعتبار أنه عارض لمحله لا يقابله، بل يجتمع معه. وأما ثالثا: فلأنه لو كان معنى قوله: يعقلان معا، ما ذكر، لكان لفظة «معا» لغوا محضا.

I say: this is open to objection. First, two opposites occurring together through one’s belonging to the other is not impossible, so no defence based on differing respects is required. What is impossible is their occurring together by both belonging to one subject. Second, if existence and nonexistence occurred together in one subject, making it both existent and nonexistent, this same defence could be applied. We could say: insofar as nonexistence negates existence, it opposes it; insofar as existence belongs to nonexistence’s subject, they occur together. Each consideration differs from the other: considering it as the negation of existence differs from considering it as belonging to existence’s subject. As negation it does not occur together with existence but opposes it; as belonging to its subject it does not oppose it but occurs together with it. Third, if ‘the two are conceived together’ meant what was stated, the word ‘together’ would be entirely redundant.

Direct witness for the argument previously available as WIT14 through Lāhījī. The second objection is substantially fuller here. | Compared with the inherited WIT14 transcription: this edition reads المتقابلين (not المقابلين), سلب للوجود (not سلب الموجود), and لغوا محضا (not لغوا); it also lacks وقد before يعقلان معا in the third objection. These are differences between the present edition and the inherited mediated transcription, not a manuscript stemma or a fresh inspection of the Lāhījī page.

Interim judgment: The secure result is a two-aspect model of representation: the known object and the cognitive form must not be numerically identified under all predicates. Lāhījī makes the form genuinely an actual quality of the knower, while the content is mentally present. The inherited extracts disclose a genuine disagreement with the position he attributes to Dawwānī.

Boundary: Neither this analysis nor the mere formation of an abstract image proves the soul’s immateriality, God’s mode of knowledge, or the independently subsisting reality of universals. Each requires further premises.

Remaining: The second collation supplies the bounded passages linked above. Follow the heat argument through Ḥillī, Qūshjī, Lāhījī and Sunni epistemology, including whether they preserve formal identity or only representational likeness. Consult the current critical report for locally closed gaps and remaining whole-work and multi-witness work.

Q08 True predication of absent and negative objects

Can true affirmative or negative propositions concern things absent from the external world, and what is the subject of such a proposition?

“The phoenix is imaginary,” “a triangle has three sides,” and “no human is currently on the moon” have different forms of truth. The issue is not solved simply by saying a subject exists mentally: judgments may refer to unrealized but possible instances, impossible combinations, or denials, and their truth-conditions must be identified without treating all their subjects as external objects.

Problem — affirmative judgments without external subjects

We truly predicate relations of impossibilities (for instance, conjunction of contradictories), yet the subjects have no external instances; the form of positive judgment cannot alone establish an external referent.

EXT15 —

ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Lāhījī ·

Inherited, not reverified

إنّا نحكم حكما إيجابيّا على ما لا تحقق له في الخارج أصلا، كقولنا: اجتماع النقيضين مستلزم لكلّ منهما ومغاير لاجتماع الضدّين.

We make an affirmative judgment about what has no actuality at all outside the mind; for example, we say that a conjunction of contradictories entails each of its members and is distinct from a conjunction of contraries.

We need a criterion separating affirming from the existence of the affirmed object.

Two different readings of “establishment”

Lāhījī marks a key distinction: the act of affirmation is not the same as the objective being/obtaining of a putative subject. Merely moving from a true affirmative sentence to an extra-mental thing equivocates. Qūshjī’s three objections, transmitted by Lāhījī, distinguish the coexistence of opposed predicates in a subject from the intellect’s joint conception of existence and its negation.

EXT16 —

ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Lāhījī ·

Inherited, not reverified

واعلم أنّ هذا الإيراد قد يورد باعتبار الإثبات وقد يورد باعتبار الثبوت.

Know that this objection can be formulated with reference to the act of affirming (ithbāt), or with reference to the obtaining of what is affirmed (thubūt).

SN05 — Sharḥ al-Mawāqif · 01

al-Jurjānī · al-Jurjānī | Sharḥ al-Mawāqif | Usul electronic recension, p. 174; marginal strata require checking | source: https://usul.ai/ar/t/sharh-al-mawaqif/174

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

إن أردتم ... أنه يتوقف على تصور ذات المعدوم، فهو ممنوع، وإن أردتم به توقفه على تصور مفهوم المعدوم، فهو مسلم ويلزم حينئذ أن يكون مفهوم المعدوم متميزا وثابتا في الذهن، ولا استحالة فيه.

If you mean that [an evident judgment] depends upon conceiving the very entity of the nonexistent, this is denied; but if you mean that it depends upon conceiving the *concept* of the nonexistent, this is granted. What follows is that the concept of the nonexistent is distinguishable and established in the mind, which is not impossible.

This is *Sharḥ al-Mawāqif*, not the same as Jurjānī’s Ḥāshiya on the Tajrīd. The online version intermixes marginal responses; exact speaker boundaries should be checked against the print before a definitive edition.

WIT14 — Al-Qūshjī’s three objections concerning existence, nonexistence and joint conception

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī (quoted by ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Lāhījī) · al-Qūshjī, Sharḥ al-Tajrīd, p.23, three objections as reproduced by Lāhījī, Shawāriq, I p.274 (mediated text)

Lāhījī printed-page electronic edition checked; mediated Qūshjī reading, not manuscript-collated

فأورد عليه الشارح القوشجي: «أما أولا: فلأن اجتماع المقابلين بعروض أحدهما للآخر ليس مستحيلا حتى يحتاج إلى الاعتذار بتغاير الجهة إنما المستحيل اجتماعهما بعروضهما لمحل واحد. وأما ثانيا: فإنه لو اجتمع الوجود والعدم في محل واحد بأن يكون موجودا ومعدوما معا، يمكن إجراء هذا العذر فيه، بأن يقال: العدم من حيث انه سلب الموجود مقابل له، ومن حيث ان الوجود عارض لمحله مجتمع معه. وأما ثالثا: فإنه لو كان معنى قوله: وقد يعقلان معا، ما ذكره، لكان لفظة معا لغوا».

Al-Qūshjī raised the following objections. First, the coexistence of opposites when one is predicated of the other is not impossible, so there is no need to excuse it by invoking different respects. What is impossible is for both opposites to be predicated of the same subject. Second, if existence and nonexistence were combined in one subject, making it both existent and nonexistent, the same excuse could be used: nonexistence is opposed to the existent as its negation, yet, since existence belongs to the subject, the two allegedly coexist. Third, if “both may be conceived together” means what the earlier commentator proposes, the word “together” would be redundant.

This is a full three-part objection by Qūshjī quoted verbatim within Lāhījī’s later commentary, which cites Sharḥ Tajrīd al-ʿaqāʾid p.23; direct Qūshjī book facsimile not yet collated. | The opponent is the old commentator’s explanation of Ṭūsī’s phrase; it is not an argument denying the principle of noncontradiction.

Formal truth cannot by itself populate the world with impossible objects.

Later direct commentary makes the restriction explicit

A twentieth-century commentator likewise denies that existence-predication presupposes an already existing quiddity. This later voice corroborates the logical distinction, not a medieval textual variant.

Muḥammad al-Ḥusaynī al-Shīrāzī · Muḥammad al-Ḥusaynī al-Shīrāzī | al-Qawl al-sadīd fī sharḥ al-Tajrīd | vol. I:56 | digital transcription read 2026-10-30, no print/manuscript collation

page-indexed Arabic transcription read; short excerpt; manuscript variants unchecked

إثبات الوجود للماهية لا يستدعي وجودها أولا، وسلبه عنها لا يقتضي تميزها وثبوتها.

Predicating existence of a quiddity does not require that it already exist; denying existence of it does not require its prior individuation and establishment.

Later direct Tajrīd commentary explains the predication error common to proof of the nonexistent as a thing. Directly inspected searchable-page extract; not independently collated against a print image or manuscript. Author is modern and is not to be conflated with the medieval Qūshjī or al-Ḥillī.

The remaining problem is to identify a suitably objective criterion of truth.

C31Q01 — The objection from heat to mental existence

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī · Sharḥ Tajrīd al-ʿaqāʾid, ed. Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Zāriʿī al-Riḍāʾī, I, printed/PDF p.128, from وأورد عليه to ما فيه ماهية الحرارة

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

وأورد عليه: أن الصورة الحاصلة من الحرارة في الذهن إما أن تكون ماهية الحرارة أو لا. فعلى الثاني لا وجود للحرارة في الذهن، بل يكون ما في الذهن أمرا مخالفا في الماهية للحرارة، فلا يصح أن للأشياء وجودين خارجيا وذهنيا. لا يقال: لا معنى لوجود الشيء في الذهن إلا وجود صورته فيه، وإن كانت مخالفة له في الحقيقة. لأنا نقول: ما ذكرناه ـ إن تم ـ دل على وجود الأشياء أنفسها في الذهن؛ لأن الحكم على المثل المذكور يقتضي ثبوته فيه، لا ثبوت أمر يخالفه في الحقيقة فيه. وعلى الأول: يلزم أن يكون الذهن حارا أو باردا؛ إذ لا معنى للحار والبارد إلا ما فيه ماهية الحرارة وماهية البرودة.

An objection was raised: the form produced by heat in the mind either is the quiddity of heat or is not. On the second alternative, heat does not exist in the mind; what is in the mind differs in quiddity from heat. It would therefore be incorrect to say that things have two modes of existence, external and mental. One cannot answer that a thing's existence in the mind means only the presence of its form there, even if that form differs in reality from it. For we say that the argument given, if sound, establishes the existence in the mind of the things themselves: judging concerning the example mentioned requires its being established there, rather than something different from it in reality. On the first alternative, however, the mind must be hot or cold, since “hot” and “cold” mean precisely that in which the quiddity of heat or cold is present.

C31Q02 — First answer: mental being does not carry external effects

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī reporting a reply · Qūshjī I, printed/PDF pp.128–129, أجيب to أول أقول فيه بحث

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

وأجيب: بأن الموجود في الذهن ماهية الحرارة والبرودة، وكذا ماهية الجبل والسماء، لكنها موجودة بوجود ظلي، وكون محل الحرارة موصوفا بها من أحكامها المتعلقة بوجودها العيني، وكذا تضادها مع البرودة إنما هو في الوجود العيني دون الظلي. وبالجملة فالصور الذهنية كلية كانت ـ كصور المعقولات ـ أو جزئية ـ كصور المحسوسات ـ مخالفة للخارجية في اللوازم المستندة إلى خصوصية أحد الوجودين، وإن كانت مشاركة لها في لوازم الماهية من حيث هي هي، وما ذكرتم من امتناعه هو حكم الخارجي؛ لأن منشأه الوجود الخارجي، فمن الحرارة يمتنع حصولها في الذهن، وتضاد عين البرودة، وعن الجبل يمتنع حصوله في الذهن، فلم قلتم إن الذهني كذلك؟

It was answered that what exists in the mind is the quiddity of heat and cold, and likewise the quiddity of a mountain and the sky, but with a shadow-like existence [wujūd ẓillī]. The subject of heat's being qualified by heat belongs to the properties tied to its concrete existence; likewise its opposition to cold concerns concrete existence rather than shadow-like existence. In general, mental forms, whether universal like intelligible forms or particular like sensible forms, differ from external forms in the consequences grounded in the specific character of either mode of existence, although they share the consequences of the quiddity considered as such. The impossibility you mentioned is a property of the external [form], grounded in external existence: it is external heat that cannot be present in the mind and is opposed to cold, and the external mountain that cannot be present there. Why assume the same holds of mental being?

Reads the printed text’s elliptical rhetorical construction as a distinction between external and mental forms. Wujūd ẓillī is shadow-like existence, not automatically nonexistence.

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī · Qūshjī I, pp.129–130, أقول فيه بحث through وكذا الكلام في الامتناع وأمثاله

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

أقول: فيه بحث؛ لأن هذا الجواب مخصوص بما إذا ادعى الخصم اتصاف الذهن بالصفات الموجودة في الخارج كالحرارة والبرودة وأمثالهما، ولا يقلع مادة الشبهة؛ فإنه لو تشبث بلوازم الماهيات كالزوجية والفردية مثلا، أو بصفات المعلومات كالامتناع وأمثاله ـ بأن يقول: لو حصلت الزوجية والفردية في الذهن لزم أن يكون الذهن زوجا وفردا؛ إذ لا معنى للزوج والفرد إلا ما حصل فيه الزوجية والفردية، وكذا لو حصل الامتناع في الذهن لزم أن يكون الذهن ممتنعا؛ إذ لا معنى للممتنع إلا ما حصل فيه الامتناع ـ لم يمكن التقصي عنه بهذا الجواب؛ إذ لا يشترط أن يقال كون محل الزوجية موصوفا بها من أحكامها المتعلقة بوجودها العيني، وكذا تضادها مع الفردية إنما هو في الوجود العيني دون الظلي؛ إذ لا وجود عينيا لأمثالهما، لأنها من لوازم الماهيات. وكذا الكلام في الامتناع وأمثاله؛ إلا لا يمكن أن يقال كون محل الامتناع موصوفا به من أحكامه المتعلقة بوجوده العيني؛ إذ لا يتصور له وجود عيني.

I say: this deserves examination. That answer is confined to cases in which the opponent claims that the mind is qualified by externally existing attributes, such as heat and cold. It does not remove the root of the difficulty. The opponent could appeal instead to consequences of quiddities, such as evenness and oddness, or attributes of known objects, such as impossibility. If evenness and oddness occur in the mind, the mind must be even and odd, since those terms mean what has evenness and oddness in it. Similarly, if impossibility occurs in the mind, the mind must be impossible, since an impossible thing means what has impossibility in it. That answer cannot evade this. One cannot stipulate that the subject of evenness is qualified by it only through its concrete existence, or that its opposition to oddness holds only in concrete rather than shadow-like existence. Such attributes have no concrete existence, since they are consequences of quiddities. The same applies to impossibility: one cannot treat the subject's qualification by impossibility as a property tied to its concrete existence, since no concrete existence of impossibility can be conceived.

The printed phrase إلا لا يمكن أن يقال is awkward in its negative context; translation follows the argument’s explicit denial of concrete existence. Retain the Arabic for review; no conjectural emendation asserted. | A substantive criticism by Qūshjī, rather than the voice of the preceding reported answer.

C31Q04 — The decisive answer: presence is different from inherence

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī · Qūshjī I, printed/PDF p.130, complete paragraph beginning والجواب الحاسم

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

والجواب الحاسم لمادة الشبهة هو الفرق بين الحصول في الذهن والقيام به؛ فإن حصول الشيء في الذهن لا يوجب اتصاف الذهن به، كما أن حصول الشيء في المكان لا يوجب اتصاف المكان بالمتمكن به، وكذا الحصول في الزمان فإنه لا يوجب اتصاف الزمان بالحاصل فيه، وإنما الموجب لاتصاف شيء بشيء هو قيامه به لا حصوله فيه، وهذه الأشياء ـ أعني: الحرارة والبرودة والزوجية والفردية والامتناع وأمثالها ـ إنما هي حاصلة في الذهن لا قائمة به، فلم يجب اتصاف الذهن بها، وإنما كانت توجب اتصاف الذهن بها لو كانت قائمة به، وليس كذلك.

The answer that removes the root of the difficulty is the distinction between being present in the mind and inhering in it. A thing's presence in the mind does not require the mind to be qualified by it, just as a thing's presence in a place does not require that place to be qualified by what occupies it. Nor does presence in time require time to be qualified by what occurs in it. What requires one thing to be qualified by another is the latter's inherence in it, rather than its mere presence in it. These things—heat, cold, evenness, oddness, impossibility, and the like—are present in the mind rather than inhering in it. The mind therefore need not be qualified by them. They would require that qualification only if they inhered in it, which they do not.

Complete objection–reported answer–counter-objection–answer chain is supplied by C31Q01–04, pp.128–130; not the entire mental-existence section. | ḥuṣūl = presence or occurrence; qiyām = inherence/subsistence in a subject. These senses must remain distinct in comparison with Yazdī’s ittiṣāf.

الحجة الثانية: أن السواد يشارك البياض في اللونية ويخالفه في فصله المختص به، فإن وجد كل من الجنس والفصل، فلا بد وأن يقوم أحدهما بالآخر، وإلا امتنع أن تلتئم منهما حقيقة واحدة، فيلزم قيام العرض بالعرض. وإن عدما أو أحدهما لزم تركب الموجود عن المعدوم، وهو محال، فيكون كل منهما ليس بموجود ولا معدوم، وهما وصفان قائمان بالسواد الموجود، فيكونان حالين. أجاب عنه: بأن كل واحد منهما كلي، والكلي ثابت في الذهن، فلا ترد عليه هذه القسمة بحسب الخارج؛ إذ لا يقبلها، وبحسب الذهن يكون موجودا في الذهن، فلا يكون قائما بالموجود في الخارج، فلا يكون حالا. وأيضا: على تقدير أن يكون كل واحد منهما موجودا، أحدهما قائما بالآخر، لم يلزم منه محال؛ إذ يجوز قيام العرض بالعرض.

The second argument: blackness shares being a colour with whiteness and differs from it by its distinctive differentia. If both genus and differentia exist, one must inhere in the other; otherwise a single reality could not be composed of them. This entails an accident's inhering in an accident. If neither exists, or one does not exist, an existent would be composed from what does not exist, which is impossible. Each must therefore be neither existent nor nonexistent. As two attributes subsisting in existent blackness, they would be two states [aḥwāl]. The answer is that each is universal, and the universal is established in the mind. This external division therefore does not apply to it, since it does not admit it. Considered mentally, it exists in the mind; it does not subsist in an external existent and so is not a state. Furthermore, even if both existed and one inhered in the other, no impossibility would follow, since an accident may inhere in an accident.

Transcribes only the upper base-text register; the separate Jurjānī register and lower minhu notes are not merged into Iṣfahānī’s voice. | Aḥwāl are the disputed intermediate states, neither existent nor nonexistent, not merely ordinary conditions.

C31I02 — Jurjānī corrects the account of universals and composition

al-Sayyid al-Sharīf al-Jurjānī · Ḥāshiyat al-Tajrīd in İSAM Tasdīd II, printed p.109 (= PDF page 111), complete gloss [17.5]

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

قوله: «الكلي ثابت في الذهن، فلا ترد عليه هذه القسمة بحسب الخارج؛ إذ لا يقبلها» فيه ضعف ظاهر؛ لأن الكلي الثابت في الذهن فقط إذا نسب إلى الخارج كان معدوما فيه، فيكون قابلا قطعا للترديد بين الموجود في الخارج والمعدوم فيه. والصواب: أن يحمل قوله «والكلي ثابت ذهنا» على أن الكليات إذا كانت أجزاء لماهية الجزئيات كانت أجزاء عقلية لها ثابتة في الذهن، ويكون حاصل الكلام أن الجنس والفصل جزءان عقليان للسواد موجودان متمايزان عنه في الذهن. وأما في الخارج فهما عين السواد، ولا محذور فيه؛ لأن جزء الموجود إنما يكون متقدما عليه بالوجود حيثما كان جزءا له، إن ذهنا فذهنا، وإن خارجا فخارجا. وتلخيصه: أن السواد في الخارج بسيط، وفي الذهن مركب من أجزاء متميزة بالماهية وبالوجود هناك فقط، كما تقرر في تركيب الماهية من الأجزاء المحمولة.

His words, “The universal is established in the mind, so this external division does not apply to it, since it does not admit it”: there is an evident weakness here. A universal established only in the mind, when referred to the external order, is nonexistent there. It therefore certainly admits division into what exists externally and what does not. The correct course is to interpret “the universal is mentally established” as meaning that universals, when parts of the quiddity of particulars, are intellectual parts established in the mind. The argument would then be that genus and differentia are two intellectual parts of blackness, existent and distinguished from it in the mind, whereas externally they are identical with blackness. No difficulty follows. A part of an existent precedes that existent in existence only in the domain in which it is a part: mentally if mentally, externally if externally. In brief, blackness is externally simple but mentally composed of parts distinguished in quiddity and existence only there, as established concerning the composition of quiddity from predicable parts.

Complete numbered gloss [17.5], excluding the editor’s apparatus and minhu annotations. An independent printed witness to Jurjānī, not a Yazdī attribution.

Q09 Nafs al-amr and objective truth

Where does a logically or mathematically correct judgment agree with reality when no corresponding material individual exists?

If “two plus two is four” remains true when no one currently entertains it, what does its correctness correspond to? The term nafs al-amr marks objective correctness without immediately committing its user to a freestanding Platonic world or to a special class of mental entities. One must distinguish the thing as it is, its conceptual presentation, and the relation of correspondence.

The Ṭūsī lemma and initial distinction

The inherited Ṭūsī units introduce correspondence to what is the case in itself; their wording alone does not locate an additional substantial “realm of facts.”

What does correspondence require when no concrete subject exists?

Truth of universally scoped suppositions

A universally quantified judgment can have a logically supposed subject, whose mental supposition need not entail a matching external individual.

EXT30 —

ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Lāhījī ·

والمراد بالأفراد الذهنية هو الأفراد المقدّرة على أن يكون الذهن ظرفا للوجود الفرضي، أعني الوجود الذي هو نفس الفرض والتقدير في الذهن.

By “mental individuals” is meant individuals supposed such that the intellect is the place of their hypothetical existence—that is, the existence constituted by intellectual supposition and positing itself.

But supposing a proposition does not make it true.

Affirmation versus objective obtaining

Lāhījī distinguishes logical assertion from ontological establishment; the two questions must not be conflated.

Know that this objection can be formulated with reference to the act of affirming (ithbāt), or with reference to the obtaining of what is affirmed (thubūt).

Now identify the standard of correctness.

Nafs al-amr and grounded relational attributions

Lāhījī states the criterion: the truth of iʿtibārī attributions is correspondence with nafs al-amr, even though the predicate need not itself be a separate extra-mental entity.

لأنّ مناط صدق الحكم بالأمور الاعتبارية هو مطابقته لما في نفس الأمر، كما سيأتي في الكتاب.

For the criterion of truth in a judgment employing conceptual or relational considerations is its correspondence with what obtains in itself (nafs al-amr), as the book will later explain.

This licenses objectivity without reification, but does not settle the ultimate metaphysics of every mathematical or modal truth.

The Ṭihrānī distinction

The inherited exposition separates the meaning of nafs al-amr from the relation of matching it; this confirms that an account of the truth-maker is an additional task. Yazdī objects to identifying nafs al-amr exclusively with the active intellect: divine knowledge has a superior claim as a criterion of reality.

H2 — Truth and nafs al amr

Ṭūsī’s lemma “In virtue of correspondence to what is the case in itself [nafs al-amr].” I say: there are two questions here. First, what does nafs al-amr mean? Second, what does correspondence to what is the case in itself mean? As for nafs al-amr, it means the thing itself, considered just as it is, apart from its being apprehended by anyone, demonstrated by a proof, or existing in a domain. Whatever occurs in a faculty of apprehension and is conceived through an instrument of conception either has an intrinsic standing other than its occurring in that faculty—as when we say, ‘A body has shape,’ ‘The human is possible,’ ‘Possibility necessarily belongs to the possible,’ and ‘Four is even.’ For a body's having shape, the human's possibility, possibility's necessarily belonging to the possible, four's evenness, and other such realities each have, within their proper bounds, an intrinsic standing that can be apprehended and demonstrated. Or it has no intrinsic standing beyond that aspect—as with the human's being necessary in itself, five's evenness, possibility's not necessarily belonging to the possible, and absolute nonexistence. These have no intrinsic standing within their proper bounds. They can neither be demonstrated nor apprehended from the way things are in themselves; they are in the mind only by supposition. In other words, nafs al-amr stands in contrast to supposition. Although the possibility of the possible exists in the intellect through consideration and abstraction, its intrinsic standing—that is, its quiddity in the broader sense—is preserved at its own level by the Real [God], without beginning or end, without anyone's supposing it in the domain of supposition or apprehending it. Five's evenness, the human's necessity, and similar things are otherwise. They have no intrinsic standing beyond their being supposed by someone in his mind and fabricated by the demon of the imaginative faculty. Thus whatever has an intrinsic standing in reality—whether it is an external existent or a mental existent, in the sense of having existence only mentally, such as possibility, human, animal, and the relation between the latter two—has two aspects when it occurs in a mind: its aspect as it is in itself, and the aspect of its being in the mind. An example is our statement ‘Four is even.’ By contrast, what has no intrinsic standing in reality, as in ‘Five is even,’ has only the aspect of its being supposed in the mind. Correspondence to nafs al-amr therefore means that the two aspects correspond: what is in the mind possesses both, as in ‘The human is possible,’ ‘The human is a body,’ and ‘Possibility is a modality of the [predicative] relation.’ The absence of correspondence in the case under discussion is a negation due to the absence of a subject: that is, there are no two aspects here to correspond with one another. Our statement ‘The human is possible’ thus has two relations, a mental relation and a relation belonging to the way things are in themselves. But ‘The human is necessary in itself’ has only a mental relation.

WIT10 — Nafs al-amr and the active intellect: exemplification rather than exclusivity

Mullā ʿAbd Allāh al-Yazdī (al-Bahābādī) · Yazdī, Ḥāshiya ʿalā ḥāshiyat Sharḥ al-Tajrīd, published PDF printed p.89; PDF image 88

Arabic visually transcribed from the published PDF page; Yazdī’s own comment

أقول: ويجوز أن لا يكون ذكر خصوص العقل الفعال للحصر، بل للتمثيل؛ فإن الظاهر أن المبادئ كلها في هذا المعنى سواء، بل علم الله تعالى أجل وأعلى، فهو بكونه الواقع ونفس الأمر أحق.

I say: It is possible that the active intellect is mentioned not as an exclusive identification, but as an illustration. For it appears that all [higher] principles stand on the same footing in this respect; indeed divine knowledge is more exalted and higher, and therefore has a still stronger claim to be regarded as actuality and *nafs al-amr*.

Rejects the inference “nafs al-amr = only the active intellect”; his argument invokes a hierarchy of cognitional foundations. Need distinguish ontological truthmaker from merely comparing representations. | Bounded passage, not the whole work; do not infer an exhaustive manuscript collation.

The appeal to divine knowledge in Q24 and fixed entities in Q26 remains a further contested explanation.

C31Y02 — The counter-objection to an account in terms of union

Yazdī reporting al-Sayyid al-Sanad and responding · Yazdī, printed p.33 (= PDF page 33), complete paragraph beginning ثم أقول

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

ثم أقول: قد اختار السيد السند ـ قدس سره ـ أن المحكي عنه هو اتحاد الموضوع مع مفهوم المحمول في الخارج. فنقول: إن كانت تلك الحكاية صادقة لزم وجود الاتحاد في الخارج، وأنه يستلزم إليه؛ وإن كانت كاذبة لم يعتبر. فإن اختار أن الاتحاد في الخارج لا أنه موجود في الخارج، فقد صار إلى ما ذكرناه سواء بسواء.

Then I say: al-Sayyid al-Sanad chose the view that what is represented is the subject's union with the concept of the predicate in the external order. We therefore say: if that representation is true, the existence of the union in the external order follows, and it entails [a regress: the printed text reads “to it”]; if it is false, it is disregarded. If he chooses to say that the union is in the external order, without saying that it exists in the external order, he has arrived at precisely what we stated.

The printed phrase وأنه يستلزم إليه is awkward; the contextual supplement “a regress” is interpretive and must not be silently substituted into Arabic. | Probable Dashtakī report by contextual title usage; p.33 has no independent identifying footnote. | The reply does not establish that predication is arbitrary. It distinguishes an externally grounded union from an added externally existing relational entity.

C31Y03 — External qualification and the status of negative predicates

Mullā ʿAbd Allāh al-Yazdī · Yazdī p.33, sequence from فهو من حيث أنه ليس في الخارج through الذاتيات

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

قوله: «فهو من حيث أنه ليس في الخارج». أي لا يوجد فيه، وإلا فالاتصاف أيضا في الخارج. قوله: «ومن حيث إنه يستدعي ملاحظة أمر خارج عن الموضوع». لا وجوده، وإلا كان من قبيل حمل الإضافات من غير فوق. قوله: «فظهر أن مطابق الحكم الحملي قد يكون ذات الموضوع فقط كما في الذاتيات». وكذا العدميات، فإنها وإن استدعت ملاحظة أمر زائد لا يستدعي وجود أمر سوى ذات الموضوع. فإن الموجود في الخارج المحكي عنه هو الذات فحسب.

His words, “insofar as it is not in the external order”: that is, it does not exist there; otherwise qualification too is in the external order. His words, “insofar as it requires considering something outside the subject”: [considering it], rather than its existence; otherwise it would be like predicating relations without an “above.” His words, “It thus becomes clear that what corresponds to a predicative judgment may be the subject's essence alone, as in essential predicates”: the same applies to negative predicates. Although these require considering something additional, they do not require anything to exist besides the subject's essence. The externally existing thing that is represented is the essence alone.

Lemmata introduced by قوله belong to the annotated text as segmented by the editor; explanatory sentences belong to the gloss under that segmentation. | The peculiar printed phrase من غير فوق is retained rather than conjecturally repaired.

C31Q01 — The objection from heat to mental existence

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī · Sharḥ Tajrīd al-ʿaqāʾid, ed. Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Zāriʿī al-Riḍāʾī, I, printed/PDF p.128, from وأورد عليه to ما فيه ماهية الحرارة

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

وأورد عليه: أن الصورة الحاصلة من الحرارة في الذهن إما أن تكون ماهية الحرارة أو لا. فعلى الثاني لا وجود للحرارة في الذهن، بل يكون ما في الذهن أمرا مخالفا في الماهية للحرارة، فلا يصح أن للأشياء وجودين خارجيا وذهنيا. لا يقال: لا معنى لوجود الشيء في الذهن إلا وجود صورته فيه، وإن كانت مخالفة له في الحقيقة. لأنا نقول: ما ذكرناه ـ إن تم ـ دل على وجود الأشياء أنفسها في الذهن؛ لأن الحكم على المثل المذكور يقتضي ثبوته فيه، لا ثبوت أمر يخالفه في الحقيقة فيه. وعلى الأول: يلزم أن يكون الذهن حارا أو باردا؛ إذ لا معنى للحار والبارد إلا ما فيه ماهية الحرارة وماهية البرودة.

An objection was raised: the form produced by heat in the mind either is the quiddity of heat or is not. On the second alternative, heat does not exist in the mind; what is in the mind differs in quiddity from heat. It would therefore be incorrect to say that things have two modes of existence, external and mental. One cannot answer that a thing's existence in the mind means only the presence of its form there, even if that form differs in reality from it. For we say that the argument given, if sound, establishes the existence in the mind of the things themselves: judging concerning the example mentioned requires its being established there, rather than something different from it in reality. On the first alternative, however, the mind must be hot or cold, since “hot” and “cold” mean precisely that in which the quiddity of heat or cold is present.

C31Q02 — First answer: mental being does not carry external effects

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī reporting a reply · Qūshjī I, printed/PDF pp.128–129, أجيب to أول أقول فيه بحث

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

وأجيب: بأن الموجود في الذهن ماهية الحرارة والبرودة، وكذا ماهية الجبل والسماء، لكنها موجودة بوجود ظلي، وكون محل الحرارة موصوفا بها من أحكامها المتعلقة بوجودها العيني، وكذا تضادها مع البرودة إنما هو في الوجود العيني دون الظلي. وبالجملة فالصور الذهنية كلية كانت ـ كصور المعقولات ـ أو جزئية ـ كصور المحسوسات ـ مخالفة للخارجية في اللوازم المستندة إلى خصوصية أحد الوجودين، وإن كانت مشاركة لها في لوازم الماهية من حيث هي هي، وما ذكرتم من امتناعه هو حكم الخارجي؛ لأن منشأه الوجود الخارجي، فمن الحرارة يمتنع حصولها في الذهن، وتضاد عين البرودة، وعن الجبل يمتنع حصوله في الذهن، فلم قلتم إن الذهني كذلك؟

It was answered that what exists in the mind is the quiddity of heat and cold, and likewise the quiddity of a mountain and the sky, but with a shadow-like existence [wujūd ẓillī]. The subject of heat's being qualified by heat belongs to the properties tied to its concrete existence; likewise its opposition to cold concerns concrete existence rather than shadow-like existence. In general, mental forms, whether universal like intelligible forms or particular like sensible forms, differ from external forms in the consequences grounded in the specific character of either mode of existence, although they share the consequences of the quiddity considered as such. The impossibility you mentioned is a property of the external [form], grounded in external existence: it is external heat that cannot be present in the mind and is opposed to cold, and the external mountain that cannot be present there. Why assume the same holds of mental being?

Reads the printed text’s elliptical rhetorical construction as a distinction between external and mental forms. Wujūd ẓillī is shadow-like existence, not automatically nonexistence.

C31Q03 — Qūshjī’s challenge using evenness and impossibility

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī · Qūshjī I, pp.129–130, أقول فيه بحث through وكذا الكلام في الامتناع وأمثاله

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

أقول: فيه بحث؛ لأن هذا الجواب مخصوص بما إذا ادعى الخصم اتصاف الذهن بالصفات الموجودة في الخارج كالحرارة والبرودة وأمثالهما، ولا يقلع مادة الشبهة؛ فإنه لو تشبث بلوازم الماهيات كالزوجية والفردية مثلا، أو بصفات المعلومات كالامتناع وأمثاله ـ بأن يقول: لو حصلت الزوجية والفردية في الذهن لزم أن يكون الذهن زوجا وفردا؛ إذ لا معنى للزوج والفرد إلا ما حصل فيه الزوجية والفردية، وكذا لو حصل الامتناع في الذهن لزم أن يكون الذهن ممتنعا؛ إذ لا معنى للممتنع إلا ما حصل فيه الامتناع ـ لم يمكن التقصي عنه بهذا الجواب؛ إذ لا يشترط أن يقال كون محل الزوجية موصوفا بها من أحكامها المتعلقة بوجودها العيني، وكذا تضادها مع الفردية إنما هو في الوجود العيني دون الظلي؛ إذ لا وجود عينيا لأمثالهما، لأنها من لوازم الماهيات. وكذا الكلام في الامتناع وأمثاله؛ إلا لا يمكن أن يقال كون محل الامتناع موصوفا به من أحكامه المتعلقة بوجوده العيني؛ إذ لا يتصور له وجود عيني.

I say: this deserves examination. That answer is confined to cases in which the opponent claims that the mind is qualified by externally existing attributes, such as heat and cold. It does not remove the root of the difficulty. The opponent could appeal instead to consequences of quiddities, such as evenness and oddness, or attributes of known objects, such as impossibility. If evenness and oddness occur in the mind, the mind must be even and odd, since those terms mean what has evenness and oddness in it. Similarly, if impossibility occurs in the mind, the mind must be impossible, since an impossible thing means what has impossibility in it. That answer cannot evade this. One cannot stipulate that the subject of evenness is qualified by it only through its concrete existence, or that its opposition to oddness holds only in concrete rather than shadow-like existence. Such attributes have no concrete existence, since they are consequences of quiddities. The same applies to impossibility: one cannot treat the subject's qualification by impossibility as a property tied to its concrete existence, since no concrete existence of impossibility can be conceived.

The printed phrase إلا لا يمكن أن يقال is awkward in its negative context; translation follows the argument’s explicit denial of concrete existence. Retain the Arabic for review; no conjectural emendation asserted. | A substantive criticism by Qūshjī, rather than the voice of the preceding reported answer.

C31Q04 — The decisive answer: presence is different from inherence

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī · Qūshjī I, printed/PDF p.130, complete paragraph beginning والجواب الحاسم

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

والجواب الحاسم لمادة الشبهة هو الفرق بين الحصول في الذهن والقيام به؛ فإن حصول الشيء في الذهن لا يوجب اتصاف الذهن به، كما أن حصول الشيء في المكان لا يوجب اتصاف المكان بالمتمكن به، وكذا الحصول في الزمان فإنه لا يوجب اتصاف الزمان بالحاصل فيه، وإنما الموجب لاتصاف شيء بشيء هو قيامه به لا حصوله فيه، وهذه الأشياء ـ أعني: الحرارة والبرودة والزوجية والفردية والامتناع وأمثالها ـ إنما هي حاصلة في الذهن لا قائمة به، فلم يجب اتصاف الذهن بها، وإنما كانت توجب اتصاف الذهن بها لو كانت قائمة به، وليس كذلك.

The answer that removes the root of the difficulty is the distinction between being present in the mind and inhering in it. A thing's presence in the mind does not require the mind to be qualified by it, just as a thing's presence in a place does not require that place to be qualified by what occupies it. Nor does presence in time require time to be qualified by what occurs in it. What requires one thing to be qualified by another is the latter's inherence in it, rather than its mere presence in it. These things—heat, cold, evenness, oddness, impossibility, and the like—are present in the mind rather than inhering in it. The mind therefore need not be qualified by them. They would require that qualification only if they inhered in it, which they do not.

Complete objection–reported answer–counter-objection–answer chain is supplied by C31Q01–04, pp.128–130; not the entire mental-existence section. | ḥuṣūl = presence or occurrence; qiyām = inherence/subsistence in a subject. These senses must remain distinct in comparison with Yazdī’s ittiṣāf.

C31I01 — Genus and differentia: the objection and both answers

Shams al-Dīn al-Iṣfahānī · Tasdīd, İSAM II, printed pp.108–109 (= PDF pages 110–111), base text only from الحجة الثانية to قيام العرض بالعرض

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

الحجة الثانية: أن السواد يشارك البياض في اللونية ويخالفه في فصله المختص به، فإن وجد كل من الجنس والفصل، فلا بد وأن يقوم أحدهما بالآخر، وإلا امتنع أن تلتئم منهما حقيقة واحدة، فيلزم قيام العرض بالعرض. وإن عدما أو أحدهما لزم تركب الموجود عن المعدوم، وهو محال، فيكون كل منهما ليس بموجود ولا معدوم، وهما وصفان قائمان بالسواد الموجود، فيكونان حالين. أجاب عنه: بأن كل واحد منهما كلي، والكلي ثابت في الذهن، فلا ترد عليه هذه القسمة بحسب الخارج؛ إذ لا يقبلها، وبحسب الذهن يكون موجودا في الذهن، فلا يكون قائما بالموجود في الخارج، فلا يكون حالا. وأيضا: على تقدير أن يكون كل واحد منهما موجودا، أحدهما قائما بالآخر، لم يلزم منه محال؛ إذ يجوز قيام العرض بالعرض.

The second argument: blackness shares being a colour with whiteness and differs from it by its distinctive differentia. If both genus and differentia exist, one must inhere in the other; otherwise a single reality could not be composed of them. This entails an accident's inhering in an accident. If neither exists, or one does not exist, an existent would be composed from what does not exist, which is impossible. Each must therefore be neither existent nor nonexistent. As two attributes subsisting in existent blackness, they would be two states [aḥwāl]. The answer is that each is universal, and the universal is established in the mind. This external division therefore does not apply to it, since it does not admit it. Considered mentally, it exists in the mind; it does not subsist in an external existent and so is not a state. Furthermore, even if both existed and one inhered in the other, no impossibility would follow, since an accident may inhere in an accident.

Transcribes only the upper base-text register; the separate Jurjānī register and lower minhu notes are not merged into Iṣfahānī’s voice. | Aḥwāl are the disputed intermediate states, neither existent nor nonexistent, not merely ordinary conditions.

C31I02 — Jurjānī corrects the account of universals and composition

al-Sayyid al-Sharīf al-Jurjānī · Ḥāshiyat al-Tajrīd in İSAM Tasdīd II, printed p.109 (= PDF page 111), complete gloss [17.5]

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

قوله: «الكلي ثابت في الذهن، فلا ترد عليه هذه القسمة بحسب الخارج؛ إذ لا يقبلها» فيه ضعف ظاهر؛ لأن الكلي الثابت في الذهن فقط إذا نسب إلى الخارج كان معدوما فيه، فيكون قابلا قطعا للترديد بين الموجود في الخارج والمعدوم فيه. والصواب: أن يحمل قوله «والكلي ثابت ذهنا» على أن الكليات إذا كانت أجزاء لماهية الجزئيات كانت أجزاء عقلية لها ثابتة في الذهن، ويكون حاصل الكلام أن الجنس والفصل جزءان عقليان للسواد موجودان متمايزان عنه في الذهن. وأما في الخارج فهما عين السواد، ولا محذور فيه؛ لأن جزء الموجود إنما يكون متقدما عليه بالوجود حيثما كان جزءا له، إن ذهنا فذهنا، وإن خارجا فخارجا. وتلخيصه: أن السواد في الخارج بسيط، وفي الذهن مركب من أجزاء متميزة بالماهية وبالوجود هناك فقط، كما تقرر في تركيب الماهية من الأجزاء المحمولة.

His words, “The universal is established in the mind, so this external division does not apply to it, since it does not admit it”: there is an evident weakness here. A universal established only in the mind, when referred to the external order, is nonexistent there. It therefore certainly admits division into what exists externally and what does not. The correct course is to interpret “the universal is mentally established” as meaning that universals, when parts of the quiddity of particulars, are intellectual parts established in the mind. The argument would then be that genus and differentia are two intellectual parts of blackness, existent and distinguished from it in the mind, whereas externally they are identical with blackness. No difficulty follows. A part of an existent precedes that existent in existence only in the domain in which it is a part: mentally if mentally, externally if externally. In brief, blackness is externally simple but mentally composed of parts distinguished in quiddity and existence only there, as established concerning the composition of quiddity from predicable parts.

Complete numbered gloss [17.5], excluding the editor’s apparatus and minhu annotations. An independent printed witness to Jurjānī, not a Yazdī attribution.

Continuous witnesses and critical qualifications · second collation

C31G02 — Actual and hypothetical qualification: a catalogue-mediated excipit

Ghiyāth al-Dīn Manṣūr’s attributed work; speaker within the reported excipit unresolved · Fahras al-makhṭūṭāt al-ʿArabiyya wa-l-Turkiyya wa-l-Fārisiyya fī Maktabat Rāghib Bāshā, vol. 6, printed/PDF p. 382, continuation of entry 1042, Ragıp Paşa 809; excipit from خامسها through حتى يصدق القضية; manuscript folio not directly inspected

خامسها: أن يكون مناط صدق القضية الإنصاف بالمحكوم به وح (وحينئذ) إن كان الإنصاف بالعنوان في نفس الأمر كانت القضية صادقة من غير اعتبار تعليق كقولنا: كل كاتب متحرك بالأصابع ما دام كاتباً، أما إذا لم يكن الإنصاف بالعنوان بحسب نفس الأمر، بل بحسب الفرض فقط فلا بد من اعتبار التعلق بذلك الوصف حتى يصدق القضية

The fifth [case]: the ground of a proposition’s truth is [the subject’s] qualification by what is predicated of it. Then, if qualification under the subject-description obtains in the fact of the matter (nafs al-amr), the proposition is true without considering a conditional dependence, as when we say: “Every writer moves the fingers for as long as he is writing.” But if qualification under that description does not obtain in the fact of the matter, and obtains only by supposition, dependence on that description must be taken into account for the proposition to be true.

WIT07 — What makes an external attribution true?

al-Sayyid al-Sanad, probably Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Dashtakī (reported by Yazdī; original uncollated) · Yazdī, printed p.33; mediated quotation; contextual attribution revised 31 October 2026

Printed p.33 inspected; title-context checked against p.12 nn.6/8 and editor’s introduction p.5; probable attribution only

قال السيد السند: تلك الحكاية، إن كانت صادقة كان متصفا في الخارج به، ولا يكفي في ذلك وجود الجسم والبياض فيه لعلاقة بينهما فيه، وإلا لصدق أن الزنجي متصف بالبياض في الخارج لوجود الزنجي والبياض كليهما فيه، وإن كان كاذبا فلا عبرة.

Al-Sayyid al-Sanad said: If that statement corresponds to the truth, the subject is actually qualified by the predicate externally. The mere external presence of a body and of whiteness does not suffice to establish the relevant relation between them: otherwise it would be true that a Black person is externally qualified by whiteness merely because both that person and whiteness exist outside the mind. But if the statement is false, it carries no weight.

Supersedes blanket Jurjānī attribution: p.12 n.6 explicitly identifies al-Sayyid al-Sanad as Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Dashtakī; n.8 distinguishes Jurjānī as al-Muḥaqqiq al-Sharīf. | The p.33 passage itself lacks a fresh identifying note. Dashtakī is contextually probable, not independently confirmed from his original gloss. | Printed Arabic has وإن كان كاذبا فلا عبرة, with masculine كان; the inherited transcription is retained here and C31Y02 supplies the subsequent argument.

Interim judgment: The best-supported result is a distinction between having a mental conception and its being objectively correct. Treating nafs al-amr as either nothing but subjective thought or automatically identical to divine knowledge begs the disputed question. The latter relation is a possible later explanation requiring its own sources.

Boundary: The inherited materials are inadequate for a complete genealogy of the technical term across al-Ījī, Jurjānī, Mīr Zāhid, and later logicians.

Remaining: The second collation supplies the bounded passages linked above. Collate works directly devoted to nafs al-amr and al-Ījī/Jurjānī/Mīr Zāhid discussions; distinguish mathematical, modal, and divine-science cases. Consult the current critical report for locally closed gaps and remaining whole-work and multi-witness work.

Q10 Modality: necessity, possibility, impossibility

Are modal determinations intrinsic, caused, or logical considerations, and how do they apply to nonexistent possibilities?

Necessity, impossibility, and possibility can be considered intrinsically or with reference to another. A contingent existent can be necessary *through its complete cause* without becoming necessary *by its essence*. Confusing these respects either makes contingency vanish when a thing exists or mistakes an intellectual modality for an independently subsisting substance.

Three modalities, and why their cognition is not their being

The possibility, necessity or impossibility of a subject is not simply a further material component that the mind detects alongside it.

When necessity, impossibility, and possibility are considered intrinsically rather than in relation to another, intelligibles are divided among them by a genuine exhaustive division.

The page also distinguishes lexical explanation from genuine definition; only the directly relevant modal conclusion is quoted.

Are these three determinations then fictions created by the mind?

Avicennan interpretation defended by Lāhījī

Lāhījī argues that Avicenna’s calling possibility “existent” need mean no more than that the mental attribution has an objective basis from which it is abstracted.

Avicenna does not mean, in calling possibility an existent meaning, that possibility is a positive property subsisting outside the mind in its own right. Rather he means that it is a meaningful determination abstracted from a basis in extra-mental existence.

Grounded intellectual considerations differ from freely invented ones.

Nafs al-amr governs the attribution

The criterion of truth for iʿtibārī modal descriptions is their correspondence with nafs al-amr, not an independent extramental property of possibility.

For the criterion of truth in a judgment employing conceptual or relational considerations is its correspondence with what obtains in itself (nafs al-amr), as the book will later explain.

Why does this not violate the principle of contradiction?

Defusing the objection from two nonexistent contradictories

Lāhījī distinguishes whether opposed concepts exist as objects from whether opposite predicates may both be truly applied. Contradiction attaches to the latter, not the former.

The meaning of both contradictories being absent in the case of terms is that neither is truly predicable of anything; it is not that the two opposed concepts lack existence or establishment in themselves.

C31Q01 — The objection from heat to mental existence

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī · Sharḥ Tajrīd al-ʿaqāʾid, ed. Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Zāriʿī al-Riḍāʾī, I, printed/PDF p.128, from وأورد عليه to ما فيه ماهية الحرارة

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

وأورد عليه: أن الصورة الحاصلة من الحرارة في الذهن إما أن تكون ماهية الحرارة أو لا. فعلى الثاني لا وجود للحرارة في الذهن، بل يكون ما في الذهن أمرا مخالفا في الماهية للحرارة، فلا يصح أن للأشياء وجودين خارجيا وذهنيا. لا يقال: لا معنى لوجود الشيء في الذهن إلا وجود صورته فيه، وإن كانت مخالفة له في الحقيقة. لأنا نقول: ما ذكرناه ـ إن تم ـ دل على وجود الأشياء أنفسها في الذهن؛ لأن الحكم على المثل المذكور يقتضي ثبوته فيه، لا ثبوت أمر يخالفه في الحقيقة فيه. وعلى الأول: يلزم أن يكون الذهن حارا أو باردا؛ إذ لا معنى للحار والبارد إلا ما فيه ماهية الحرارة وماهية البرودة.

An objection was raised: the form produced by heat in the mind either is the quiddity of heat or is not. On the second alternative, heat does not exist in the mind; what is in the mind differs in quiddity from heat. It would therefore be incorrect to say that things have two modes of existence, external and mental. One cannot answer that a thing's existence in the mind means only the presence of its form there, even if that form differs in reality from it. For we say that the argument given, if sound, establishes the existence in the mind of the things themselves: judging concerning the example mentioned requires its being established there, rather than something different from it in reality. On the first alternative, however, the mind must be hot or cold, since “hot” and “cold” mean precisely that in which the quiddity of heat or cold is present.

C31Q02 — First answer: mental being does not carry external effects

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

وأجيب: بأن الموجود في الذهن ماهية الحرارة والبرودة، وكذا ماهية الجبل والسماء، لكنها موجودة بوجود ظلي، وكون محل الحرارة موصوفا بها من أحكامها المتعلقة بوجودها العيني، وكذا تضادها مع البرودة إنما هو في الوجود العيني دون الظلي. وبالجملة فالصور الذهنية كلية كانت ـ كصور المعقولات ـ أو جزئية ـ كصور المحسوسات ـ مخالفة للخارجية في اللوازم المستندة إلى خصوصية أحد الوجودين، وإن كانت مشاركة لها في لوازم الماهية من حيث هي هي، وما ذكرتم من امتناعه هو حكم الخارجي؛ لأن منشأه الوجود الخارجي، فمن الحرارة يمتنع حصولها في الذهن، وتضاد عين البرودة، وعن الجبل يمتنع حصوله في الذهن، فلم قلتم إن الذهني كذلك؟

It was answered that what exists in the mind is the quiddity of heat and cold, and likewise the quiddity of a mountain and the sky, but with a shadow-like existence [wujūd ẓillī]. The subject of heat's being qualified by heat belongs to the properties tied to its concrete existence; likewise its opposition to cold concerns concrete existence rather than shadow-like existence. In general, mental forms, whether universal like intelligible forms or particular like sensible forms, differ from external forms in the consequences grounded in the specific character of either mode of existence, although they share the consequences of the quiddity considered as such. The impossibility you mentioned is a property of the external [form], grounded in external existence: it is external heat that cannot be present in the mind and is opposed to cold, and the external mountain that cannot be present there. Why assume the same holds of mental being?

Reads the printed text’s elliptical rhetorical construction as a distinction between external and mental forms. Wujūd ẓillī is shadow-like existence, not automatically nonexistence.

C31Q03 — Qūshjī’s challenge using evenness and impossibility

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī · Qūshjī I, pp.129–130, أقول فيه بحث through وكذا الكلام في الامتناع وأمثاله

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

أقول: فيه بحث؛ لأن هذا الجواب مخصوص بما إذا ادعى الخصم اتصاف الذهن بالصفات الموجودة في الخارج كالحرارة والبرودة وأمثالهما، ولا يقلع مادة الشبهة؛ فإنه لو تشبث بلوازم الماهيات كالزوجية والفردية مثلا، أو بصفات المعلومات كالامتناع وأمثاله ـ بأن يقول: لو حصلت الزوجية والفردية في الذهن لزم أن يكون الذهن زوجا وفردا؛ إذ لا معنى للزوج والفرد إلا ما حصل فيه الزوجية والفردية، وكذا لو حصل الامتناع في الذهن لزم أن يكون الذهن ممتنعا؛ إذ لا معنى للممتنع إلا ما حصل فيه الامتناع ـ لم يمكن التقصي عنه بهذا الجواب؛ إذ لا يشترط أن يقال كون محل الزوجية موصوفا بها من أحكامها المتعلقة بوجودها العيني، وكذا تضادها مع الفردية إنما هو في الوجود العيني دون الظلي؛ إذ لا وجود عينيا لأمثالهما، لأنها من لوازم الماهيات. وكذا الكلام في الامتناع وأمثاله؛ إلا لا يمكن أن يقال كون محل الامتناع موصوفا به من أحكامه المتعلقة بوجوده العيني؛ إذ لا يتصور له وجود عيني.

I say: this deserves examination. That answer is confined to cases in which the opponent claims that the mind is qualified by externally existing attributes, such as heat and cold. It does not remove the root of the difficulty. The opponent could appeal instead to consequences of quiddities, such as evenness and oddness, or attributes of known objects, such as impossibility. If evenness and oddness occur in the mind, the mind must be even and odd, since those terms mean what has evenness and oddness in it. Similarly, if impossibility occurs in the mind, the mind must be impossible, since an impossible thing means what has impossibility in it. That answer cannot evade this. One cannot stipulate that the subject of evenness is qualified by it only through its concrete existence, or that its opposition to oddness holds only in concrete rather than shadow-like existence. Such attributes have no concrete existence, since they are consequences of quiddities. The same applies to impossibility: one cannot treat the subject's qualification by impossibility as a property tied to its concrete existence, since no concrete existence of impossibility can be conceived.

The printed phrase إلا لا يمكن أن يقال is awkward in its negative context; translation follows the argument’s explicit denial of concrete existence. Retain the Arabic for review; no conjectural emendation asserted. | A substantive criticism by Qūshjī, rather than the voice of the preceding reported answer.

C31Q04 — The decisive answer: presence is different from inherence

ʿAlī al-Qūshjī · Qūshjī I, printed/PDF p.130, complete paragraph beginning والجواب الحاسم

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

والجواب الحاسم لمادة الشبهة هو الفرق بين الحصول في الذهن والقيام به؛ فإن حصول الشيء في الذهن لا يوجب اتصاف الذهن به، كما أن حصول الشيء في المكان لا يوجب اتصاف المكان بالمتمكن به، وكذا الحصول في الزمان فإنه لا يوجب اتصاف الزمان بالحاصل فيه، وإنما الموجب لاتصاف شيء بشيء هو قيامه به لا حصوله فيه، وهذه الأشياء ـ أعني: الحرارة والبرودة والزوجية والفردية والامتناع وأمثالها ـ إنما هي حاصلة في الذهن لا قائمة به، فلم يجب اتصاف الذهن بها، وإنما كانت توجب اتصاف الذهن بها لو كانت قائمة به، وليس كذلك.

The answer that removes the root of the difficulty is the distinction between being present in the mind and inhering in it. A thing's presence in the mind does not require the mind to be qualified by it, just as a thing's presence in a place does not require that place to be qualified by what occupies it. Nor does presence in time require time to be qualified by what occurs in it. What requires one thing to be qualified by another is the latter's inherence in it, rather than its mere presence in it. These things—heat, cold, evenness, oddness, impossibility, and the like—are present in the mind rather than inhering in it. The mind therefore need not be qualified by them. They would require that qualification only if they inhered in it, which they do not.

Q11 Definition, proof, and explanatory demonstration

When is an argument merely inferential (innī), when explanatory (limmī), and what qualifies as a demonstration?

Knowing that something is so is not always the same as knowing why it is so. Demonstration requires conditions on premises, inference and the explanatory middle. This differs from the claim that every valid inference must be a strictly scientific demonstration, and from the claim that direct knowledge by presence is a defective syllogism.

The logical discipline

Quṭb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī describes the middle term joining premises and insists on the greater intelligibility of definitions. These are technical rules that help diagnose where the explanatory link sits.

This is neither an inference nor a demonstration in the technical terminology of logic. Certainly, if one argued from the Necessary Existent to His attributes and effects, it would be a demonstration through the reason why (limmī). This accords with the Philosopher's statement that the way of the truthful is to take Him as witness for other things, rather than to infer Him from other things. The author [Ṭūsī] follows this course in his book by arguing from the necessity of God's existence to His attributes. [Ibn Sīnā, quoted from al-Mabdaʾ wa-l-maʿād:] 'We established the Necessary Existent neither by way of His acts nor by way of His motion. Thus this inference was neither an indication nor a pure demonstration. No pure demonstration proves the First; rather, our reasoning was akin to a demonstration, because it argued from the state of existence that existence requires something necessary.' [Ṭihrānī:] I say: The commentator called it a limmī inference—that is, a demonstration—only because it resembles one, as the Philosopher himself put it. [Lāhījī, quoted from the Shawāriq:] What makes this route like a limmī demonstration is what the Philosopher indicated: the Necessary can be established by this reasoning even if He had effected nothing and no effect had appeared from Him. Inferential demonstrations (innī) proceed from acts and effects, unlike limmī demonstrations. Since this path does not start from effects, it resembles a limmī proof; but since it does not start from a cause, it is not one.

Q12 Individuation, unity, and relational categories

What individuates a substance, and are unity, plurality, relation and causality real features or second intelligibles?

A father is father only relative to a child; “father” cannot be a free-standing external item unrelated to its correlate. But not every reciprocal relational description entails a separate real accident. Unity likewise may be conceived of actual beings without adding a new independent substance called unity. The issue therefore combines the analysis of categories with the status of relational predicates.

Ṭūsī on unity and relational categories

The matn distinguishes the one and the many and treats many relations and unity as second intelligibles, then places reciprocity among the characteristic properties of relations.

This should not be deduced from an unrelated passage on mental existence.

Unity analysed by al-Ḥillī

Al-Ḥillī develops the claim that unity and plurality as predicates are intellectual considerations, using the difficulty of making unity itself a further external entity.
