Can successive existences nevertheless constitute one enduring individual?

Objection against succession of existences

Lāhījī argues that, if successive existence-instances are potential during motion, the moving essence never has the actual existence required to be a mover. The reply requires an account of identity across ontological renewal, not just the image of intensifying heat.

Ṭūsī’s lemma “Its existence is self-evident.” Having explained the concept of motion through one of its properties—namely, its being a perfection of a body under that qualification—the author states that its existence is self-evident and requires no demonstration. Know that a body which, for example, successively occupies several spatial positions has a condition, namely succession and change with respect to place. There is no doubt that this condition actually obtains for the body in external reality as long as it is between its starting point and terminus. This condition is called ‘motion as being-in-transit’ [al-ḥaraka al-tawassuṭiyya], and it is this whose existence is self-evident. In virtue of this condition, the body has relations to the intermediate boundaries between the starting point and terminus. These relations are plainly multiple and distinct, corresponding to the possible divisions of the distance. It was already explained that the body occurs at each of these intermediate boundaries without either resting or moving at that boundary. Nevertheless, these occurrences can be retained in imagination, one after another, in order and by stages, so that something extended is produced in imagination from them. This extended thing, produced from the occurrences related to those boundaries, is called ‘motion as traversal’ [al-ḥaraka al-qaṭʿiyya]. It exists in imagination, not in external reality, because the relations do not exist externally. Thus the body's being between the starting point and terminus exists externally when its relation to the intermediate boundaries is not considered; when that relation is considered, it does not exist externally but exists in imagination. Reason analogously concerning motion in the other categories.

Compare Q17 on matter’s identity and Q20 on the soul’s development.

Interim judgment: The lesson is to distinguish the metaphysics of an undergoing subject, the temporal structure of change and the intellect’s or imagination’s synthetic representation. The inherited evidence is strong for the distinction but not yet for a complete theory of intrinsic potency and act.

Boundary: The title “continuity of motion” cannot substitute for the missing proofs of continuity, potentiality, and the contrary theories of motion.

Remaining: Collate Ṭūsī’s underlying physical passages and commentators, then include Ibn Sīnā’s motion and Ṣadrā’s substantial motion as parallel rather than direct Tajrīd glosses.

Q19 Origination, eternity, and causal necessity

Does metaphysical contingency entail a temporal beginning, and how do substantial generation and perpetual preservation interact?

A world may be argued to be contingent in existence without that argument already proving that it began at some finite past time. Conversely, a proof of temporal origination may depend on a theory of atoms, accidents, free choice or temporal succession. The present question therefore separates the mode of being caused from the chronology of a caused world.

The beginning/necessity distinction

The argument of Q13 makes contingency the reason for needing a cause. It cannot be turned directly into a demonstration of temporal beginning. Temporal origination appears at another explanatory level.

The distinction blocks an invalid shortcut both for philosophical eternalists and for proponents of temporal creation.

Al-Taftāzānī’s objection to a necessitarian premise

Al-Taftāzānī rejects an argument that presupposes an eternal Maker must produce by necessity of nature. A voluntary agent can bring about a temporal effect when willing it.

Q20 Soul, faculties, imagination, and acquired perfection

Which cognitional operations belong to the soul, to an organ, or to an instrument, and can repeated activity perfect an intrinsic capacity?

The soul’s definition as first perfection is not equivalent to declaring it a material form in the body. Its faculties include sensation, representation, intellect, desire and volition; these can operate through bodily instruments, while intellectual understanding invites a further claim about immateriality. A *malaka* is an acquired capacity, not the momentary occurrence of one cognitive act.

The soul as a first perfection of an organic body

Al-Ḥillī begins from the standard account of the soul as the first perfection of an organic natural body. A definition of soul through its operation on a body is not yet a proof of its immateriality.

فإن ما يجد الإنسان من نفسه عند عرض المسائل علم بالقوة يجد من نفسه ملكة وقدرة على الجواب لهذه المسائل المذكورة. وهذه القوة أقرب إلى الوجود مما كانت، أي من القوة التي كانت قبل السؤال، فإن للقوة مراتب بحسب البعد والقرب من الوجود، ولا يكون للإنسان علما بجواب كل واحد من تلك المسائل على الخصوص ما لم يكن عنده صورة كل واحد واحد. وواجب الوجود منزه عن هذه الأشياء: حلول الصورة فيه، وكون علمه بالقوة، فلا يكون علمه بالموجودات على الوجه المذكور.

What someone discovers within himself when questions are put to him is knowledge in potency: he finds a habitual disposition and capacity to answer those questions. This potency is nearer actuality than before the question was posed, since potencies have degrees according to their remoteness from, or nearness to, existence. But one does not have distinct knowledge of the answer to every single one of those questions unless one possesses its particular form. The Necessary Existent is exempt from all these features: the inherence of a form within Him and the possession of knowledge only potentially. His knowledge of existents cannot take the form just described.

The passage distinguishes (a) potency prior to being asked, (b) acquired readiness/habit (malaka, qudra), and (c) determinate actual knowledge. 'Quwwa' here is cognitive potency, and 'qudra' the capacity to answer, not the same technical meaning. Compare with Suhrawardī base text and Shahrāzūrī before attributing the wording of each lemma to Quṭb. The preceding passage on p. 349 argues that actual knowledge of a necessary concomitant is not automatically the actual knowledge of what it entails.

Q21 Final causality, providence, and the good

Can ends account for natural operations and divine providence without making God act to obtain something He lacks?

Final causes can explain why a maker acts or why a natural process occurs, but the end may be conceptually prior to an act while becoming actual only afterward. Applied to God this structure becomes controversial: if a divine act serves a purpose, does God acquire some perfection from it, or can there be wisdom and benefit without need?

The efficient/final order

Al-Ḥillī explains how the envisaged end moves the agent before the action while the achieved end follows it in existence. This distinguishes priority in explanation from priority in time.

T10 — How a final cause can be prior and posterior

al-Ḥillī · Al-ʿAllāma al-Ḥillī | Kashf al-murād, ed. Āmulī, p. 198, discussion of the final cause. | Arabic source: https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/3439/198?lang=ar

قال: والغاية علة بماهيتها لعلية العلة الفاعلية، معلولة في وجودها للمعلول. أقول: الغاية لها اعتباران يحصل لها باعتبارهما التقدم والتأخر بالنسبة إلى المعلول؛ وذلك لأن الفاعل إذا تصور الغاية فعل الفعل ثم حصلت الغاية بحصول الفعل. فماهية الغاية علة لعلية الفاعل؛ إذ لولا تلك الماهية وحصولها في علم الفاعل لما أثر ولا فعل الفعل. فإن الفاعل للبيت يتصور الاستكنان أولًا فيتحرك إلى إيجاد البيت، ثم يوجد الاستكنان بحصول البيت. فماهية الاستكنان علة لعلية الفاعل ووجوده معلول للبيت؛ ولا امتناع في أن يكون الشيء الواحد متقدمًا ومتأخرًا باعتبارين.

Ṭūsī says: “The end [الغاية], in respect of its quiddity, is the cause of the efficient cause's being a cause; in respect of its existence, it is an effect of what is produced.” I say: An end has two aspects, by virtue of which it is prior and posterior to the effect. The agent first conceives the end, acts, and only then does the end come to exist when the action has produced its result. Thus the quiddity of the end is a cause of the efficient cause's causal activity: without that quiddity and its occurrence in the agent's knowledge, the agent would not bring about the action. Someone building a house first conceives shelter, then proceeds to construct the house; when the house exists, shelter comes to be available. The quiddity of shelter thus explains the agent's activity, while shelter's existence is consequent upon the house. There is no impossibility in the same thing being prior and posterior in two different respects.

TRANSLATOR’S NOTE “Cause” changes explanatory sense across the sentence: an end as conceived can motivate the productive action, while the end's realization follows the completed product. This is not an argument that every agent, including God, acts to gain a perfection.

Without the distinction, final causes appear self-contradictory.

A shared causal classification

The explanatory tradition surrounding the *Mawāqif* agrees that the final cause is “for whose sake” a thing is produced and that it is produced as a result in external order. The explicit source is indexed under Q15.

Interim judgment: The dispute is over the precise meaning of an end as an explanatory cause. Human builders act to gain goods; divine action cannot be explained by God’s deficient state seeking completion. Whether real finality belongs to created natures and divine providence remains a further substantive question.

Boundary: Aquinas’s account of God as the end of creatures is a useful later comparison, not a substitute for the full kalām objections and their internal replies.

Remaining: Collate original later glosses within Sharḥ al-Mawāqif, Qūshjī, and Lāhījī; add direct Sunni accounts of divine purpose.

Q22 Divine simplicity, emanation, and the one-from-one rule

Can an absolutely simple First explain multiple differentiated effects, and what is the force of relational or conceptual multiplicity?

The “one from one” principle is easily misstated as “anything causes only one thing.” The philosopher’s stronger formulation concerns what proceeds from an utterly simple cause insofar as it is one, without other conditions or differentiating respects. Critics ask whether these qualifications rescue the proof or presuppose the conclusion; and whether a freely choosing agent falls under it at all.

The initial direct commentary

Al-Ḥillī connects Ṭūsī’s statement about the one cause to the First Intellect and the explanation of derivative multiplicity through relations. What counts as a sufficient differentiating respect remains the question.

T12 — The First Intellect and the failure of merely relational multiplicity

al-Ḥillī · Al-ʿAllāma al-Ḥillī | Kashf al-murād, ed. Āmulī, pp. 174–175, continuous passage across the page break. | Arabic source: https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/3439/174?lang=ar

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

قال: ثم تعرض الكثرة باعتبار كثرة الإضافات. أقول: لما بيّن أن العلة الواحدة لا يصدر عنها إلا معلول واحد، لزم أن تكون الموجودات بأسرها في سلسلة واحدة، بحيث يكون أي موجود فرضته علة لأي موجود فرضته أو معلولًا له، إما قريبة أو بعيدة، فلا يوجد شيئان يستغني أحدهما عن الآخر، والوجود يكذب هذا. فأوجبوا وقوع كثرة في المعلول الأول غير حقيقية بل إضافية يمكن أن يتكثر بها التأثير. قالوا: لأن المعلول الأول بالنظر إلى ذاته ممكن، وبالنظر إلى علته واجب، وله ماهية ووجود مستفاد من فاعله، وهو يعقل ذاته لتجرده ويعقل مبدأه؛ وهذه جهات كثيرة إضافية يقع بها التكثر ولا تثلم وحدته، ويصدر عنه باعتبار كل جهة شيء. وهذا الكلام عندنا في غاية السقوط، لأن هذه الجهات لا تصلح للتأثير؛ لأنها أمور اعتبارية ومساوية لغيرها ولا تكون شروطًا فيه.

Ṭūsī says: “Multiplicity then supervenes by reason of a multiplicity of relations [الإضافات].” I say: Once it had been established that only one effect proceeds from one cause, it would follow that all existing things formed a single chain, so that any two things whatever would stand to one another as cause and effect, directly or indirectly. There could then be no two things independent of one another. But actuality contradicts this. The philosophers therefore posited a multiplicity in the first effect—not a real multiplicity, but one of relations—through which its causal activity could be diversified. They say that the first effect is possible [ممكن] when considered in itself but necessary [واجب] in relation to its cause; it possesses a quiddity and an existence received from its agent; and, being immaterial, it knows itself and its principle. These form a multiplicity of relational respects that do not compromise its unity, and from each respect something proceeds. We regard this argument as profoundly unsatisfactory. These respects are incapable of exercising causal influence: they are merely conceptual considerations [أمور اعتبارية], comparable to other such considerations, and cannot function as conditions of the effect.

TRANSLATOR’S NOTE This is a targeted criticism of the proposed transition from the First Intellect to the multiplicity of the cosmos; it is not by itself a formal proof against every possible one-from-one principle. The extensive metaphysical footnote in the Āmulī edition is the modern editor's, not al-Ḥillī's.

Qūshjī reconstructs and contests the inference

Qūshjī isolates the absolute-unity hypothesis, notes the exception claimed for a voluntary agent with multiple acts of willing, reproduces an argument from differing respects of sourcehood, and turns that argument against its own concept of sourcehood.

T13 — The scope of the rule and a challenge to its demonstration

al-Qūshjī · ʿAlī al-Qūshjī | Sharḥ al-Tajrīd, ed. al-Zāriʿī al-Riḍāʾī, vol. I, printed pp. 570–571 (selected opening and response). | Arabic source: https://archive.org/details/charhTajridKochaji

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

قال: ومع وحدته يتحد المعلول. أقول: الفاعل إذا كان واحدًا في ذاته، ولم يكن له صفة، ولم يكن فعله مشروطًا بأمر، لم يجز عند الحكماء أن يصدر عنه أكثر من واحد، خلافًا لأكثر المتكلمين. وقد يزعم أن عدم جواز ذلك في الموجب بالذات وجوازه في الفاعل المختار، وكلاهما متفق عليه، وإنما النزاع بينهم في أن المبدأ الأول موجب أو مختار. والحق أن الفاعل المختار إذا تعددت إراداته أو تعلقاتها، على ما ذهب إليه المتكلمون، كان خارجًا عما نحن بصدده، إذ فيه كثرة باعتبار تعدد إراداته أو تعلقاتها، فلا يكون واحدًا من كل الوجوه. احتج الحكماء بوجوه: الأول: لو كان الواحد الحقيقي مصدرًا لأمرين كانت مصدريته لهذا غير مصدريته لذاك؛ فإن كان كل واحد منهما نفس الواحد الحقيقي كان لأمر واحد حقيقتان مختلفتان، وإن دخل فيه واحد منهما لزم التركيب، فلم يكن واحدًا من جميع الوجوه. [... حذف هنا فرع من البرهان يتعلق بفرض خروج الجهتين عن الذات ...] وأجيب تارة بالنقض، وتقريره أنه لو تم هذا الدليل لزم مثله في صفة المصدريّة؛ فإنا نقول: لو صدر عن الواحد الحقيقي شيء، فمصدريته لذلك الشيء أمر مغاير له، لكونه نسبة بين غيرين، فهو إما داخل فيه فيلزم تركيبه، أو خارج عنه معلول له، فتنتقل المسألة إلى مصدرية هذه النسبة، حتى يتسلسل.

Ṭūsī says: “When the cause is one, its effect is one.” I say: If an agent is one in its essence, has no [additional] attribute, and its activity is not conditional upon anything else, the philosophers hold that more than one effect cannot proceed from it. Most theologians disagree. One might claim that its impossibility in the case of an agent acting by the necessity of its nature [الموجب بالذات], and its possibility in the case of a voluntary agent [الفاعل المختار], are both agreed upon, and that the real dispute is simply whether the First Principle is necessary or voluntary. The correct point is that a voluntary agent whose acts of will or their objects are multiple, as the theologians maintain, falls outside the present case. Such an agent has multiplicity in respect of its acts of will or their relations, and so is not one in every respect. The philosophers offer several proofs. The first is this: if something absolutely one were the source of two effects, its being-source of the first [مصدريته لهذا] would differ from its being-source of the second. If each were identical with the absolutely one, the same thing would have two distinct realities; but if either entered into its constitution, composition would follow, and it would not be absolutely one. [The further alternative, where the respects are external to the First, is omitted here.] One response is to turn the argument back upon its own notion of sourcehood [المصدرية]. If the demonstration were valid, the same problem would arise with the cause's being-a-source: when something proceeds from what is absolutely one, its sourcehood for that effect is a relational property differing from it, since it is a relation between two distinct things. This property must either enter into the cause—entailing composition—or be an effect external to it. In the latter case we must ask about the cause's sourcehood of that relation, and so on without end.

TRANSLATOR’S NOTE Qūshjī does not simply replace the philosophical thesis with a bare denial. He first narrows the condition of “one in every respect”, including the possibility of multiple willing-relations, and then exposes a regress problem in the first proposed demonstration. The paragraph is one stage in a larger dispute. A bracketed editorial ellipsis marks an omitted alternative in the philosophers’ initial proof, rather than representing the response as immediately adjacent in the original. This selection does not imply a final verdict on the whole principle.

The disagreement is about the proof, its scope, and what counts as an independent source of differentiation.

Lāhījī qualifies the principle

Lāhījī insists on unity from every respect and discusses whether freedom or necessity, as differently construed, changes the conclusion. His defence is neither a trivial proposition nor a demonstration of the entire Neoplatonic sequence.

T14 — A qualified defence of the one-from-one principle

al-Lāhījī · ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Lāhījī | Shawāriq al-ilhām, ed. Asad ʿAlīzāda, vol. II, printed pp. 295–297 (excerpt through the Avicennian formulation). | Arabic source: https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/14865/296?lang=ar

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

قال: ومع وحدته يتحد المعلول. أقول: ومنها أن الفاعل المستقل إذا كان واحدًا من جميع الجهات، بحيث لا يكون فيه كثرة الأجزاء، ولا كثرة الوجود والماهية، ولا يكون متصفًا بصفة حقيقية زائدة في الخارج أو اعتبارية زائدة في العقل، ولا يتوقف فعله على شرط وآلة وقابل؛ فلا يمكن أن يصدر عنه في مرتبة واحدة إلا معلول واحد، على ما ذهب إليه الحكماء خلافًا للمتكلمين. وإليه أشار بقوله «ومع وحدته يتحد المعلول»، سواء كان الفاعل موجبًا أو مختارًا اختياره وإرادته نفس ذاته؛ والحكماء يسمون لمثل هذا المختار الفاعل بالرضا. وأما إذا كانت إرادته واختياره زائدة على ذاته، وهو الذي يسمونه الفاعل بالقصد، فهو خارج عما نحن فيه؛ لأن فيه اثنينيّة بالفعل، سواء تعددت إرادته أو تعلقها أو لا، فلا يكون واحدًا من جميع الجهات. وأما بيان ذلك فقال الشيخ في الإشارات: «تنبيه: مفهوم أن علة ما بحيث تجب عنها أ غير مفهوم أن علة ما بحيث يجب عنها ب». وإذا كان الواحد يجب عنه شيئان، فمن حيثيتين مختلفتي المفهوم مختلفتي الحقيقة، فإما أن يكونا من مقوماته، أو من لوازمه، أو بالتفريق.

Ṭūsī says: “When the cause is one, its effect is one.” I say: Among the principles is this: if an independently acting cause is one in every respect—containing neither a plurality of parts nor a plurality of existence and quiddity, possessing no real additional attribute outside the mind or additional conceptual attribute in the intellect, and having an act that does not depend on a condition, instrument, or recipient—then only one effect can proceed from it at a single level. This is the philosophers' view, against that of the theologians. This is what Ṭūsī indicates when he says that unity of cause entails unity of effect. It applies whether the agent acts necessarily or acts voluntarily with a choice and will identical with its essence. Philosophers call the latter kind an agent acting by satisfaction or approval [الفاعل بالرضا]. If, by contrast, its will and choice are additional to its essence—the type they call an agent acting by intention [الفاعل بالقصد]—it falls outside the issue. Such an agent contains an actual duality, whether or not its acts of will or their objects are multiple, and is not one in every respect. For its demonstration, Avicenna says in the Ishārāt: “The concept of a cause insofar as A necessarily proceeds from it is different from the concept of a cause insofar as B necessarily proceeds from it.” If two things necessarily proceed from what is one, they do so through two distinct respects, distinct in concept and in reality. These must either constitute the cause, be among its concomitants, or be distributed between the two.

TRANSLATOR’S NOTE This passage is a qualified rather than indiscriminate endorsement. The logical condition of the rule excludes a purportedly simple source with an additional willing-state, instrumental condition, or receptive substrate. The quotation from Avicenna is translated here as reported by Lāhījī, not independently collated against a critical Ishārāt edition.

Its compatibility with divine freedom remains disputed.

The Qūnawī–Ṭūsī exchange

Qūnawī challenges how relational multiplicity could explain real differentiation without partitioning the First and considers one effused existence with numerous determinations. Ṭūsī answers that conceptual and negative considerations can differentiate explanatory respects without multiplying the First Essence.

A9 — Qūnawī challenges the explanatory work of distinctions in the First Intellect

al-Qūnawī · Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Qūnawī · Question 4 (first critical paragraph, selected)

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

المسألة الرابعة: الواحد لا يصدر عنه إلا واحد. هذه المسألة يتفرع عليها من أمهات المسائل مسائل شتى كمسألة العقول وعلّة ترتيبها وعلّة صدور الكثرة من العقل الأوّل المشهود له بالوحدة وجعل الاعتبارات المفروضة فيه علّة لصدور الكثرة منه أو جزء علّة هذا مع وجوب اعترافهم بأنّ تلك الاعتبارات ليست بأمور وجودية. فإنهم لو لم يعترفوا بذلك، لزمهم الإقرار بصدور الكثرة من الحقّ، لأنّ الصادر منه على هذا التقدير العقل الأول واعتباراته الثلاثة أو إثبات أنّ تلك الاعتبارات مع كونها ليست بأمور وجودية يجب أن تكون علّة لوجود الكثرة. وكل ذلك محال.

Fourth question: “From one, only one proceeds” [الواحد لا يصدر عنه إلا واحد]. From this foundational question many other questions branch out: those concerning the intellects, the cause of their ordered arrangement, and the cause of the emergence of multiplicity from the First Intellect, which is acknowledged to be one. Among them is the making of the various considerations [الاعتبارات] posited in that intellect into causes, or partial causes, of multiplicity proceeding from it. Yet the philosophers must concede that these considerations are not existential realities. If they do not concede this, they must admit that multiplicity proceeds from the Real, for what issues from Him would then be the First Intellect together with its three considerations. Alternatively they must maintain that considerations which are not existential realities can nevertheless be causes of real multiplicity. All this is impossible.

READING NOTE Qūnawī attacks an explanatory transition: from different descriptions or relations of one intellect to numerically different produced realities. Whether such relations are extramental, conceptual, or causally relevant is the issue. | Arabic source: https://www.ibnalarabi.com/qunawi/tusi.php?id=5

ونحن نقول لهم: إذ قد اعترفتم بأنّ الماهيات غير مجعولة وليست بأمور وجودية والوجود المشترك بين جميع الماهيات واحد مع التحقق بأنّ المسمّى عالما ليس بأمر زائد على ماهيات متّصفة بوجود واحد يشترك فيه العقل وغيره، فلم لا يجوز أن يكون ذلك الأمر الواحد الصادر من الحق الواحد هو هذا الوجود العام المشترك، ويدخل فيه العقل الأول وغيره، وتكون الموجودات بأجمعها مرتبطة بالحق لا بالسلسلة المذكورة، وتكون العقول وكلّ ما يسمّى واسطة شروطا يحصل الفعل الإيجادي عندها بالوجود الواحد الفائض من الحق؟ فالوسائط معدّات بمعنى أنها توجب تعيّن الاستعدادات الجزئية بواسطة الوجود. والحق هو المفيض، كما ذهبوا إليه في الأسباب السفلية من أنها تعدّ، والفعّال يفيض. ويظهر إذ ذاك أنّ تعلّق العلم الإلهي بالأشياء هو على النحو الكلي والتفصيلي معا من جهة الوجود الواحد المشترك لا من جهة العلل واللوازم، كما ذكر.

We say to them: since you have acknowledged that quiddities are unmade, that they are not existential realities, and that the existence common to all quiddities is one—and since what is called “the world” is nothing over and above quiddities qualified by one existence shared by the First Intellect and everything else—why should it not be permissible that the one thing proceeding from the One Real be precisely this common universal existence, embracing the First Intellect and the others? All existents would then be connected to the Real, not merely through the chain just described. The intellects and whatever else is called an intermediary would be conditions in the presence of which the productive act takes place through the one existence overflowing from the Real. Intermediaries would be preparers [معدّات], in the sense that they bring about the determination of particular receptivities through existence. The Real is the one who bestows [المفيض], just as the philosophers themselves say of lower causes that they prepare while the Agent bestows. It would then become evident that divine knowledge relates to things both universally and in detail, by virtue of the one common existence—not merely by way of causes and their consequences, as they claimed.

READING NOTE Here the word “common” belongs to Qūnawī’s proposal; Ṭūsī’s Question-3 reply challenges its interpretation as an extramental universal. Note the difference between a preparatory condition [مُعِدّ] and the agent that bestows existence [مفيض]. | Arabic source: https://www.ibnalarabi.com/qunawi/tusi.php?id=5

A11 — Ṭūsī: one from one in one respect

al-Ṭūsī · Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī · Reply to Question 4 (opening argument)

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

أقول: إني أبيّن ما فهمت من كلامهم. فإن كان موافقا لما عليه الأمر، فذلك وإن لم يكن، فلا عجب في مثل هذه المضائق أن تزلّ قدمي، كما زلّ أقدام كثير من العقلاء. فقولهم: الواحد لا يصدر عنه إلا الواحد، مرادهم أنه لا يصدر عنه باعتبار واحد إلا واحد، وذلك أنهم يجوّزون أن يصدر عن الواحد أشياء كثيرة باعتبارات مختلفة، كما أنّ الواحد تكون له النصفية باعتبار الاثنين معه، والثلثية باعتبار الثلاثة معه، وعدم الانقسام باعتبار وحدته لا غير. ولمّا كان المبدأ الأول عندهم واحدا من كل الوجوه، كان معرفة الوجه في صدور الكثير منه محتاجا إلى لطف قريحة.

I shall explain what I have understood of their statements. If it accords with things as they are, so much the better; if not, it is hardly surprising that my foot should slip in difficulties of this kind, just as many intelligent people have slipped. By “from one, only one proceeds,” they mean that from it, **under one consideration** [باعتبار واحد], only one proceeds. They allow many things to proceed from a single thing under different considerations. Thus something one is a half in relation to two, a third in relation to three, and indivisible when considered simply in its unity. Since, according to them, the First Principle is one in every respect, explaining how multiplicity proceeds from it requires great subtlety of thought.

READING NOTE The emphatic restriction “under one consideration” is essential. Without it the formulation seems immediately contradicted by every ordinary agent with multiple effects. Ṭūsī next offers a combinatorial example, not reproduced in this selection. | Arabic source: https://www.ibnalarabi.com/qunawi/tusi.php?id=5

وقد ظهر أنّ هذه الاعتبارات ليست مفروضة وليست بعلّة تامة لشيء. إنما هي اعتبارات انضافت إلى مبدأ واحد. فتكثر بسببها معلولاته. ولا يجب كون الاعتبارات أمورا وجودية عينية، بل يكفي كونها عقلية، فإنّ الفاعل الواحد قد يفعل بسبب اختلاف أمور عقلية أو عدمية أفعالا كثيرة.

It has become clear that these considerations are not mere arbitrary suppositions, nor are they complete causes [علل تامة] of anything. They are considerations attaching to one principle, in consequence of which its effects become multiple. These considerations need not be concrete extramental realities [أمور وجودية عينية]; it suffices that they be intellectual. A single agent can perform many acts on account of differences that are intellectual or privative [عدمية].

The important concession is that an explanatory difference is not necessarily an additional concrete constituent. | Arabic source: https://www.ibnalarabi.com/qunawi/tusi.php?id=5

One must assess whether conceptual distinctions can bear the requested causal weight.

Interim judgment: There are two principal opposed strategies: real differentiating principles in secondary effects and intellectually distinguished respects grounded in the source or its relation to what proceeds. Qūnawī’s alternative shifts what counts as the “one” first effect. A coherent reading cannot infer either the universal First Intellect scheme or a doctrine of one diffused existence from the short rule alone.

Boundary: The full Dawwānī–Dashtakī response chain is still missing. A late editor’s Akbarī note attached to al-Ḥillī must not be mislabelled as al-Ḥillī’s own position.

Remaining: Map every objection/reply of the direct commentaries, the Qūnawī correspondence, and Shīrāzī’s doctrines of causation and multiplicity.

Q23 The Necessary: existence, essence and proof

Does the dependence of all contingent things entail a Necessary Existent, and can the proof avoid treating a group as a separate caused object?

Ṭūsī offers several anti-regress arguments. Al-Ḥillī questions the initial proof and separately reconstructs an argument from the totality. Dawwānī presents and tests the latter in detail, records al-Kātibī’s objections, and tries to establish the necessity of an unconditioned ground without circularity. These are distinct arguments and must not be merged.

Ṭūsī: several distinct proofs, not one

The initial proof from necessary causes and the totality argument are distinct Tajrīd lemmata (210 and 213). The former reasons that a chain of beings necessary through others needs an intrinsically necessary cause; the latter tests whether all causes of a totality could lie among its parts. Lemma 572 applies the anti-regress conclusion to proving a Maker.

ولا يتراقى معروضاهما في سلسلة واحدة إلى غير النهاية لأن كل واحد منها ممتنع الحصول بدون علة واجبة لكن الواجب بالغير ممتنع أيضا فيجب وجود علة لذاتها هي طرف.

Their subjects‎ [المعروض]‎ cannot ascend without end in a single series: no member can occur without a necessary cause‎ [العلة]‎, yet what is necessary through another cannot [occur without a cause] either. There must therefore be an intrinsically [necessary] cause that is an endpoint.

How could the whole be necessitated by something that itself depends on infinitely many members of that whole?

Before accepting either proof, ask whether the premise is independent of the conclusion.

Al-Ḥillī: a reservation and a separate totality proof

Al-Ḥillī records a reservation concerning the first proof, then sets out the totality proof: the collective is contingent, cannot cause itself, and supposedly cannot be caused by a member. His statement that the totality is possible because its members are possible is precisely the premise later scrutinized.

One candidate analysis treats the “totality” merely as several effects considered together; its explanation might then be several causes, without the further demand for a numerically single cause of the group.

Dawwānī reconstructs an opponent’s use of a complete efficient cause but warns that definitions of completeness and the role of constituents matter. The proof’s decisive point is ruling out a cause that is one of the collection’s parts.

Al-Kātibī’s objection and Dawwānī’s critique

Dawwānī reports al-Kātibī’s explicit challenge to the claim that the totality is caused by all its members. He then rejects the transfer from each part’s priority to the priority of all parts together; a group cannot become an efficient cause simply because each constituent bears some causal relation.

Distributive priority of individual parts does not automatically transfer to the plurality as a whole. EDITORIAL LIMIT: The conclusion is restricted to the transfer from distributive to collective predication.

Thus, at least one version of the collective proof fails unless its central mereological premise is supplied.

A distinct route: necessity through another is conditional

A causally sufficient thing may itself be caused, so sufficiency for an effect does not entail intrinsic necessity. Dawwānī instead treats necessity-through-another as a conditional: if the antecedent cause is posited, the consequent is required. Infinitely many such conditionals do not, merely by their number, posit an existing unconditioned antecedent.

A causally sufficient member may itself have a cause; this sufficiency alone does not establish intrinsic necessity. EDITORIAL LIMIT: Keep necessary-through-another distinct from Necessary-in-itself.

This supplies a fresh argument for why an actual contingent order calls for an unconditioned actuality, although its full formal validity remains to be tested.

The final anti-circularity check

Dawwānī challenges an argument that effectively defines dependence as dependence on the noncontingent. That already assumes the conclusion. The project must distinguish need, sufficiency, necessity-through-another, the actuality of the series, and intrinsic necessity.

published-page-checked short extract; no manuscript variants collated

وإن أريد عدم استقلاله في نوعه بمعنى أنه محتاج إلى ما لا يكون ممكنا فهو أول المسألة

The absence of ontological self-sufficiency establishes dependence, but it is not identical to proving a terminal noncontingent cause. EDITORIAL LIMIT: Do not smuggle the existence of a Necessary Being into the definition of the contingent.

Only now do the broader comparison with al-Rāzī, Taftāzānī, and Aquinas, and the ontological question of manifestation (Q27), become meaningful.

Separate theological and mystical extensions

Ṭūsī’s divine-existence lemma, the direct Qūnawī–Ṭūsī exchange, and Jāmī’s later argument need to be read after the demonstrations. The existence of a first cause alone does not establish identity of created and divine being or an Akbarī account of manifestation.

A8 — Ṭūsī: necessary existence is not the common mental universal

al-Ṭūsī · Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī · Conclusion of Reply to Question 3 (complete final paragraph)

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

الفرق هو أنّ وجود الحق عيني، ليس له وجود عارض له، والوجود العام عقلي، لا يتحقق في غير العقل، ويكون له وجود آخر عارض له، إذا اعتبر كونه في العقل. والحق الذي لا مرية فيه أنّ واجب الوجود لذاته لا يمكن أن يكون إلا شيء عينيّ وجوده عين ذاته، ولا يمكن أن يكون الموصوف بهذه الصفة إلا واحدا من كل جهة واجبا من كلّ اعتبار.

The difference is that the existence of the Real is extramental [عيني]: no further existence inheres in it. Universal existence is intellectual [عقلي]; it obtains only in the intellect, and when considered as being in the intellect it has a further existence inhering in it. The indubitable truth is that what is necessary in existence through itself [واجب الوجود لذاته] can only be an extramental reality whose existence is identical with its essence [ذات]. Only one can have this characteristic: one in every respect, necessary from every consideration.

READING NOTE Ṭūsī’s distinction between a mental universal and an extramental reality is not, without further argument, a complete reply to the Akbarī account of the one reality of existence, which need not treat “existence” as a universal genus. | Arabic source: https://www.ibnalarabi.com/qunawi/tusi.php?id=4

C2 — Jāmī’s argument from the reality of existence

Jāmī · ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Jāmī · al-Durra al-fākhira, section §18–19, printed p. 8 (selected)

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

فنقول: لا شكّ أنّ مبدأ الموجودات موجود، فلا يخلو إمّا أن يكون حقيقة الوجود أو غيره، لا جائز أن يكون غيره ضرورة احتياج غير الوجود في وجوده إلى غير هو الوجود، والاحتياج ينافي الوجوب، فتعيّن أن يكون حقيقة الوجود. فإن كان مطلقا ثبت المطلوب وإن كان متعيّنا يمتنع أن يكون التعيّن داخلا فيه وإلّا لتركّب الواجب، فتعيّن أن يكون خارجا. فالواجب محض ما هو الوجود والتعيّن صفة عارضة. فإن قلت: لم لا يجوز أن يكون التعيّن عينه؟ قلت: إن كان التعيّن بمعنى ما به التعيّن يجوز أن يكون عينه، لكن لا يضرّنا، فإنّ ما به تعيّنه، إذا كان ذاته، ينبغي أن يكون هو في نفسه غير متعيّن وإلّا تسلسل. وإن كان بمعنى التشخّص لا يجوز أن يكون عينه لأنّه من المعقولات الثانية الّتي لا يحاذى بها أمر في الخارج.

We say: there is no doubt that the principle of existents itself exists. It must therefore be either the very reality of existence [حقيقة الوجود] or something other than it. It cannot be something other than existence, because whatever is other than existence depends, for its existing, upon something distinct from itself—namely, existence—and dependence [الاحتياج] is incompatible with necessity [الوجوب]. Thus the principle must be the reality of existence. If it is unrestricted [مطلق], the desired conclusion follows. If it is determined [متعيّن], its determination cannot be an intrinsic constituent of it, since the Necessary would then be composite. The determination must therefore be external to it. The Necessary is sheer existence, and determination is an adventitious qualification. You may ask: why could its determination not be identical with it? I answer: if “determination” means *that by which* it is determined, it may be identical with it; but this does not harm our argument. For if the ground of its determination is its own essence, it must in itself be undetermined, on pain of an infinite regress. If, on the other hand, “determination” means individuation [التشخص], it cannot be identical with it; individuation is a second intelligible [معقول ثان] corresponding to no independent item in extramental reality.

READING NOTE A representative argumentative section, not an adequate substitute for the complete later objections and glosses. Compare Qūnawī’s common existence and Ṭūsī’s rejection of an extramental universal. An English translation by Nicholas Heer already exists (*The Precious Pearl*, 1979); this is an independent working rendering. | Arabic source: https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/9247/84?lang=ar

TIH06 — Ṭihrānī: the proof of the Necessary is neither strictly innī nor strictly limmī

Hāshim al-Ḥusaynī al-Ṭihrānī · Hāshim al-Ḥusaynī al-Ṭihrānī, Tawḍīḥ al-murād, I, 425; citations of Ibn Sīnā, al-Mabdaʾ wa-l-maʿād, and Lāhījī, Shawāriq.

New continuation: printed/digital text; manuscript collation pending

فليس هذا دليلا ولا برهانا على اصطلاح علم الميزان، نعم إذا استدل بالواجب الوجود على صفاته وآثاره لكان برهانا لميا كما يجيء في كلام الشيخ عن قريب أن طريقة الصديقين أنهم يستشهدون به لا عليه، أي يستشهدون بالواجب الوجود على غيره لا عليه بغيره، والمصنف رحمه الله تعالى سلك هذا المسلك في كتابه إذ هو استدل بوجوب وجوده على صفاته. قال الشيخ الرئيس في كتاب المبدأ والمعاد بعد الفراغ من تقرير هذا المنهج: أنا أثبتنا الواجب الوجود لا من جهة أفعاله ولا من جهة حركته، فلم يكن القياس (أي هذا القياس) دليلا ولا أيضا برهانا محضا، فالأول ليس عليه برهان محض، بل كان قياسا شبيها بالبرهان لأنه استدلال من حال الوجود أنه يقتضي واجبا الخ. أقول: فالشارح إنما أطلق عليه الاستدلال اللمي أي البرهان لأنه يشبه به كما وقع في كلام الشيخ. وقال صاحب الشوارق: إن وجه كون هذا الطريق أشبه بالبرهان أي اللمي هو ما أشار إليه الشيخ من أن الواجب وإن لم يفعل شيئا ولم يظهر منه أثر يمكن بهذا القياس أن يثبت، وذلك لأن القياسات الإنية إنما تكون من الأفعال والآثار بخلاف اللمية، فهذا الطريق لكونه لا من جهة الآثار يشبه اللم، ومن جهة أنه ليس من العلة ليس به.

This is neither an inference nor a demonstration in the technical terminology of logic. Certainly, if one argued from the Necessary Existent to His attributes and effects, it would be a demonstration through the reason why (limmī). This accords with the Philosopher's statement that the way of the truthful is to take Him as witness for other things, rather than to infer Him from other things. The author [Ṭūsī] follows this course in his book by arguing from the necessity of God's existence to His attributes. [Ibn Sīnā, quoted from al-Mabdaʾ wa-l-maʿād:] 'We established the Necessary Existent neither by way of His acts nor by way of His motion. Thus this inference was neither an indication nor a pure demonstration. No pure demonstration proves the First; rather, our reasoning was akin to a demonstration, because it argued from the state of existence that existence requires something necessary.' [Ṭihrānī:] I say: The commentator called it a limmī inference—that is, a demonstration—only because it resembles one, as the Philosopher himself put it. [Lāhījī, quoted from the Shawāriq:] What makes this route like a limmī demonstration is what the Philosopher indicated: the Necessary can be established by this reasoning even if He had effected nothing and no effect had appeared from Him. Inferential demonstrations (innī) proceed from acts and effects, unlike limmī demonstrations. Since this path does not start from effects, it resembles a limmī proof; but since it does not start from a cause, it is not one.

SPEAKER BREAKS: the 'Shaykh al-Raʾīs' is Ibn Sīnā, not the author of Tawḍīḥ; 'ṣāḥib al-Shawāriq' means Lāhījī. The challenge is rigorous: demonstrating that a necessary being must exist by examining existence differs from inferring a cause from its effects, yet is not a strict explanatory syllogism from a prior cause. فيكون الفرق بين هذا المذهب، ومذهب الحكماء: أنهم يخصون الواجبية بمرتبة واحدة؛ هي تلك الحقيقة بشرط أن لا يتعين بشيء من الماهيات. والصوفية يجعلون الواجبية لتلك الحقيقة؛ لا بشرط أن يتعين بشيء من الماهيات، فيكون كل حقيقة وجودية واجبة، إذا اعتبرت من حيث هي هي، مقطوعة النظر عن التعين، وممكنة باعتبار أخذها بشرط التعين، فيكون الممكنات في الحقيقة هي التعينات، والواجب هو الحقيقة المطلقة، فلا يلزم تعدد وتكثر فيما هو واجب، ولا كون شيء من الممكنات فردا للواجب، ولا حاجة إلى أن يقال: إن تلك الحقيقة غير متعينة في حد ذاتها؛ كالكلي الطبيعي، أو أنها متعينة بتعين؛ لا ينافي شيئا من التعينات، كما ارتكبوه ليرد عليه ما أشرنا إليه سابقا، بل هي متعينة بنفس ذاتها. وهذا التعين ينافي جميع التعينات، حيث يمتنع أن يؤثر فيها شيء من التعينات، ويقارنها مقارنة تأثير؛ كمقارنة العوارض المشخصة للماهيات، وإنما المقارنة التي للتعينات معها هي مقارنة تأثر وانفعال؛ منها كمقارنة المعلول للعلة.

The difference between this position and that of the philosophers would therefore be that the philosophers restrict necessity to one rank: that reality on condition that it is not determined by any quiddity. The Sufis ascribe necessity to that reality without stipulating its determination by any quiddity. Every existential reality, considered just as it is and apart from determination, would thus be necessary, while it would be contingent when taken under the condition of determination. The contingent things would in reality be the determinations, and the Necessary would be the unrestricted reality. Neither plurality in what is necessary nor any contingent thing's being an instance of the Necessary follows. There is no need to say that this reality is intrinsically undetermined, like the natural universal, or that it has a determination compatible with all determinations, as its interpreters proposed, thereby inviting our earlier objection. Rather, it is determined through its very essence. This determination excludes all [such other] determinations in the sense that none can affect it or accompany it as an affecting factor, as individuating accidents accompany quiddities. The determinations accompany it instead as things affected by it and receptive to it, as an effect accompanies its cause.

The restrictive clause explains ينافي: causal invulnerability, not an unqualified denial of any relation to determinations. | lā bi-sharṭ is being taken without a condition; bi-sharṭ lā imposes a negative condition.

C31L04 — The alternative argument: whatever differs from existence is dependent

ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Lāhījī reporting an alternative interpretation · Shawāriq I, printed p.464 to opening of 465; PDF pages 465–466; electronic p.471

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

وقد يوجه بحيث لا يلزم القول بالانبساط، ومخالطته مع التعينات، لعدم إمكان عروض الوجود الذي هو الواجب القائم بذاته لشيء من الماهيات. والدليل على كون الوجود هو الواجب: أن كل مفهوم مغاير لحقيقة الوجود كالإنسان مثلا، فإنه ما لم ينضم إليه الوجود بوجه من الوجوه في نفس الأمر لم يكن موجودا فيها قطعا، وما لم يلاحظ العقل انضمام الوجود إليه لم يمكن له الحكم بكونه موجودا. فكل مفهوم مغاير للوجود، فهو في كونه موجودا في نفس الأمر محتاج إلى غيره الذي هو الوجود، وكل ما هو محتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره فهو ممكن، إذ لا معنى للممكن إلا ما يحتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره، سواء كان ذلك الغير موجدا له أو وجودا له، وكل مفهوم مغاير للوجود ممكن، ولا شيء من الممكن بواجب، فلا شيء من المفهومات المغايرة للوجود بواجب. وقد ثبت بالبرهان أن الواجب موجود، فهو لا يكون إلا الوجود الذي هو موجود بذاته، ويستغني في كونه موجودا عن غير ذاته، وإن كان المتبادر من لفظ الموجود بحسب اللغة ما قام به الوجود، فإن المتبع هو ما أدى إليه البرهان لا غير.

It may also be interpreted without entailing that existence spreads or mingles with determinations, since the existence which is the self-subsisting Necessary cannot be an accident of any quiddity. The argument that existence is the Necessary is this. Any concept different from the reality of existence, such as “human,” certainly does not exist in objective actuality unless existence is joined to it in some manner. Unless the intellect considers existence joined to it, it cannot judge it to exist. Every concept different from existence therefore depends, for its existence in objective actuality, on something other than itself, namely existence. Whatever depends on another for being existent is contingent: a contingent is precisely what needs another in order to exist, whether that other produces it or is its existence. Every concept different from existence is contingent; nothing contingent is necessary; hence no concept different from existence is necessary. It has been demonstrated that the Necessary exists. It must therefore be existence, which exists through itself and needs nothing other than its essence in order to exist. Even if the linguistic sense first suggested by “existent” is something in which existence subsists, what must be followed is the result of demonstration alone.

This is the argument under report, not Lāhījī’s final endorsement. Nafs al-amr means objective actuality here.

C31L05 — Existence as a real particular; existent as a universal predicate

Lāhījī reporting al-Muḥaqqiq al-Sharīf and Dawwānī · Shawāriq I, printed p.465; PDF page 466; electronic p.472

Printed page image inspected; normalized Arabic transcription and fresh working translation

ولما وجب كون الواجب جزئيا حقيقيا متعينا بنفس ذاته، فإنما بذاته وجب أن يكون الوجود أيضا لكونه هو الواجب كذلك، فلا يكون الوجود مفهوما كليا ليمكن له أفراد، فهو جزئي حقيقي ليس فيه إمكان تعدد ولا انقسام، وقائم بذاته منزه عن كونه عارضا لغيره، فيكون الواجب هو الوجود المطلق؛ أي المعرى عن التقيد بغيره والانضمام إليه. وعلى هذا لا يتصور عروض الوجود للماهيات الممكنة، فليس معنى كونها موجودة إلا أن لها نسبة مخصوصة إلى حضرة الوجود القائم بذاته، وتلك النسبة على وجوه مختلفة وأنحاء شتى يتعذر الاطلاع على ماهياتها، فالموجود كلي وإن كان الوجود جزئيا حقيقيا. كذا ذكره المحقق الشريف ملخصا لما ذكره بعض محققي مشايخهم، وأنه قال: ولا يعلمه إلا الراسخون في العلم، وتبعه المحقق الدواني في اختيار هذا التوجيه، ونسبه إلى ذوق المتألهين. وهو إنما يناسب مذهب المتكلمين النافين لكون الوجود ذا أفراد حقيقية كما لا يخفى.

Since the Necessary must be a real particular determined through its own essence, existence too, because it is the Necessary, must be so. Existence would not be a universal concept capable of having instances, but a real particular incapable of multiplicity or division, subsisting through itself and exempt from being an accident of another. The Necessary would thus be unrestricted existence: existence stripped of restriction by, or conjunction with, anything else. On this account existence cannot be an accident of contingent quiddities. Their being existent means only that they have a specific relation to the presence of self-subsisting existence. This relation takes different forms and diverse modes whose quiddities cannot be apprehended. Thus “existent” is universal although “existence” is a real particular. Al-Muḥaqqiq al-Sharīf stated this as a summary of what one of their accomplished masters had said, adding that only those firmly rooted in knowledge know it. Al-Muḥaqqiq al-Dawwānī followed him in choosing this interpretation and attributed it to the “taste of the theosophers” [dhawq al-mutaʾallihīn]. This, however, accords only with the theologians' position denying that existence has real instances, as is evident.

Here al-Muḥaqqiq al-Sharīf is the reported source conventionally identified as Jurjānī; do not confuse with the distinct title al-Sayyid al-Sanad in Yazdī. | A mediated account of Dawwānī’s adoption; not a transcript of any of the five original glosses.

ولعمري أن هذا التوجيه لا يسمن ولا يغني من جوع، فإن كون الوجود موجودا بذاته ومستغنيا في كونه موجودا عن غير ذاته، إنما يسلم في الوجود القائم بذاته، وهو الذي لا يمكن أن يكون قائما بماهية من الماهيات، ولا شبهة في كونه واجب الوجود، فمن أين يلزم أنه لا يكون وجود غير ذلك قائما بالماهيات الممكنة وأن يكون كل حقيقة وجودية قائمة بذاتها؟ وما ذكر من وجوب كون الوجود جزئيا حقيقيا إنما هو في حقيقة وجودية قائمة بذاتها، فمن أين يلزم أن مفهوم الوجود الذي هو الكون في الأعيان ليس بكلي، وليس له أفراد حقيقية بعضها قائم بذاته وبعضها قائم بالماهيات الممكنة؟ فإن بني على ذلك ما بني عليه مذهب المتكلمين، من وجوه الإشكالات المذكورة، فوجوه الدفع أيضا قد عرفت، مع أن الكلام في هذا البيان المنقول، وأنه كيف دل على ذلك المطلوب؟ وإنما بسطنا في هذه المسألة بهذا التطويل الذي لم يكن عنه من محيد، لكونها أهم أصول المعرفة وأعظم مسائل التوحيد.

By my life, this interpretation neither nourishes nor relieves hunger. That existence exists through itself and needs nothing other than its essence in order to exist is conceded only of self-subsisting existence, which cannot subsist in a quiddity. There is no doubt that this is necessarily existent. But how does it follow that there cannot be an existence other than it, subsisting in contingent quiddities, or that every existential reality must subsist through itself? The requirement that existence be a real particular concerns only a self-subsisting existential reality. How does it follow that the concept of existence, namely being in concrete reality, is not universal and does not have real instances, some self-subsisting and others subsisting in contingent quiddities? If this conclusion is based on the objections supporting the theologians' position, you have already learned their answers. Moreover, our present question concerns this transmitted argument: how does it establish that conclusion? We have treated this question at such unavoidable length because it is among the most important foundations of knowledge and the greatest questions concerning divine unity.

Completes the Ishāra ʿirfāniyya main text; printed p.467 opens a new numbered question. Does not establish the completeness of the whole Shawāriq.

Interim judgment: The whole/parts proof is historically contested and its “cause of the totality” premise must not be smuggled in. The conditional-necessity strategy avoids some mereological pitfalls, but a complete demonstration still owes the link between actually existing dependent beings and a noncontingent existential ground.

Boundary: One must not infer the impossibility of all infinite structures from a restriction argued only for a per se dependent causal series; nor infer Akbarī numerical unity of existence from the existence of a Necessary First Cause.

Q24 Divine knowledge, particulars and exemplarity

How can divine cognition include changing individuals without acquired forms or change within the divine essence?

How can the first cause possess detailed knowledge of its effects, including temporal particulars, without receiving knowledge from those effects, undergoing temporal change, or becoming a composite repository of distinct forms? Read this as a connected historical dialectic rather than conflating Avicenna’s account with every defence of knowledge by presence.

The opening problem: timeless knowledge of temporal order

Ṭūsī separates God’s relation to events from temporal succession. Knowing earlier and later things does not require becoming earlier and later oneself. This is a necessary starting distinction but does not yet show how the intelligible objects are present to God.

A13 — Ṭūsī: knowledge of temporal particulars without being in time

al-Ṭūsī · Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī · Reply to Question 4 (continuous selected passage)

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

ولمّا نفوا عنه الكون في الزمان، جعلوا نسبة جميع الأزمنة — ماضيها ومستقبلها وحالها — إليه نسبة واحدة. فقالوا: كما يكون العالم بالأمكنة إذا لم يكن مكانيّا، يكون عالما بأنّ زيدا في أيّ جهة من جهات عمرو، وكيف تكون الإشارة منه إليه وكم بينهما من المسافة، وكذلك في جميع ذرّات العالم، ولا يجعل نسبة شيء منها إلى نفسه لكونه غير مكاني، كذلك العالم بالأزمنة إذا لم يكن زمانيا، يكون عالما بأنّ زيدا في أي زمان يولد وعمروا في أي زمان، وكم يكون بينهما من المدة. وكذلك في جميع الحوادث المرتبطة بالأزمنة. ولا يجعل نسبة شيء منها إلى زمان يكون حاضرا له، فلا يقول: هذا مضى، وهذا ما حصل بعد، وهذا موجود الآن، بل يكون جميع ما في الأزمنة حاضرا عنده متساوي النسبة إليه مع علمه بنسب البعض إلى البعض وتقدّم البعض على البعض.

Because they deny that God exists within time, they assign to Him the same relation to every time—past, future, or present. Just as a knower of places who is not spatial can know in which direction Zayd stands relative to ʿAmr, how each is situated with respect to the other, and the distance between them, down to every particle in the world, without making any of those places a place occupied by the knower—so a knower of times who is not temporal knows at what time Zayd is born and at what time ʿAmr is born, and how much time separates them. He likewise knows every event connected with times. But He does not refer any event to a time that is present *to Him*. He does not say, “This has passed,” “This has not yet happened,” or “This exists now.” Rather, everything in time is present to Him, with an equal relation to Him, while He knows the relations among temporal things and the precedence of some over others.

READING NOTE Do not translate this as denying God knowledge of individual events. The distinction is between knowing their objective temporal relations and occupying a changing temporal standpoint. Ṭūsī is reporting and defending the philosophers’ position. | Arabic source: https://www.ibnalarabi.com/qunawi/tusi.php?id=5

There remains an internal difficulty: how can multiplicity be known distinctly without composition in the divine essence?

The Avicennian dilemma of intelligible forms

An Ibn Sīnā text quoted by Lāhījī asks whether the forms of things known are parts of the First, accidental concomitants, or separate realities. If parts, divine composition threatens; if concomitants, the grounding of their possibility and their relation to divine necessity require analysis. This is a mediated quotation, not an independently re-collated Shifāʾ manuscript.

Lāhījī against externally subsisting knowledge-forms

Lāhījī argues that placing the intelligible forms in separate entities or in the first effect merely moves the explanatory problem. The forms become part of the generated order and need an account of the prior knowledge that orders them; requiring another representation threatens regress.

Among the indications that God’s knowledge does not differ before and after things come to exist is that it remains in one state from eternity to eternity, and does not change as what is known passes from nonexistence to existence.

Invariance of divine cognition is incompatible with supposing that the external presence of objects makes divine knowledge more complete. Directly inspected searchable-page extract; not independently collated against a print image or manuscript. The source continues with a religious report and a criticism of a form of presence-based account; only the author’s thesis is translated here.

An adequate theory must permit distinct divine knowledge of particulars without succession, an external dependency, or regress.

The separate question of imaginal and reflexive knowledge

Quṭb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī’s example of knowing a necessary consequent concerns a distinction between knowledge of a thing and knowledge of what follows from it. It is an analogue useful for defining the problem, not a direct solution to divine omniscience.

No position has yet earned a demonstration of how multiplicity without composition is possible; the conditions of success are made explicit.

Interim judgment: A coherent solution must satisfy four constraints: explanatory priority of the first cause; unchanging divine knowledge; determinate knowledge of particulars; and exclusion of real composition or a regress of explanatory representations. The witnessed Ibn Sīnā, Ibn Rushd, and Lāhījī passages supply complementary tensions, not an already established consensus.

Q25 Prophecy, rational warrant and extraordinary cognition

What can reason establish about prophecy, and when do revelatory disclosures exceed rather than cancel rational demonstration?

Why should revelation be necessary or fitting if reason has its own powers? The *Tajrīd* gives reasons involving the completion of rational guidance and the social-moral functions of law, then discusses miracle as warrant of a claimant’s truthfulness. Mystical experiences raise a related but distinct kind of cognition; they do not automatically establish prophetic mission.

Ṭūsī’s layered account

The lemmata argue for the benefits of prophecy, support of rational duty, divine assistance, and the signification of miracles. The claims about obligatoriness and divine wisdom must be interpreted against the particular theological premises about grace.

The epistemic question is what authorises a public messenger, not simply what an individual experiences.

Ṭihrānī’s rational/prophetic distinction

Ṭihrānī explicitly discusses reason’s need for guidance, revelation and the disputed nature of proofs for prophethood. His sample bears directly on the balance of reason and mission.

TIH07 — Ṭihrānī: revelation, reason, and the disputed proof of prophetic necessity

Hāshim al-Ḥusaynī al-Ṭihrānī · Hāshim al-Ḥusaynī al-Ṭihrānī, Tawḍīḥ al-murād, I, printed pp. 643–644; section “fī wujūb al-biʿtha”.

قول المصنف: وهي واجبة لاشتمالها الخ — يدل هذا الكلام أن للإنسان تكاليف عقلية وتكاليف سمعية، وهو المشهور. ولكن المفيد رحمه الله تعالى قال في أوائل المقالات: إن العقل لا ينفك عن سمع وإن التكليف لا يصح إلا بالرسل، واتفقت الإمامية على أن العقل يحتاج في علمه ونتائجه إلى السمع، وأنه غير منفك عن سمع ينبه الغافل على كيفية الاستدلال، وأنه لا بد في أول التكليف وابتدائه في العالم من رسول. أقول: الحق مع المفيد رحمه الله وإن خالفه أقوام حتى بعض الإمامية بظاهر كلامهم، لأن العقل البشري له مقام القبول والاستعداد فلا بد له في مقام الحكم والاستدلال من تنبيه وإفاضة من العالين ولو قبل هذه النشأة، وأما الأشاعرة فيعزلون العقل بالكلية على أصلهم كما مر. قول الشارح: بأن التكاليف السمعية الخ — إيضاح هذا الاستدلال أن الإنسان بمجرد عقله يعمل بالتكاليف العقلية، ولكن الشرع إذا أتى بالتكاليف الأخرى وواظب الإنسان عليها كان للعمل بالتكاليف العقلية أقرب وأحفظ فيحصل اللطف في حكم العقل بالشرع. أقول: هذا الاستدلال لضعفه لا يقوم على ساق، والحق أن علة وجوب البعثة هي علة حسنها، وهي تلك الفوائد التي أنهاها المصنف إلى قوله: فيحصل اللطف للمكلف.

[Ṭihrānī introducing the author's lemma:] 'It [the prophetic mission] is obligatory because it includes ...' This implies that human beings have rational duties and duties known through revelation, as is commonly held. However, al-Mufīd said in Awāʾil al-maqālāt that reason is never without hearing [revealed teaching], and that imposition of duty is not sound except through messengers. He reports the Imāmī agreement that reason needs revealed instruction for its knowledge and results, and requires a message that alerts the heedless to the manner of inference, so that at the beginning of religious obligation there must be a messenger. [Ṭihrānī:] I say that al-Mufīd is right, despite dissent, even among some Imāmīs in the apparent sense of their remarks. For human reason occupies a state of receptivity and preparedness; in judging and inferring it therefore needs an awakening and effusion from higher beings, even if that occurs before this earthly life. The Ashʿarīs, by contrast, exclude reason entirely according to their principle, as discussed earlier. [Explaining the commentator's argument:] A human being observes rational duties by reason alone. But if religious law brings further duties and a person perseveres in them, that person comes closer to and better preserves the performance of rational duties. Thus revelation becomes a gracious assistance (luṭf) to rational judgment. [Ṭihrānī:] I say: This argument is too weak to stand. Rather, the reason that prophetic missions are obligatory is the same reason they are good: the benefits that the author itemized up to his words 'and grace is thereby realized for the responsible person'.

These paragraphs cover the page break between printed pp. 643–644. This is a dispute WITHIN the discussion of prophetic missions; not a blanket claim that unveiled mystical experience displaces rational proof. Ṭihrānī explicitly endorses al-Mufīd on reason's need for guidance yet rejects the commentator's narrower argument for prophetic necessity. His claim about Ashʿarīs is a polemical attribution, not a neutral fact about all Sunni theology. The initial al-Mufīd text is quoted here in Ṭihrānī's reporting; direct verification against Awāʾil al-maqālāt remains outstanding.

A separate appeal to spiritual unveiling is *not* a substitute for public certification.

An independent Sunni statement on miracle as evidence

Al-Māwardī’s treatment of prophetic signs connects extraordinary information to verification of a prophet’s truthfulness. It is an independent control, not a *Tajrīd* commentary.

Q26 Fixed entities, divine knowledge, and unactualized possibilities

Are the Akbarī aʿyān thābita fixed objects in divine knowledge, and how do they differ from Muʿtazilī nonexistents and nafs al-amr?

An unactualised possibility may be intelligible without possessing independent external existence. The Akbarī discussion of aʿyān thābita adds determinations in divine knowledge and a theory of manifestation. It should not be translated directly into the older Muʿtazilī claim that a nonexistent possible quiddity is an established external thing. The relevant senses of “fixed,” “known,” “made,” and “existent” must be kept distinct.

The question — fixed, but in which respect?

Qūnawī distinguishes a quiddity as unmade in its determination within eternal divine knowledge from the quiddity’s actual realization through outpouring. This is a claim about divine knowledge and ontological determination, not automatically a claim that an independent external thing exists before it is created.

A5 — Are possible quiddities themselves made?

al-Qūnawī · Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Qūnawī · Question 2 (opening and first horn of the dilemma)

المسألة الثانية: هل الماهيات الممكنة مجعولة أو غير مجعولة؟ وعلى كلا التقديرين، فهل هي من كونها ماهيات فقط أمور وجودية بمعنى أنّ لها ضربا من الوجود أو هي أمور عدمية؟ إن كانت غير مجعولة، فلا جائز أن تكون وجودية، لأنه يلزم من ذلك مساوقتها للواجب في وجوب الوجود الذاتي وفي صرافة الوحدة الذاتية، ولم تكن حينئذ ممكنة، بل واجبة لخلوّها عن وصف الإمكان والفقر المستلزم لاستفادة الوجود من الغير.

Second question. Are possible quiddities [الماهيات الممكنة] made [مجعولة], or are they not made? Whichever answer is given, are they—considered simply as quiddities—existential realities possessing some manner of existence, or are they nonexistential? If they are unmade, they cannot be existential realities. For that would put them on the same footing as the Necessary in intrinsic necessity of existence [وجوب الوجود الذاتي] and in the sheer unity of essence. They would no longer be possible, but necessary, since they would lack the possibility and poverty entailed by receiving existence from another.

READING NOTE The question is not simply whether the objects of divine knowledge are “real.” It asks what is produced by the act of making: quiddity itself, its existence, or its determination. Does the account introduce plurality in God?

The doctrine of relations

Qūnawī explicitly identifies divine knowledge with the essence in the register of oneness, locating plurality in the respect of its epistemic relations.

But is that sufficient to establish determinate realities without a distinct mode of existence?

Ṭūsī’s twofold existence distinction

For Ṭūsī, an essence considered as essence is just itself; determinate existent instances depend on intellectual or external existence. This does not deny that thinkers can conceive possibilities, but it rejects independent establishment of nonexistents.

al-Ṭūsī · Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī · Reply to Question 2 (continuous selection)

Inherited extract: direct source/voice/collation still needs full audit

بل الحقّ أنّ جميع الماهيات والموجودات مجعولة، جاعلها اللّه سبحانه وتعالى. وإذا قلنا: الماهيات الممكنة صارت منسوبة إلى الوجود، فإنّ الإمكان لا يمكن أن توصف به الماهية من حيث هي ماهية فقط، إنما يمكن أن توصف به إذا قيست إلى الوجود أو إلى العدم. وأما قوله: «هل هي من كونها ماهيات فقط أمور وجودية؟». فالجواب: لا، فإنّ الماهية من حيث هي ماهية فقط لا يمكن أن تكون شيئا غير الماهية. وأما إذا فسّره بقوله: «هل لها ضرب من الوجود؟». فالجواب: نعم، فإنّ الماهية إذا تصوّرت، حدث لها وجود عقلي. وإذا فرضت في الأعيان، كان لها وجود عيني. والوجود العيني لا يكون إلّا من موجدها، والوجود العقلي يكون ممن تعقّلها. وكلا الوجودين ممكن له. وإذا قالوا: للماهية وجود قبلها، أرادوا به تعقّلها الذي يكون سببا لوجودها العيني. وهو العلم الفعلي. وإذا قالوا: لها وجود معها، أرادوا به الوجود العيني. وإذا قالوا: لها وجود بعدها، أرادوا به تعقّلها بعد وجودها، يعني العلم الانفعالي. وإذا نظر إلى الماهية فقط، لم يكن في القصد العقلي إلا الماهية، ولم يكن الوجود ولا العدم داخلين في ذلك النظر. ولذلك قالوا: إنها ليست بموجودة ولا معدومة.

Rather, the truth is that all quiddities and existents are made: God—glorified and exalted—is their maker. When we say that possible quiddities are related to existence, possibility [الإمكان] is not attributable to quiddity precisely insofar as it is quiddity alone. It can be attributed when quiddity is compared with existence or nonexistence. As for the question, “Are quiddities, simply as quiddities, existential realities?” the answer is no. Quiddity, precisely insofar as it is quiddity, can be nothing other than quiddity. But if the question means, “Do they have some manner of existence?” the answer is yes. When a quiddity is conceived, it acquires intellectual existence [وجود عقلي]; when it is posited among extramental individuals, it has extramental existence [وجود عيني]. Extramental existence comes only from its producer; intellectual existence arises through whoever conceives it. Both modes of existence are possible for it. When they say that a quiddity has an existence before itself, they mean the conception of it that causes its extramental existence: this is productive knowledge [العلم الفعلي]. When they say it has existence accompanying it, they mean extramental existence. When they say it has an existence after itself, they mean its being conceived after its extramental existence—receptive knowledge [العلم الانفعالي]. If quiddity alone is considered, nothing is intended by the intellect except quiddity itself; neither existence nor nonexistence enters into that consideration. Hence it is said that quiddity is neither existent nor nonexistent.

READING NOTE The final denial is made in the restricted consideration of quiddity in itself. It should not be read as granting independently existing nonexistent objects. Q27 Existence itself, dependent existents, and manifestation

Can there be one independent existence with many dependent determinations, and does an analysis of need prove such unity?

To say “the Necessary is existence itself” is not yet to say that finite beings have no distinct existential actuality. This chapter follows a specific attempt to bridge that gap. It asks whether contingent quiddities are dependent upon one extramental reality of existence, and whether their multiplicity is existentially real, graded, or confined to determinations and relations.

Jurjānī proposes a rational reformulation

In the second mystical gloss Jurjānī considers existence as a singular, intrinsically individuated, self-subsisting reality to which other things stand in particular relations. He presents this as a difficult intelligible possibility, not a straightforward deduction from a verbal universal. Lāhījī’s p.468 provides the initial reading of qualified manifestations as gradations of one existential reality.

Existence would then be one reality, differentiated in its manifestations—which are the quiddities—according to intensity and weakness, perfection and deficiency.

Lāhījī initially formulates a potential interpretation, not his final demonstration of numerical unity. | Bounded passage, not the whole work; do not infer an exhaustive manuscript collation.

The passage must be read as part of a sequence, not labelled a blanket endorsement of all Sufi statements.

Jurjānī’s third gloss argues and receives an objection

The extended third gloss reasons from the intrinsic dependence of quiddities to the Necessary’s self-subsisting existence, then distinguishes a shared concept of existent from an indivisible extra-mental existence. Crucially it entertains the objection: dependence on one’s *own* existence does not automatically make one dependent on an alien cause. On p.469 he contrasts the philosophers’ bi-sharṭ lā with the Sufis’ lā bi-sharṭ; this is a different modal treatment of determination.

JRG03 — Jurjānī, gloss III: an argument for existence itself and the objection from dependence

al-Sayyid al-Sharīf al-Jurjānī · al-Jurjānī, Ḥāshiyat Sharḥ al-Tajrīd, gloss III; Garrett 865 fols. 62b–63b and Yahuda 5373 fols. 88a–89a; Nicholas Heer, Five Unedited Texts, pp. 2–3.

Heer printed page 3 inspected; manuscript collation and exhaustive variants pending

واعلم أن هذه المباحث التي أوردها الشارح في كون الوجود عين الواجب أو زائدا عليه هي الكلمات الواردة على ألسن القوم في هذا المقام. وههنا مقالة أخرى قد أشرنا فيما سبق أنها مما لا يدركها إلا أولو البصائر والألباب الذين خصوا بحكمة بالغة وفصل الخطاب. فلنفصلها هيهنا بقدر ما يفي به قوة التقرير ويحيط به دائرة التحرير، فنقول وبالله التوفيق فنعم الرفيق: كل مفهوم مغاير للوجود كالإنسان مثلا فإنه ما لم ينضم إليه الوجود بوجه من الوجوه في نفس الأمر لم يكن موجودا فيها قطعا، وما لم يلاحظ العقل انضمام الوجود إليه لم يمكن له الحكم بكونه موجودا، فكل مفهوم مغاير للوجود فهو في كونه موجودا في نفس الأمر يحتاج إلى غيره الذي هو الوجود، وكل ما هو محتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره فهو ممكن إذ لا معنى للممكن إلا ما يحتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره، فكل مفهوم مغاير للوجود فهو ممكن، ولا شيء من الممكن بواجب، فلا شيء من المفهومات المغايرة للوجود بواجب. وقد ثبت بالبرهان أن الواجب موجود، فهو لا يكون إلا عين الوجود الذي هو موجود بذاته لا بأمر مغاير لذاته. ولما وجب أن يكون الواجب جزئيا حقيقيا قائما بذاته ويكون تعينه بذاته لا بأمر زائد على ذاته وجب أن يكون الوجود أيضا كذلك إذ هو عينه فلا يكون الوجود مفهوما كليا يمكن أن يكون له أفراد بل هو في حد ذاته جزئي حقيقي ليس فيه إمكان تعدد ولا انقسام وقائم بذاته منزه عن كونه عارضا لغيره، فيكون الواجب هو الوجود المطلق أي المعرى عن التقيد بغيره والانضمام إليه. وعلى هذا لا يتصور عروض الوجود للماهيات الممكنة، فليس معنى كونها موجودة إلا أن لها نسبة مخصوصة إلى حضرة الوجود القائم بذاته، وتلك النسبة على وجوه مختلفة وأنحاء شتى يتعذر الاطلاع على ماهياتها، فالموجود كلي وإن كان الوجود جزئيا حقيقيا. هذا ملخص ما ذكره بعض المحققين من مشايخنا، قال: ولا يعلمه إلا الراسخون في العلم. فإن قلت: الذي يتبادر إلى الذهن من لفظ الوجود مفهوم لا يمنع الشركة، فكيف يكون جزئيا حقيقيا؟ وأيضا المفهوم من لفظ الوجود ما قام به الوجود كما اشتهر في كلامهم، فكيف يفسر بمعنى لا يفهمه أحد؟ قلت: الجواب عن الأول أن الكلام في حقيقة الوجود لا فيما يتبادر إلى الأذهان من مدلول اللفظ. فإنه يجوز أن يكون مفهوما كليا وعارضا اعتباريا لتلك الحقيقة الممتنعة عن الاشتراك في حد ذاتها كمفهوم الواجب بالقياس إلى حقيقته. وعن الثاني أن المعتبر هو البرهان وما يؤدي إليه لا الاشتهار في ألسنة الأقوام وعقول الأوهام. نعم، يتجه على المقدمة القائلة بأن كل ما هو محتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره فهو ممكن، منع لطيف، وهو أن المحتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غير موجود ممكن قطعا، لا المحتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره هو وجوده. ويندفع بنظر دقيق وهو أن ما احتاج في موجوديته إلى غيره فقد استفاد ذلك من غيره وصار معلولا له موقوفا في ذلك عليه وكل ما هو كذلك فهو ممكن سواء سمي ذلك الغير الموقوف عليه وجوده أو موجده. ومما يؤيد كون الوجود عين الواجب أن الوجود في حد ذاته ينافي العدم وهو أبعد المفهومات عن قبول العدم لأن ما عداه لا يمتنع عن قبول العدم لذاته بل بواسطة الوجود ولا شك أن الواجب هو الذي ينافي العدم لذاته لا ما ينافيه بواسطة غيره. ماذا تقول فيمن يرى أن الوجود مع كونه عين الواجب وغير قابل للتجزؤ والانقسام قد انبسط على هياكل الموجودات وظهر فيها فلا يخلو عنه شيء من الأشياء، بل هو حقيقتها وعينها وإنما امتازت وتعددت بتقيدات وتعينات اعتبارية، ويمثل ذلك بالبحر وظهوره في صور الأمواج المتكثرة مع أنه ليس هناك إلا حقيقة البحر فقط؟ قلت: قد سلف من كلامنا أن هذا طور وراء طور العقل لا يتوصل إليه إلا بالمشاهدات الكشفية دون المناظرات العقلية. وكل ميسر لما خلق له والله المستعان وعليه التكلان.

Know that the questions the commentator introduced about whether existence is identical with the Necessary Existent or additional to Him are the expressions current among the group in this discussion. There is another position, previously indicated, whose grasp belongs only to those of insight and understanding who have received profound wisdom and decisive speech. Let us set it out as far as exposition permits, seeking God's help. Every concept other than existence—for example, humanity—cannot exist in reality unless existence is joined to it in some respect. Nor can the intellect judge it to exist without considering that conjunction. Thus whatever is conceptually different from existence requires something other than itself—existence—for its actuality. Whatever needs another for its actuality is possible, for possibility is just such a need. Every concept other than existence is therefore possible; nothing possible is necessary; hence none of those other concepts is the Necessary. Now demonstration establishes that the Necessary exists. It must therefore be existence itself, which exists through itself rather than through a distinct constituent. Since the Necessary must be an individual reality subsisting through itself and individuated by itself rather than through something added, existence itself must be so too, because it is identical with the Necessary. Existence is not, on that understanding, a universal with several extramental instances: in itself it is an individual reality incapable of multiplication or division, independent of a substrate, never an accident of something else. The Necessary is accordingly absolute existence—that is, existence free of limitation by, or conjunction with, another thing. Existence cannot in this account inhere in possible quiddities. That they exist means only that they stand in a distinctive relation to the presence of self-subsistent existence. These relations are diverse in modes and kinds; their essences resist comprehension. Thus the predicate “existent” has universal application, even though existence itself is an individual reality. This summarizes what some investigating masters among our teachers said; one of them adds that only those firmly rooted in knowledge know it. If you object: What occurs to the mind on hearing 'existence' is a concept open to common participation. How can it be a genuine individual? Moreover, on the customary account 'existent' signifies that in which existence inheres; how can one explain it by something nobody understands? I reply: First, we are concerned with the reality of existence, not with the mental content conveyed by the word. The latter can be universal and an intellectual attribute of a reality that itself admits no shared instantiation, as the concept of the Necessary relates to its reality. Second, what counts is demonstration and its conclusions, not a notion's circulation in common speech or imagination. There is, however, a subtle objection to the premise that anything needing something else in order to exist is possible: one may concede this when what is needed is some OTHER existent, but not when what is needed is the thing's own existence. A careful response is that whatever derives its actuality from another is thereby an effect dependent upon it; anything so dependent is possible, whether that upon which it depends is called its 'existence' or its 'giver of existence'. Another supporting argument for identifying existence with the Necessary is that existence as such excludes nonexistence. Among our concepts it is the furthest from admitting nonexistence; everything else is free of nonexistence only through existence, whereas the Necessary excludes nonexistence intrinsically. What, then, of one who holds that existence, although identical with the Necessary and not divisible into parts, extends over the structures of all existents and appears within them, so that nothing is devoid of it and it is their very reality, with differences and multiplicity arising solely from conceptual restrictions and determinations—like the sea appearing as many waves when there is in truth only the sea? I reply: As was said earlier, this is a sphere beyond the sphere of reason. It is approached through unveiled witnessings, not rational disputations. Each is facilitated toward that for which he was created. God is the source of help, and upon Him is reliance.

ARGUMENT MAP (speaker carefully distinguished): (1) Report of the masters, introduced as a position rather than an unqualified dogma; (2) need for 'existence' -> possibility; (3) necessity -> existence itself; (4) difference between universal concept and indivisible reality; (5) explicitly stated subtle objection that needing 'one's existence' does not automatically mean needing ANOTHER existent; (6) reply by treating borrowed actuality as dependency; (7) final sea/waves thesis is withheld from rational demonstration. The sentence 'fa-l-mawjūd kullī wa-in kāna al-wujūd juzʾiyyan ḥaqīqiyyan' is an especially significant terminological distinction, and requires comparison with Garrett manuscript before final printing. Arabic manually rekeyed from Heer's published transcription (PDF printed pp. 2–3); punctuation editorial. A word-by-word diplomatic collation with the manuscripts and Heer's variants has not been completed. | TEXTUAL WITNESS: Hussein b. Muʿīn al-Dīn al-Maybudī quotes this direct Tajrīd gloss in his Persian Sharḥ Dīwān, printed p. 50, ed. Ḥasan Raḥmānī and Sayyid Ibrāhīm Ashk Shīrīn (https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/17503/118?lang=ar). Both that witness and Heer's published Arabic read «ولما وجب» (causal 'since') rather than «ولو وجب» ('if'); the working translation now follows the former.
