مذهب سخيف لان موضوع القضية فى العلوم لا بدّ ان يكون كليا شاملا لجميع الافراد المحققة والمقدرة فى نفس الامر لما بين فى صناعة البرهان من المنطق وان كانت القضية الخارجية متداولة فى السنة اهل المحاورة من العرف. قول الشارح : فيلزم مع اتصاف الذهن الخ اى مع انا نعلم ان هذه الامور منتفية عن الذهن لزم على فرض الاتصاف اجتماع الضدين لانا نتصور هذه الامور معا. قول الشارح : ليس هو ماهية الحرارة الخ اى ليس فى الذهن حقيقة الحرارة والسواد بل فيه صورتهما المجردة عن المادة الخارجية بالتجريد العقلى المخالفة للحقيقة فى كثير من اللوازم وعبر الشارح رحمه‌الله عن الحقيقة بالماهية وحاصل الجواب ان الماهية واحدة فى الخارج والذهن واما الوجودان فمتغايران وحيث ان كثيرا من اللوازم والآثار يدور مدار الوجود الخارجى فالماهية الموجودة بالوجود الذهنى ليست لها تلك الآثار.

Ṭūsī’s lemma “And it is divided …” This division is made with reference to the existent itself. Thus, for example, when an individual instance of the human exists externally, the human is said to exist with external existence; when an individual instance is represented in the imagination, or its quiddity is impressed upon the soul, it is said to exist with mental existence. The claim is therefore established by appeal to affirmative real propositions, which require the existence of their subject: the establishment of something for something presupposes the establishment of that for which it is established. Since a real proposition need not have all its instances—or many of them—existing [externally], they must have existence in the mind. Al-Ḥillī’s lemma “A genuine division” A genuine division is one whose two alternatives cannot both apply and cannot both fail to apply. A proposition containing such a division is called a strict disjunctive proposition, as when we say: ‘A number is either even or odd.’ The present case is similar: existence is either external or mental; existence can neither lack both nor combine both. ‘Genuine division’ may also be applied to a disjunction in which neither alternative can change into the other, even if combination or exclusion is possible. Consider: ‘An existent is either eternal in itself or eternal through another.’ An existent can fall under neither alternative and instead originate in time. But what is eternal in itself—the Necessary Existent—cannot change into what is eternal through another—the world, according to the philosophers—or vice versa. This differs from ‘A human is either at rest or in motion’: a human at rest can become one in motion, and vice versa, although combination and exclusion are impossible. The commentator may intend this second meaning by ‘genuine division.’ Al-Ḥillī’s lemma “Know that the term ‘proposition’ is used …” Propositions have four classifications, according to subject, predicate, modality, and copula. According to the subject, they divide into mental propositions, whose subject is in the mind—that is, its qualification by the predicate is in respect of the mind, as in ‘Animal is a genus’ and ‘A genus is either higher or lower.’ Natural propositions are among mental propositions: in these, the judgment does not take individuals into account but concerns the nature itself, as in ‘Animal is a part of human.’ The other division is external propositions, whose subject is external. These are external propositions in the broad sense, and they have three subdivisions: real propositions, external propositions in the narrower sense, and singular propositions. Examples are, respectively, ‘Body is finite,’ ‘Those in the army were killed,’ and ‘Zayd is standing.’ Real propositions divide into universal, particular, and unquantified propositions. All this is explained in logic. Al-Ḥillī’s lemma “And this is an unsound doctrine …” The pronoun refers, as is apparent, to his statement ‘its subject is taken with reference to external reality.’ His meaning is that taking the subject with reference to external reality in scientific investigations is an unsound doctrine. For the subject of a proposition in the sciences must be universal, encompassing all the instances actually realized or supposed in the way things are in themselves [nafs al-amr], as has been explained in the demonstrative part of logic—even though external propositions are current in ordinary conversation. Al-Ḥillī’s lemma “It would therefore follow, with the mind’s being qualified …” That is: although we know that these properties are absent from the mind, the supposition that it is qualified by them would entail the conjunction of contraries, because we conceive these properties together. Al-Ḥillī’s lemma “It is not the quiddity of heat …” That is, what is in the mind is not the reality of heat and blackness, but their form, abstracted from external matter by intellectual abstraction, which differs from that reality in many concomitants. The commentator—God have mercy on him—has used ‘quiddity’ to express ‘reality.’ The substance of the answer is that the quiddity is one in external reality and in the mind, whereas the two existences differ. Since many concomitants and effects depend upon external existence, the quiddity existing with mental existence does not have those effects.

قول المصنف : باعتبار المطابقة لما فى نفس الامر اقول : هاهنا بحثان الاول : ما معنى نفس الامر؟ والثانى : ما معنى المطابقة لما فى نفس الامر؟ اما نفس الامر : فمعناه ذات الشيء من حيث هو هو مع قطع النظر من ان يدركه مدرك او يقام عليه برهان او يوجد فى ظرف فما يقع فى مدرك من المدارك ويتصور بآلة من آلات التصور فاما ان يكون له نفسية غير حيثية كونه واقعا فى ذلك المدرك كقولنا : الجسم متشكل والانسان ممكن والامكان لازم للممكن والاربعة زوج فان تشكل الجسم وامكان الانسان ولزوم الامكان للممكن وزوجية الاربعة وامثالها من الواقعيات هى امور لها فى حدودها نفسيات يمكن ادراكها واقامة البرهان عليها واما ان لا يكون له نفسية غير تلك الحيثية كوجوب الانسان بالذات وزوجية الخمسة وعدم لزوم الامكان للممكن والعدم المطلق فانها ليس لها فى حدودها نفسيات ولا يمكن اقامة البرهان عليها ولا ادراكها من نفس الامر بل هى فى الذهن ليس الا بالفرض وبعبارة اخرى ان نفس الامر فى مقابل الفرض فان امكان الممكن وان كان يكون وجوده فى العقل بالاعتبار والانتزاع ولكن نفسيته اى ماهيته بالمعنى الاعم فى مرتبتها محفوظة بحفظ الحق ازلا وابدا من دون ان يفرضه فارض فى صقع الفرض او يدركه مدرك بخلاف زوجية الخمسة ووجوب الانسان وامثالهما فانها ليست كذلك بل ليس لها نفسية الا مفروضيتها من فارض فى ذهنه ومصنوعيتها من شيطان المتخيلة فما كان له نفسية واقعية سواء كان من الموجودات الخارجية او الموجودات الذهنية بمعنى انه لم يكن له وجود الا ذهنا كالامكان والانسان والحيوان والنسبة بينهما فله حيثيتان اذا وقع فى ذهن من الاذهان : الحيثية النفس الامرية وحيثية كونه فى الذهن كقولنا : الاربعة زوج بخلاف ما لم يكن له نفسية واقعية كقولنا : الخمسة زوج فانه ليس له إلا حيثية كونه مفروضا فى الذهن فمعنى المطابقة لنفس الامر هو تطابق الحيثيتين بان يكون ما فى الذهن واجدا لهما كما فى قولنا : الانسان ممكن والانسان جسم والامكان كيفية النسبة وعدم المطابقة فيما نحن فيه هو السلب بانتفاء الموضوع اى لم يكن له حيثيتان حتى تتطابقا فقولنا : الانسان ممكن له نسبتان نسبة ذهنية ونسبة نفس الامرية واما قولنا : الانسان واجب بذاته فليس له الا نسبة ذهنية.

Ṭūsī’s lemma “In virtue of correspondence to what is the case in itself [nafs al-amr].” I say: there are two questions here. First, what does nafs al-amr mean? Second, what does correspondence to what is the case in itself mean? As for nafs al-amr, it means the thing itself, considered just as it is, apart from its being apprehended by anyone, demonstrated by a proof, or existing in a domain. Whatever occurs in a faculty of apprehension and is conceived through an instrument of conception either has an intrinsic standing other than its occurring in that faculty—as when we say, ‘A body has shape,’ ‘The human is possible,’ ‘Possibility necessarily belongs to the possible,’ and ‘Four is even.’ For a body's having shape, the human's possibility, possibility's necessarily belonging to the possible, four's evenness, and other such realities each have, within their proper bounds, an intrinsic standing that can be apprehended and demonstrated. Or it has no intrinsic standing beyond that aspect—as with the human's being necessary in itself, five's evenness, possibility's not necessarily belonging to the possible, and absolute nonexistence. These have no intrinsic standing within their proper bounds. They can neither be demonstrated nor apprehended from the way things are in themselves; they are in the mind only by supposition. In other words, nafs al-amr stands in contrast to supposition. Although the possibility of the possible exists in the intellect through consideration and abstraction, its intrinsic standing—that is, its quiddity in the broader sense—is preserved at its own level by the Real [God], without beginning or end, without anyone's supposing it in the domain of supposition or apprehending it. Five's evenness, the human's necessity, and similar things are otherwise. They have no intrinsic standing beyond their being supposed by someone in his mind and fabricated by the demon of the imaginative faculty. Thus whatever has an intrinsic standing in reality—whether it is an external existent or a mental existent, in the sense of having existence only mentally, such as possibility, human, animal, and the relation between the latter two—has two aspects when it occurs in a mind: its aspect as it is in itself, and the aspect of its being in the mind. An example is our statement ‘Four is even.’ By contrast, what has no intrinsic standing in reality, as in ‘Five is even,’ has only the aspect of its being supposed in the mind. Correspondence to nafs al-amr therefore means that the two aspects correspond: what is in the mind possesses both, as in ‘The human is possible,’ ‘The human is a body,’ and ‘Possibility is a modality of the [predicative] relation.’ The absence of correspondence in the case under discussion is a negation due to the absence of a subject: that is, there are no two aspects here to correspond with one another. Our statement ‘The human is possible’ thus has two relations, a mental relation and a relation belonging to the way things are in themselves. But ‘The human is necessary in itself’ has only a mental relation.

قول المصنف : وهى من حيث هى ليست الا هى معنى هذا الكلام ان الماهية من حيث هى ماهية اى من حيث هى فى مرتبة نفسها ولا يعتبر معها شيء لا يحمل عليها شيء من الاشياء حتى ذاتياتها ولوازمها الا نفسها لان حيثية نفسها غير حيثية غيرها ولو كان ذاتيا او لازما لها ، نعم يلاحظ الذاتيات واللوازم بنحو الاندماج والاندكاك معها لا بنحو التفصيل ، فالانسان مثلا من حيث هو هو انسان ليس غير حتى انه ليس بحيوان لان حمل الحيوان عليه يستلزم اخراجه من صرافة نفسه وعن مرتبته وادخاله فى اعتبار حيثية هى مصححة حمل الحيوان عليه وتلك الحيثية انه كل له جزء عقلى هو الحيوان ، فاذا اريد ان يحمل على الماهية شيء غير نفسها فلا بد ان يعتبر معها غير نفسها ما هو مصحح ومناط لحمل ذلك الشيء عليها. وليس معناه انها من حيث هى هى اى فى مرتبة نفسها ليس شيء من الاشياء عينا لها ولا جزء منها الا هى كما يظهر من كلمات بعض الاكابر لمكان الاستثناء اذ هو يثبت لما بعده ما ينفى عما قبله وبالعكس فيصير المعنى باعتبار بعد الاستثناء ان الماهية فى مرتبة نفسها هى نفسها وجزئها وهذا باطل بالضرورة لانها فى مرتبتها ليست بجزئها لان الجزء متقدم على الماهية بالماهية كما ان لازم الماهية كالامكان مثلا متأخر عن الماهية بالماهية. [حُذفت هنا ملاحظتان قصيرتان في النص والنحو.] قول الشارح : الفا ولا شيئا من الاشياء اى ليس الفا ولا شيئا من الاشياء غير الألف ولا بمقابلاتها ، اى ليس الانسان مثلا من حيث هو هو بالف ولا بمقابله وليس بواحد ولا بمقابله وليس بكلي ولا بمقابله وليس بموجود ولا بمقابله وليس بحيوان ولا بمقابله وهكذا الى ان يحصى جميع الاشياء ، بل هو انسان فقط. ان قلت : هل هذا الا ارتفاع النقيضين فكيف جوزوه فى هذا المقام ، قلت : ليس هذا بارتفاع النقيضين لان معناه ان النقيضين ليسا بنفس الماهية ، نعم اذا قلنا ان الانسان فى مرتبة نفسها ليس بإنسان وليس بلا انسان فهو ارتفاع النقيضين ولكنا نقول ان الانسان فى مرتبة نفسها انسان لا شيء غيره ، وببيان اخر ان الانسان فى مقام الموضوعية انسان لا غير واما اذا نظرنا الى المحمولات فهو اما موجود واما لا موجود وكذا اما كلى أو لا كلى وهكذا وارتفاع النقيضين واجتماعهما راجعان الى المحمولات فافهم.

Ṭūsī’s lemma “Considered just as it is, it is nothing but itself.” The meaning of this statement is that quiddity, insofar as it is quiddity—that is, insofar as it is at its own level, with nothing else considered alongside it—has nothing predicated of it except itself, not even its essential constituents or its concomitants. For the respect in which it is itself differs from the respect in which something else is considered, even if that other thing is essential to it or concomitant with it. Its essential constituents and concomitants may indeed be considered as enfolded and subsumed within it, but not in a differentiated manner. Thus the human, for example, considered just as it is, is human and nothing else—even ‘animal’ is not [predicated of it in this consideration]. For predicating ‘animal’ of it requires taking it out of the purity of itself and its own level, and introducing the consideration of a respect that warrants predicating ‘animal’ of it: namely, that it is a whole with an intellectual part, animal. Hence, if something other than the quiddity itself is to be predicated of it, something other than itself must be considered alongside it, to warrant and ground the predication of that thing. The statement does not mean that, considered just as it is—that is, at its own level—nothing is identical with it or a part of it except itself, as appears from the formulations of some eminent authorities. This is because of the exception: an exception affirms of what follows it what it denies of what precedes it, and conversely. Thus, in respect of what follows the exception, the meaning would become that the quiddity, at its own level, is identical with itself and is a part of itself. This is self-evidently false, since at its own level it is not a part of itself: the part is prior to the quiddity in respect of quiddity, just as a concomitant of quiddity—possibility, for example—is posterior to the quiddity in respect of quiddity. [Two short textual and grammatical notes omitted.] Al-Ḥillī’s lemma “A, nor any of the things …” That is, it is neither A, nor anything other than A, nor their opposites. Thus the human, for example, considered just as it is, is neither A nor its opposite; neither one nor its opposite; neither universal nor its opposite; neither existent nor its opposite; neither animal nor its opposite; and so on until every item has been enumerated. Rather, it is human only. If you object, ‘Is this anything other than the exclusion of both contradictories? How, then, have they allowed it here?’ I reply: this is not the exclusion of both contradictories, for its meaning is that neither contradictory is the quiddity itself. Certainly, if we said that the human, at the level of itself, is neither human nor nonhuman, that would be the exclusion of both contradictories. But we say that the human, at the level of itself, is human and nothing else. To put it another way, in its capacity as subject, the human is human and nothing else; but when we consider the predicates, it is either existent or nonexistent, either universal or nonuniversal, and so on. The exclusion or conjunction of contradictories concerns the predicates. Understand this.

Ṭūsī’s lemma “Reciprocity is necessary in it.” This is one of the three properties of the relative, namely the requirement of reciprocity. Know that inʿikās occurs either in a proposition—in the sense explained in logic—or in a simple term. In the latter case, two things are such that each can properly be related to the other, either directly or through a preposition, obligatorily or optionally. The same preposition may occur on both sides, or the preposition on one side may differ from that on the other. Thus we say: ‘The father is the father of the son, and the son is the son of the father’; ‘The slave is the master's slave, and the master is the slave's master’—or ‘a slave to the master and a master to the slave’; ‘The passer-by passes by what is passed, and what is passed is passed by the passer-by’; and ‘The knower knows the known, and the known is known to the knower.’ If one of two things is related to the other, but the other is not related back to it, this property is absent, and neither is designated ‘a relative.’ Rather, what has thus been related is called ‘a related term’ in their terminology, even though grammarians call it a muḍāf. Examples are ‘a person's head,’ ‘the elder of the people,’ ‘Zayd's slave,’ and ‘part of the book.’ Although the head, elder, slave, and part are related to these things, they are not relatives, because reciprocity is absent. They become relatives when related instead to the possessor of the head, the younger, the master, and the whole. This property is not restricted to the relative in common usage; it also applies to the relative in the strict sense. Here we agree with al-ʿAllāma, the commentator, and the earlier commentator, and disagree with the commentator al-Qūshjī, who says: ‘As for the relative in the strict sense, there is no relation in it such that reciprocity could be conceived in it, for one does not say, “Fatherhood is fatherhood in relation to sonship.”’ We also disagree with the author of al-Shawāriq, who says: ‘This property belongs only to the relative in common usage. The author's statement, “is necessary in it,” therefore means in the relative in common usage—or in the relative without qualification, but insofar as it is realized in the relative in common usage.’ For reciprocity in the relative in common usage obtains only in virtue of the relative in the strict sense. Just as one can properly say, ‘The father is a father in relation to the son,’ one can properly say, ‘Fatherhood is fatherhood in relation to sonship.’ We see no difference between them except that the father is related to the son through the relation inhering in him, whereas fatherhood is related to sonship through itself. Moreover, their position conflicts with the apparent meaning of the author's words. The pronoun in his statement, ‘Reciprocity and co-implication are necessary in it,’ refers back to ‘the relative’ at the beginning of his discussion. For co-implication applies to it, and not only to the relative in common usage: this is certain and agreed upon. The unity of the context therefore requires reciprocity to apply to it as well.

Ṭūsī’s lemma “Its existence is self-evident.” Having explained the concept of motion through one of its properties—namely, its being a perfection of a body under that qualification—the author states that its existence is self-evident and requires no demonstration. Know that a body which, for example, successively occupies several spatial positions has a condition, namely succession and change with respect to place. There is no doubt that this condition actually obtains for the body in external reality as long as it is between its starting point and terminus. This condition is called ‘motion as being-in-transit’ [al-ḥaraka al-tawassuṭiyya], and it is this whose existence is self-evident. In virtue of this condition, the body has relations to the intermediate boundaries between the starting point and terminus. These relations are plainly multiple and distinct, corresponding to the possible divisions of the distance. It was already explained that the body occurs at each of these intermediate boundaries without either resting or moving at that boundary. Nevertheless, these occurrences can be retained in imagination, one after another, in order and by stages, so that something extended is produced in imagination from them. This extended thing, produced from the occurrences related to those boundaries, is called ‘motion as traversal’ [al-ḥaraka al-qaṭʿiyya]. It exists in imagination, not in external reality, because the relations do not exist externally. Thus the body's being between the starting point and terminus exists externally when its relation to the intermediate boundaries is not considered; when that relation is considered, it does not exist externally but exists in imagination. Reason analogously concerning motion in the other categories.

JRG01 — Jurjānī, gloss I: the challenge of radical unity and the protest of reason

al-Sayyid al-Sharīf al-Jurjānī · al-Jurjānī, Ḥāshiyat Sharḥ al-Tajrīd, gloss I; Garrett 865 fols. 16a–16b, Yahuda 5373 fols. 87b–88a; ed./transcription Nicholas Heer, Five Unedited Texts, p. 2.

Heer printed introduction and edition verified; manuscript collation pending

قيل عليه: ذهب جماعة من الصوفية إلى أن ليس في الواقع إلا ذات واحدة لا تركيب فيها أصلا، بل لها صفات متعددة هي عينها، وهي حقيقة الوجود المنزهة في حد ذاتها عن شوائب العدم وسمات نقصان الإمكان، ولها تقيدات بقيود اعتبارية بحسب ذلك تتراءى موجودات متمايزة فيتوهم من ذلك تعدد حقيقي، فلما لم يقم برهان على بطلان ذلك لم يتم ما ذكره من عدم اتحاد الماهيات ولا يتم أيضا اشتراك الوجود بل لا يثبت وجود ممكن أصلا. أقول: هذا خروج عن طور العقل، فإن بداهته شاهدة بتعدد الموجودات تعددا حقيقيا، وإنما ذوات وحقائق مختلفة بالحقيقة دون الاعتبار فقط. والذاهبون إلى تلك المقالة يدعون استنادها إلى مكاشفاتهم ومشاهداتهم، وأنه لا يمكن الوصول إليها بمباحث العقل ودلالته، بل هو معزول هناك كالحس في إدراك المعقولات. وأما المتقيدون بدرجات العقل والقائلون بأن ما يشهد له العقل فمقبول وما يشهد عليه فمردود، وأنه لا طور وراءه، فيزعمون أن تلك المكاشفات والمشاهدات على تقدير صحتها مأولة بما يوافق العقل، فهم بشهادة بداهته عندهم مستغنون عن إقامة برهان على بطلان أمثال ذلك ويعدون تجويزها مكابرة لا يلتفت إليها.

[Objection reported:] A group of Sufis maintain that in reality there is nothing but one essence, in which there is absolutely no composition. It has multiple attributes that are identical with it. It is the reality of existence, itself purified of the taints of nonexistence and the marks of the deficiency of possibility. Through its restrictions by conceptual or relational qualifications, distinct existents appear; on that account, real plurality is imagined. Since no demonstration has established the falsity of this, the commentator's assertion that quiddities are not identical remains unproved, as does the common predication of existence; indeed, no possible existent is established at all. [I say:] This lies outside the province of reason. Reason's immediate evidence testifies that existents are genuinely multiple and are essences and realities different in truth, not merely in consideration. Those who hold that view claim support from their unveilings and contemplative witnessings; they maintain it cannot be attained by rational inquiries or their indications. Reason is displaced here, just as sense is in grasping intelligibles. By contrast, those who restrict themselves to the degrees of reason, holding that what reason confirms is accepted and what it rejects is rejected, and that there is no sphere beyond it, allege that, supposing those unveilings and witnessings genuine, they must be interpreted in agreement with reason. Such persons consider reason's immediate testimony sufficient to dispense with a demonstration against doctrines of this sort and deem their admission an obstinacy unworthy of attention.

VOICE: “qīla ʿalayhi” introduces an objection ascribed to a group of Sufis; “aqūlu” is Jurjānī's response. The response describes TWO epistemic orientations; it does not flatly settle which construal of unity Jurjānī himself finally endorses. It is crucial that he identifies the alleged loss of independently existent possibles as a cost of the radical reading. In the second and third glosses he explores a more rationally constrained unity thesis and also marks the limits of dialectical proof. Arabic normalized for spacing and punctuation from Nicholas Heer's transcribed Arabic, PDF printed p. 2; final diplomatic manuscript collation outstanding.

JRG02 — Jurjānī, gloss II: singular reality and the qualified existence of others

al-Sayyid al-Sharīf al-Jurjānī · al-Jurjānī, Ḥāshiyat Sharḥ al-Tajrīd, gloss II; Garrett 865 fol. 22a; Nicholas Heer, Five Unedited Texts, p. 2.

Heer printed introduction and edition verified; manuscript collation pending

وأما إذا قلنا إن [حقيقة] الوجود هي حقيقة مشخصة في حد ذاتها لا تعدد فيها بوجه من الوجوه، وهي قائمة بذاتها لا تطرق إليها عدم أصلا ولا إمكان قطعا، وهي حقيقة الواجب تعالى، ومعنى كون غيره موجودا هو أن لتلك الحقيقة المستغنية عن القيام بغيرها نسبة مخصوصة إلى ذلك الغير، وإن كانت تلك النسبة مجهولة الكيفية، فذلك كلام يعجز عن إدراكه إلا أولو البصائر الذين خصوا من عنده تعالى بفطنة ثاقبة عالية وأوتوا من لدنه حكمة بالغة. وسيرد عليك تفاصيل هذه المعاني إن شاء الله تعالى.

But if we say that the [reality of] existence is a reality individuated in itself, in which there is no multiplicity in any respect, that it is self-subsistent, in no way subject to nonexistence and altogether incapable of possibility, and that it is the reality of the Necessary Existent—so that for anything other than It to exist means that this reality, which needs nothing else in which to subsist, has a certain particular relation to that other thing, even if the manner of this relation is unknown—then this is discourse whose comprehension escapes all save those endowed with insight, whom He Most High has specially granted penetrating intelligence and to whom He has given consummate wisdom. Details of these meanings will come to you, God willing.

Here the “other's” being is explained through a special relation (nisba makhṣūṣa) to the Necessary's unique reality of existence. The relation's mode remains unknown; it is NOT asserted that the other has a divine essence. Brackets around ḥaqīqa are in Heer's transcription, not silently supplied by this edition. PDF printed p. 2; manuscript collation outstanding.

JRG03 — Jurjānī, gloss III: an argument for existence itself and the objection from dependence

al-Sayyid al-Sharīf al-Jurjānī · al-Jurjānī, Ḥāshiyat Sharḥ al-Tajrīd, gloss III; Garrett 865 fols. 62b–63b and Yahuda 5373 fols. 88a–89a; Nicholas Heer, Five Unedited Texts, pp. 2–3.

Heer printed page 3 inspected; manuscript collation and exhaustive variants pending

واعلم أن هذه المباحث التي أوردها الشارح في كون الوجود عين الواجب أو زائدا عليه هي الكلمات الواردة على ألسن القوم في هذا المقام. وههنا مقالة أخرى قد أشرنا فيما سبق أنها مما لا يدركها إلا أولو البصائر والألباب الذين خصوا بحكمة بالغة وفصل الخطاب. فلنفصلها هيهنا بقدر ما يفي به قوة التقرير ويحيط به دائرة التحرير، فنقول وبالله التوفيق فنعم الرفيق: كل مفهوم مغاير للوجود كالإنسان مثلا فإنه ما لم ينضم إليه الوجود بوجه من الوجوه في نفس الأمر لم يكن موجودا فيها قطعا، وما لم يلاحظ العقل انضمام الوجود إليه لم يمكن له الحكم بكونه موجودا، فكل مفهوم مغاير للوجود فهو في كونه موجودا في نفس الأمر يحتاج إلى غيره الذي هو الوجود، وكل ما هو محتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره فهو ممكن إذ لا معنى للممكن إلا ما يحتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره، فكل مفهوم مغاير للوجود فهو ممكن، ولا شيء من الممكن بواجب، فلا شيء من المفهومات المغايرة للوجود بواجب. وقد ثبت بالبرهان أن الواجب موجود، فهو لا يكون إلا عين الوجود الذي هو موجود بذاته لا بأمر مغاير لذاته. ولما وجب أن يكون الواجب جزئيا حقيقيا قائما بذاته ويكون تعينه بذاته لا بأمر زائد على ذاته وجب أن يكون الوجود أيضا كذلك إذ هو عينه فلا يكون الوجود مفهوما كليا يمكن أن يكون له أفراد بل هو في حد ذاته جزئي حقيقي ليس فيه إمكان تعدد ولا انقسام وقائم بذاته منزه عن كونه عارضا لغيره، فيكون الواجب هو الوجود المطلق أي المعرى عن التقيد بغيره والانضمام إليه. وعلى هذا لا يتصور عروض الوجود للماهيات الممكنة، فليس معنى كونها موجودة إلا أن لها نسبة مخصوصة إلى حضرة الوجود القائم بذاته، وتلك النسبة على وجوه مختلفة وأنحاء شتى يتعذر الاطلاع على ماهياتها، فالموجود كلي وإن كان الوجود جزئيا حقيقيا. هذا ملخص ما ذكره بعض المحققين من مشايخنا، قال: ولا يعلمه إلا الراسخون في العلم. فإن قلت: الذي يتبادر إلى الذهن من لفظ الوجود مفهوم لا يمنع الشركة، فكيف يكون جزئيا حقيقيا؟ وأيضا المفهوم من لفظ الوجود ما قام به الوجود كما اشتهر في كلامهم، فكيف يفسر بمعنى لا يفهمه أحد؟ قلت: الجواب عن الأول أن الكلام في حقيقة الوجود لا فيما يتبادر إلى الأذهان من مدلول اللفظ. فإنه يجوز أن يكون مفهوما كليا وعارضا اعتباريا لتلك الحقيقة الممتنعة عن الاشتراك في حد ذاتها كمفهوم الواجب بالقياس إلى حقيقته. وعن الثاني أن المعتبر هو البرهان وما يؤدي إليه لا الاشتهار في ألسنة الأقوام وعقول الأوهام. نعم، يتجه على المقدمة القائلة بأن كل ما هو محتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره فهو ممكن، منع لطيف، وهو أن المحتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غير موجود ممكن قطعا، لا المحتاج في كونه موجودا إلى غيره هو وجوده. ويندفع بنظر دقيق وهو أن ما احتاج في موجوديته إلى غيره فقد استفاد ذلك من غيره وصار معلولا له موقوفا في ذلك عليه وكل ما هو كذلك فهو ممكن سواء سمي ذلك الغير الموقوف عليه وجوده أو موجده. ومما يؤيد كون الوجود عين الواجب أن الوجود في حد ذاته ينافي العدم وهو أبعد المفهومات عن قبول العدم لأن ما عداه لا يمتنع عن قبول العدم لذاته بل بواسطة الوجود ولا شك أن الواجب هو الذي ينافي العدم لذاته لا ما ينافيه بواسطة غيره. ماذا تقول فيمن يرى أن الوجود مع كونه عين الواجب وغير قابل للتجزؤ والانقسام قد انبسط على هياكل الموجودات وظهر فيها فلا يخلو عنه شيء من الأشياء، بل هو حقيقتها وعينها وإنما امتازت وتعددت بتقيدات وتعينات اعتبارية، ويمثل ذلك بالبحر وظهوره في صور الأمواج المتكثرة مع أنه ليس هناك إلا حقيقة البحر فقط؟ قلت: قد سلف من كلامنا أن هذا طور وراء طور العقل لا يتوصل إليه إلا بالمشاهدات الكشفية دون المناظرات العقلية. وكل ميسر لما خلق له والله المستعان وعليه التكلان.

Know that the questions the commentator introduced about whether existence is identical with the Necessary Existent or additional to Him are the expressions current among the group in this discussion. There is another position, previously indicated, whose grasp belongs only to those of insight and understanding who have received profound wisdom and decisive speech. Let us set it out as far as exposition permits, seeking God's help. Every concept other than existence—for example, humanity—cannot exist in reality unless existence is joined to it in some respect. Nor can the intellect judge it to exist without considering that conjunction. Thus whatever is conceptually different from existence requires something other than itself—existence—for its actuality. Whatever needs another for its actuality is possible, for possibility is just such a need. Every concept other than existence is therefore possible; nothing possible is necessary; hence none of those other concepts is the Necessary. Now demonstration establishes that the Necessary exists. It must therefore be existence itself, which exists through itself rather than through a distinct constituent. Since the Necessary must be an individual reality subsisting through itself and individuated by itself rather than through something added, existence itself must be so too, because it is identical with the Necessary. Existence is not, on that understanding, a universal with several extramental instances: in itself it is an individual reality incapable of multiplication or division, independent of a substrate, never an accident of something else. The Necessary is accordingly absolute existence—that is, existence free of limitation by, or conjunction with, another thing. Existence cannot in this account inhere in possible quiddities. That they exist means only that they stand in a distinctive relation to the presence of self-subsistent existence. These relations are diverse in modes and kinds; their essences resist comprehension. Thus the predicate “existent” has universal application, even though existence itself is an individual reality. This summarizes what some investigating masters among our teachers said; one of them adds that only those firmly rooted in knowledge know it. If you object: What occurs to the mind on hearing 'existence' is a concept open to common participation. How can it be a genuine individual? Moreover, on the customary account 'existent' signifies that in which existence inheres; how can one explain it by something nobody understands? I reply: First, we are concerned with the reality of existence, not with the mental content conveyed by the word. The latter can be universal and an intellectual attribute of a reality that itself admits no shared instantiation, as the concept of the Necessary relates to its reality. Second, what counts is demonstration and its conclusions, not a notion's circulation in common speech or imagination. There is, however, a subtle objection to the premise that anything needing something else in order to exist is possible: one may concede this when what is needed is some OTHER existent, but not when what is needed is the thing's own existence. A careful response is that whatever derives its actuality from another is thereby an effect dependent upon it; anything so dependent is possible, whether that upon which it depends is called its 'existence' or its 'giver of existence'. Another supporting argument for identifying existence with the Necessary is that existence as such excludes nonexistence. Among our concepts it is the furthest from admitting nonexistence; everything else is free of nonexistence only through existence, whereas the Necessary excludes nonexistence intrinsically. What, then, of one who holds that existence, although identical with the Necessary and not divisible into parts, extends over the structures of all existents and appears within them, so that nothing is devoid of it and it is their very reality, with differences and multiplicity arising solely from conceptual restrictions and determinations—like the sea appearing as many waves when there is in truth only the sea? I reply: As was said earlier, this is a sphere beyond the sphere of reason. It is approached through unveiled witnessings, not rational disputations. Each is facilitated toward that for which he was created. God is the source of help, and upon Him is reliance.

ARGUMENT MAP (speaker carefully distinguished): (1) Report of the masters, introduced as a position rather than an unqualified dogma; (2) need for 'existence' -> possibility; (3) necessity -> existence itself; (4) difference between universal concept and indivisible reality; (5) explicitly stated subtle objection that needing 'one's existence' does not automatically mean needing ANOTHER existent; (6) reply by treating borrowed actuality as dependency; (7) final sea/waves thesis is withheld from rational demonstration. The sentence 'fa-l-mawjūd kullī wa-in kāna al-wujūd juzʾiyyan ḥaqīqiyyan' is an especially significant terminological distinction, and requires comparison with Garrett manuscript before final printing. Arabic manually rekeyed from Heer's published transcription (PDF printed pp. 2–3); punctuation editorial. A word-by-word diplomatic collation with the manuscripts and Heer's variants has not been completed. | TEXTUAL WITNESS: Hussein b. Muʿīn al-Dīn al-Maybudī quotes this direct Tajrīd gloss in his Persian Sharḥ Dīwān, printed p. 50, ed. Ḥasan Raḥmānī and Sayyid Ibrāhīm Ashk Shīrīn (https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/17503/118?lang=ar). Both that witness and Heer's published Arabic read «ولما وجب» (causal 'since') rather than «ولو وجب» ('if'); the working translation now follows the former. Al-Maybudī's quotation adds «ولو كان ذلك الغير وجوده» within the possible-being premise, whereas the Heer working base text used here lacks that clause. It also reads «عين الواجب» where Heer has «عين الوجود» in the immediately following conclusion. These are documented variant readings, NOT silently harmonized readings; manuscript collation is still needed.

LAH01 — Lāhījī, Ishāra ʿirfāniyya: degrees of a single reality of existence

إشارة عرفانية: اعلم أن ما نقلنا من بعضهم سابقا في توجيه كلام الصوفية في وحدة الوجود مما يناسب مذهب الحكماء على ما حققنا من تحقق الحقائق المختلفة للوجود. فإنه إذا كان للوجود حقائق مختلفة متحققة ويمكن أن يتفطن بكون تلك الحقائق غير مختلفة بتمام الحقيقة، بل بالشدة والضعف. فيكون الوجود حقيقة واحدة متفاوتة في المظاهر التي هي الماهيات بحسب الشدة والضعف، والكمال والنقص. ولما كانت الوجودات المتفاوتة قائمة بالماهيات متعينة بتعيناتها، لم

An allusion for those versed in mystical knowledge. Know that the earlier interpretation we cited from certain thinkers of the Sufis' discourse on unity of existence accords with the philosophers' doctrine, on the analysis we have given that distinct realities of existence obtain. For if existence has distinct, actual realities, one can discern that these realities differ not in their whole reality but in intensity and weakness. Existence would then be one reality, varying in its manifestations—namely the quiddities—according to intensity and weakness, perfection and imperfection. And since these differentiated existences subsist in quiddities and are determined through their determinations, they do not ... [sentence continues on p. 469].

The section begins mid-page. This is the *beginning* of the named Ishāra, NOT the preceding proof of simplicity. Translation intentionally ends at a page break; continue with LAH02. Lāhījī here presents a potentially reconciling reading, not yet his subsequent challenge. Footnote 5 analogizes degrees of whiteness in snow and paper, not differences of man, horse and sheep. LAH02 — Lāhījī: what the philosophers and the Sufis locate in the Necessary

يلزم أن يكون اختلافها في نفس حقيقة الوجود، ليلزم التشكيك في الذاتي، بل في تعيناتها التابعة للماهيات المختلفة. وهذا في الحقيقة اختلاف في ظهور آثار الوجود قلة وكثرة. بل لما كان اختلاف الوجودات كما عرفت تبعا لاختلاف الماهيات، فمع قطع النظر عن الماهيات لا اختلاف في حقيقة الوجود من حيث هي أصلا. فيكون الفرق بين هذا المذهب، ومذهب الحكماء، أنهم يخصون الواجبية بمرتبة واحدة؛ هي تلك الحقيقة بشرط أن لا يتعين بشيء من الماهيات. والصوفية يجعلون الواجبية لتلك الحقيقة؛ لا بشرط أن يتعين بشيء من الماهيات. فيكون كل حقيقة وجودية واجبة، إذا اعتبرت من حيث هي هي، مقطوعة النظر عن التعين. وممكنة باعتبار أخذها بشرط التعين. فتكون الممكنات في الحقيقة هي التعينات. والواجب هو الحقيقة المطلقة، فلا يلزم تعدد وتكثر فيما هو واجب، ولا كون شيء من الممكنات فردا للواجب.

... it does not follow that their difference is within the reality of existence itself, thereby introducing gradation into what is essential; rather, the difference lies in their determinations that follow upon differing quiddities. In truth, this is a difference in the appearance of existence's effects, in greater and lesser measure. Indeed, because the differences among existences, as explained, follow upon the differences among quiddities, if we abstract from quiddities there is no difference whatsoever in the reality of existence considered in itself. The difference between this doctrine and that of the philosophers is therefore that the philosophers reserve necessity for one level: that reality on condition that it is not determined by any quiddity. The Sufis, however, ascribe necessity to that reality without the condition of its not being determined by a quiddity. Every existent reality is thus necessary when considered as it is in itself, abstracting from determination, and is possible when taken on condition of determination. Possibles are therefore in truth the determinations, while the Necessary is the absolute reality. Consequently, there is neither multiplication nor plurality in what is Necessary, nor does any possible thing become an instance of the Necessary.

Faithful to the named comparison between a philosophical 'bi-sharṭ lā' (on the condition of no determination) and a Sufi 'lā bi-sharṭ' (without the condition of no determination). These qualifying constructions are not interchangeable. A reading of this PAGE ALONE must not be presented as Lāhījī's final assent: by p. 473 he objects to an inferred monopoly of independent existence. The critical middle pages 470–472 have not yet been obtained; this remains a discontinuous edition.

إنما يسلم في الوجود القائم بذاته، وهو الذي لا يمكن أن يكون قائما بماهية من الماهيات. ولا شبهة في كونه واجب الوجود. فمن أين يلزم أنه لا يكون وجود غير ذلك قائما بالماهيات الممكنة وأن يكون كل حقيقة وجودية قائمة بذاتها؟ وما ذكر من وجوب كون الوجود جزئيا حقيقيا، إنما هو في حقيقة وجودية قائمة بذاتها. فمن أين يلزم أن مفهوم الوجود الذي هو الكون في الأعيان ليس بكلي، وليس له أفراد حقيقية بعضها قائم بذاته وبعضها قائم بالماهيات الممكنة؟ فإن بنى على ذلك ما بنى عليه مذهب المتكلمين، من وجوه الإشكالات المذكورة، فوجوه الدفع أيضا قد عرفت مع أن الكلام في هذا البيان المنقول، وأنه كيف يدل على ذلك المطلوب؟ وإنما ثبتنا في هذه المسألة بهذا التطويل الذي لم يكن عنه من محيد، لكونها أهم أصول المعرفة وأعظم مسائل التوحيد.

That is granted only for existence subsisting through itself, which cannot subsist in any quiddity; there is no doubt that such existence is necessary. But whence does it follow that there cannot be some other existence subsisting in possible quiddities, or that every reality of existence must subsist through itself? The argument that existence must be a real individual applies only to a reality of existence that subsists through itself. How, then, does it follow that the concept of existence—being in external realities—is not universal, with genuine instances, some subsisting through themselves and others in possible quiddities? If the objections the theologians advance are built upon the interpretation in question, their replies too have already been explained. But our present discussion concerns this reported argument and how it is supposed to demonstrate the conclusion claimed. We have remained so long with this question, with no way to avoid doing so, because it is among the most important principles of knowledge of God and the greatest questions of divine unity.

This is a counter-argument, not a Sufi slogan. The question is whether the uniqueness of an intrinsically necessary individual existence implies that there cannot be dependent existences. The quantifier is critical: all real existence need not be independent simply because one independent existence is necessary. Footnote 1 clarifies 'ʿalā dhālika' as referring to the Sayyid's interpretation; footnote 2 identifies the 'reported explanation' as the Sufis'. This page is the CONCLUSION of a longer dialectic, and should not be presented as an uninterrupted full Ishāra until pp. 470–472 are checked.

فليس هذا دليلا ولا برهانا على اصطلاح علم الميزان، نعم إذا استدل بالواجب الوجود على صفاته وآثاره لكان برهانا لميا كما يجيء في كلام الشيخ عن قريب أن طريقة الصديقين أنهم يستشهدون به لا عليه، أي يستشهدون بالواجب الوجود على غيره لا عليه بغيره، والمصنف رحمه الله تعالى سلك هذا المسلك في كتابه إذ هو استدل بوجوب وجوده على صفاته. قال الشيخ الرئيس في كتاب المبدأ والمعاد بعد الفراغ من تقرير هذا المنهج: أنا أثبتنا الواجب الوجود لا من جهة أفعاله ولا من جهة حركته، فلم يكن القياس (أي هذا القياس) دليلا ولا أيضا برهانا محضا، فالأول ليس عليه برهان محض، بل كان قياسا شبيها بالبرهان لأنه استدلال من حال الوجود أنه يقتضي واجبا الخ. أقول: فالشارح إنما أطلق عليه الاستدلال اللمي أي البرهان لأنه يشبه به كما وقع في كلام الشيخ. وقال صاحب الشوارق: إن وجه كون هذا الطريق أشبه بالبرهان أي اللمي هو ما أشار إليه الشيخ من أن الواجب وإن لم يفعل شيئا ولم يظهر منه أثر يمكن بهذا القياس أن يثبت، وذلك لأن القياسات الإنية إنما تكون من الأفعال والآثار بخلاف اللمية، فهذا الطريق لكونه لا من جهة الآثار يشبه اللم، ومن جهة أنه ليس من العلة ليس به.

This is neither an inference nor a demonstration in the technical terminology of logic. Certainly, if one argued from the Necessary Existent to His attributes and effects, it would be a demonstration through the reason why (limmī). This accords with the Philosopher's statement that the way of the truthful is to take Him as witness for other things, rather than to infer Him from other things. The author [Ṭūsī] follows this course in his book by arguing from the necessity of God's existence to His attributes. [Ibn Sīnā, quoted from al-Mabdaʾ wa-l-maʿād:] 'We established the Necessary Existent neither by way of His acts nor by way of His motion. Thus this inference was neither an indication nor a pure demonstration. No pure demonstration proves the First; rather, our reasoning was akin to a demonstration, because it argued from the state of existence that existence requires something necessary.' [Ṭihrānī:] I say: The commentator called it a limmī inference—that is, a demonstration—only because it resembles one, as the Philosopher himself put it. [Lāhījī, quoted from the Shawāriq:] What makes this route like a limmī demonstration is what the Philosopher indicated: the Necessary can be established by this reasoning even if He had effected nothing and no effect had appeared from Him. Inferential demonstrations (innī) proceed from acts and effects, unlike limmī demonstrations. Since this path does not start from effects, it resembles a limmī proof; but since it does not start from a cause, it is not one.

SPEAKER BREAKS: the 'Shaykh al-Raʾīs' is Ibn Sīnā, not the author of Tawḍīḥ; 'ṣāḥib al-Shawāriq' means Lāhījī. The challenge is rigorous: demonstrating that a necessary being must exist by examining existence differs from inferring a cause from its effects, yet is not a strict explanatory syllogism from a prior cause. Page 425, HTML transcription, printed page number confirmed. Translation is bounded and opens in a continued sentence.

قول المصنف: وهي واجبة لاشتمالها الخ — يدل هذا الكلام أن للإنسان تكاليف عقلية وتكاليف سمعية، وهو المشهور. ولكن المفيد رحمه الله تعالى قال في أوائل المقالات: إن العقل لا ينفك عن سمع وإن التكليف لا يصح إلا بالرسل، واتفقت الإمامية على أن العقل يحتاج في علمه ونتائجه إلى السمع، وأنه غير منفك عن سمع ينبه الغافل على كيفية الاستدلال، وأنه لا بد في أول التكليف وابتدائه في العالم من رسول. أقول: الحق مع المفيد رحمه الله وإن خالفه أقوام حتى بعض الإمامية بظاهر كلامهم، لأن العقل البشري له مقام القبول والاستعداد فلا بد له في مقام الحكم والاستدلال من تنبيه وإفاضة من العالين ولو قبل هذه النشأة، وأما الأشاعرة فيعزلون العقل بالكلية على أصلهم كما مر. قول الشارح: بأن التكاليف السمعية الخ — إيضاح هذا الاستدلال أن الإنسان بمجرد عقله يعمل بالتكاليف العقلية، ولكن الشرع إذا أتى بالتكاليف الأخرى وواظب الإنسان عليها كان للعمل بالتكاليف العقلية أقرب وأحفظ فيحصل اللطف في حكم العقل بالشرع. أقول: هذا الاستدلال لضعفه لا يقوم على ساق، والحق أن علة وجوب البعثة هي علة حسنها، وهي تلك الفوائد التي أنهاها المصنف إلى قوله: فيحصل اللطف للمكلف.

[Ṭihrānī introducing the author's lemma:] 'It [the prophetic mission] is obligatory because it includes ...' This implies that human beings have rational duties and duties known through revelation, as is commonly held. However, al-Mufīd said in Awāʾil al-maqālāt that reason is never without hearing [revealed teaching], and that imposition of duty is not sound except through messengers. He reports the Imāmī agreement that reason needs revealed instruction for its knowledge and results, and requires a message that alerts the heedless to the manner of inference, so that at the beginning of religious obligation there must be a messenger. [Ṭihrānī:] I say that al-Mufīd is right, despite dissent, even among some Imāmīs in the apparent sense of their remarks. For human reason occupies a state of receptivity and preparedness; in judging and inferring it therefore needs an awakening and effusion from higher beings, even if that occurs before this earthly life. The Ashʿarīs, by contrast, exclude reason entirely according to their principle, as discussed earlier. [Explaining the commentator's argument:] A human being observes rational duties by reason alone. But if religious law brings further duties and a person perseveres in them, that person comes closer to and better preserves the performance of rational duties. Thus revelation becomes a gracious assistance (luṭf) to rational judgment. [Ṭihrānī:] I say: This argument is too weak to stand. Rather, the reason that prophetic missions are obligatory is the same reason they are good: the benefits that the author itemized up to his words 'and grace is thereby realized for the responsible person'.

These paragraphs cover the page break between printed pp. 643–644. This is a dispute WITHIN the discussion of prophetic missions; not a blanket claim that unveiled mystical experience displaces rational proof. Ṭihrānī explicitly endorses al-Mufīd on reason's need for guidance yet rejects the commentator's narrower argument for prophetic necessity. His claim about Ashʿarīs is a polemical attribution, not a neutral fact about all Sunni theology. The initial al-Mufīd text is quoted here in Ṭihrānī's reporting; direct verification against Awāʾil al-maqālāt remains outstanding.

Quṭb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī · Quṭb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī, Sharḥ Ḥikmat al-ishrāq, printed p. 346, ch. 10.

إذا كان عدم الحجاب كافيا في العلم الإشراقي الحضوري، ونور الأنوار نور محض، لا يمكن احتجابه عن ذاته ولا احتجاب غيره من الموجودات العقلية والحسية عنه. فنور الأنوار ظاهر لذاته، أي مدرك لها، على ما سبق بيانه في كل مجرد، وغيره ظاهر له، فيكون مدركا له، «لا يعزب عنه مثقال ذرة في السماوات ولا في الأرض» إذ لا يحجبه شيء عن شيء. وإذ لم يحجبه شيء عن شيء، فيدرك جميع الأشياء بالإشراق الحضوري، الذي هو أشرف أنحاء الإدراك، لا بصور في ذاته، فيتكثر ذاته المقدسة وجهاته، لكونه فاعلا وقابلا، مع أن جهة الفعل غير جهة القبول، فلا يكون واحدا حقيقيا.

If the absence of a veil suffices for illuminative, presentational knowledge, and the Light of Lights is pure light, it cannot be veiled from itself, nor can other intelligible and sensible existents be veiled from it. Thus the Light of Lights is manifest to itself—that is, knows itself, as explained previously for every immaterial being—and other things are manifest to it, and therefore known by it: 'Not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or the earth escapes Him,' since nothing conceals one thing from Him by another. Since nothing conceals any thing from Him, He knows all things through knowledge by presence and illumination, the noblest mode of cognition, not through forms inhering in His essence. Were such forms to inhere in Him, His sacred essence and aspects would be multiplied, because He would be both agent and recipient, although the aspect of acting differs from that of receiving; He would no longer be genuinely one.

This is a *parallel Illuminationist primary source* from a commentary on Suhrawardī's Ḥikmat al-ishrāq, not a Tajrīd ḥāshiya. The chapter opening on this same page discusses visual perception and the elimination of the opacity/barrier model; this bounded argument is the theological application. Printed text on web is a mixed commentary context: a close critical edition must compare the base lemma with the Shīrāzī gloss before assigning each sentence exclusively to Shīrāzī.

New continuation: printed/digital text; manuscript collation pending

فإن ما يجد الإنسان من نفسه عند عرض المسائل علم بالقوة يجد من نفسه ملكة وقدرة على الجواب لهذه المسائل المذكورة. وهذه القوة أقرب إلى الوجود مما كانت، أي من القوة التي كانت قبل السؤال، فإن للقوة مراتب بحسب البعد والقرب من الوجود، ولا يكون للإنسان علما بجواب كل واحد من تلك المسائل على الخصوص ما لم يكن عنده صورة كل واحد واحد. وواجب الوجود منزه عن هذه الأشياء: حلول الصورة فيه، وكون علمه بالقوة، فلا يكون علمه بالموجودات على الوجه المذكور.

What someone discovers within himself when questions are put to him is knowledge in potency: he finds a habitual disposition and capacity to answer those questions. This potency is nearer actuality than before the question was posed, since potencies have degrees according to their remoteness from, or nearness to, existence. But one does not have distinct knowledge of the answer to every single one of those questions unless one possesses its particular form. The Necessary Existent is exempt from all these features: the inherence of a form within Him and the possession of knowledge only potentially. His knowledge of existents cannot take the form just described.

The passage distinguishes (a) potency prior to being asked, (b) acquired readiness/habit (malaka, qudra), and (c) determinate actual knowledge. 'Quwwa' here is cognitive potency, and 'qudra' the capacity to answer, not the same technical meaning. Compare with Suhrawardī base text and Shahrāzūrī before attributing the wording of each lemma to Quṭb. The preceding passage on p. 349 argues that actual knowledge of a necessary concomitant is not automatically the actual knowledge of what it entails.

TAF01 — al-Taftāzānī: the common concept of existence and the competing ontologies

Saʿd al-Dīn al-Taftāzānī · al-Taftāzānī, Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid, digital numbered p. 61 (Usul.ai, 1981 edition metadata), existence as shared concept vs real ontology.

Usul.ai page 61 checked 2026-10-29; printed-page/MS collation pending

قال: البحث الثاني: المنقول عن الشيخ أبي الحسن الأشعري أن وجود كل شيء عين ذاته، وليس للفظ الوجود مفهوم واحد مشترك بين الوجودات، بل الاشتراك لفظي. والجمهور على أن له مفهوما واحدا مشتركا بين الوجودات، إلا أنه عند المتكلمين حقيقة واحدة تختلف بالقيود والإضافات، حتى أن وجود الواجب هو كونه في الأعيان على ما يعقل من كون الإنسان، وإنما الاختلاف في الماهية، فالوجود معنى زائد على الماهية في الواجب والممكن جميعا. وعند الفلاسفة وجود الواجب مخالف لوجود الممكن في الحقيقة، واشتراكهما في مفهوم الكون اشتراك معروضين في لازم خارجي غير مقوم، وهو في الممكن زائد على الماهية عقلا، وفي الواجب نفس الماهية، بمعنى أنه لا ماهية للواجب سوى الوجود الخاص المجرد عن مقارنة الماهية، بخلاف الإنسان فإن له ماهية هو الحيوان الناطق ووجودا هو الكون في الأعيان. فوقع البحث في ثلاث مقامات: أنه مشترك معنى، وأنه زائد ذهنا، وأنه في الواجب زائد أيضا. والإنصاف أن الأولين بديهيان، والمذكور في معرض الاستدلال تنبيهات. فعلى الأول وجوه: الأول أنا إذا نظرنا في الحادث جزمنا بأن له مؤثرا مع التردد في كونه واجبا أو ممكنا، عرضا أو جوهرا، متحيزا وغير متحيز، ومع تبدل اعتقاد كونه ممكنا إلى اعتقاد كونه واجبا إلى غير ذلك من الخصوصيات، فبالضرورة يكون الأمر المقطوع به الباقي مع التردد في الخصوصيات وتبدل الاعتقادات مشتركا بين الكل.

[The section introduces a reported position:] The view transmitted from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī is that the existence of each thing is identical with that thing's essence and that 'existence' has no one concept shared by existents; the word is common only by homonymy. The majority maintain that it has one concept common to existents. According to the theologians, however, it is one reality differentiated by qualifications and relations, such that the Necessary's existence is His being in the external world, just as one understands a human being's existence. The difference lies in quiddity: existence is additional to the quiddity of the Necessary and of the possible alike. According to the philosophers, the Necessary's existence differs in reality from possible existence; their shared concept of 'being' pertains to subjects possessing a non-constitutive concomitant. In possibles, existence is intellectually additional to quiddity; in the Necessary it is His very essence, meaning He has no quiddity beyond His specific existence, unmixed with any other quiddity. A human being, by contrast, has the quiddity 'rational animal' and existence as being in the external world. Three questions arise: whether existence has one meaning; whether it is additional in intellect; and whether it is also additional in the Necessary. Fairness demands that the first two are self-evident; the arguments advanced are reminders. The first reminder for shared meaning is that, upon considering a newly arisen thing, we are certain that it has an agent while remaining undecided whether that agent is necessary or possible, accident or substance, spatial or non-spatial; our opinion of these particularities may change. Necessarily, then, what remains certain throughout these doubts and changes is common to all the alternatives.

SOURCE AND VOICE: “al-manqūl ʿan al-Shaykh Abī al-Ḥasan” explicitly attributes the first view to al-Ashʿarī as reported by al-Taftāzānī; it is NOT a direct quotation from al-Ashʿarī. The “majority,” “theologians” and “philosophers” are a doxographical map offered by al-Taftāzānī, not uniformly accepted self-descriptions. The first reminder supports a shared concept/predicable and does NOT by itself prove the identity of extramental realities. The following printed page explicitly warns that none of these proofs demonstrates that real existences are ontically identical. The final two reminders, further objection/reply and printed edition collation remain to be incorporated in full. Digital page 61 identified on Usul.ai, edition metadata first edition 1401/1981; printed pagination has not been independently checked against facsimile.

وأما تفصيلا فعن الأول أن قيامه بالماهية من حيث هي هي، لا بالماهية المعدومة ليلزم التناقض، ولا بالماهية الموجودة ليلزم الدور أو التسلسل. فإن قيل: إن أريد بالماهية من حيث هي هي ما لا يكون الوجود أو العدم نفسها ولا جزءا منها على ما قيل فغير مفيد، لأن العروض كاف في لزوم المحالات؛ وإن أريد ما لا يكون موجودا ولا معدوما لا بالعروض ولا بغيره فالتناقض فيه أظهر، لأن اللاوجود نقيض الوجود بلا نزاع ولا اشتباه. قلنا: المراد ما لا يعتبر فيه الوجود ولا العدم، وإن كان لا ينفك عن أحدهما في الخارج. فإن قيل: عدم الانفكاك عن أحدهما كاف في لزوم المحال، لأنه إن قارن العدم فيناقض أو الوجود فيدور أو يتسلسل. قلنا: قيام الوجود بالماهية أمر عقلي، ليس كقيام البياض بالجسم ليلزم تقدمها عليه بالوجود تقدما ذاتيا أو زمانيا فتلزم المحالات، بل غاية الأمر أنه يلزم تقدمها عليه بالوجود العقلي ولا استحالة فيه، لجواز أن تلاحظ وحدها من غير ملاحظة وجود خارجي أو ذهني، ويكون لها وجود ذهني لا بملاحظة العقل؛ فإن عدم الاعتبار غير اعتبار العدم. وإن اعتبر العقل وجودها الذهني لم يلزم التسلسل، بل ينقطع بانقطاع الاعتبار. وعن الثاني أنا نختار أن الوجود موجود ولا نسلم لزوم التسلسل؛ وإنما يلزم لو كان وجوده أيضا زائدا عليه وليس كذلك، بل وجوده عينه وإنما النزاع في غيره، والأدلة إنما قامت عليه. وتحقيق ذلك أنه لما كان تحقق كل شيء بالوجود فبالضرورة يكون تحققه بنفسه من غير احتياج إلى وجود آخر يقوم به، كما أنه لما كان التقدم والتأخر فيما بين الأشياء بالزمان كانا فيما بين أجزائه بالذات من غير افتقار إلى زمان آخر. فإن قيل فيكون كل وجود واجبا إذ لا معنى له سوى ما يكون تحققه بنفسه. قلنا ممنوع، فإن معنى وجود الواجب بنفسه أنه مقتضى ذاته من غير احتياج إلى فاعل، ومعنى تحقق الوجود بنفسه أنه إذا حصل للشيء إما من ذاته كما في الواجب أو من غيره كما في الممكن لم يفتقر تحققه إلى وجود آخر يقوم به.

In reply to the first objection, the inherence of existence pertains to the quiddity as such: not to a nonexistent quiddity (which would be contradictory), nor to an already existent one (which would cause a circle or an infinite regress). An objector presses: If 'quiddity as such' only means that neither existence nor nonexistence is identical with it or part of it, that does not solve the paradox; and if it means a quiddity neither existent nor nonexistent in any sense, that is yet more contradictory. We answer that neither existence nor nonexistence is being taken into consideration, although in external reality the thing cannot be without one or the other. The objector replies that this inseparability is enough to restore the paradox: if nonexistence accompanies it, there is contradiction; if existence does, there is circularity or regress. We answer: existence's 'inherence' in quiddity is an affair of intellect, not like whiteness's inherence in a body, which would entail that the substrate has priority of existence, whether essentially or temporally. At most the quiddity has priority in intellectual consideration, and there is nothing impossible about this. The intellect may consider it alone, without considering its external or mental existence, even while it has mental existence independently of that particular act of considering. For *not considering* something is different from *considering its absence*. And if the intellect considers its mental existence in turn, this does not force a real infinite regress: it ends when the act of considering ends. As to the second objection, we can affirm that existence itself exists without conceding a regress. The regress would follow only if its existence too were additional to it, which it is not; its existence is identical with itself. The disagreement concerns other things, to which the proofs pertain. Since all things are actual through existence, existence necessarily is actual through itself without requiring another existence inhering in it—just as, although priority and posteriority among things are by time, those relations among time's own parts are by time's very essence, without requiring a further time. If one then objects that each existence would be necessary because each is actual through itself, we reject the inference. For the Necessary to exist through itself is for existence to be demanded by its essence without need of an agent. For existence itself to be actual through itself merely means that, whether it comes to a thing from its essence (as with the Necessary) or from another (as with a possible), its actuality needs no second existence inhering in it.

STRUCTURE: direct response to two opposite attempts to treat the existential addition like a real accident in a previously actual subject. Taftāzānī makes the unconsidered/nonexistent distinction precise: ʿadam al-iʿtibār ≠ iʿtibār al-ʿadam. He also sharply differentiates (i) being self-actualizing in the sense of existence's not needing another 'existence' and (ii) the Necessary's causal independence. These are central checks on loose analogies between vertical preservation, participation and formal mediation. Digital Arabic source p. 69 has an unpunctuated transcription; punctuation and paragraphing here are editorial. The surrounding objections are on p. 68, and a further continuation follows the selected excerpt on p. 69; neither should be treated as included in this bounded unit.

والحاصل أنه على تقدير وقوع التشكيك بالشدة أو الزيادة في الذاتي ثلاث احتمالات: الأول: أن لا يشتمل الأشد والأزيد على أمر ليس في الأضعف والأنقص. وهذا يستلزم أن لا يكون هاهنا تشكيك أصلا لا في الذاتي ولا في غيره. الثاني: أن يتحقق ذلك الأمر ويكون داخلا في مفهوم المشكك؛ وهذا يستلزم عدم اشتراكهما ضرورة انتفاء جزئه في الأضعف. الثالث: أن يتحقق ويكون خارجا عن مفهومه. هذا وإن لم يستلزم انتفاء التشكيك مطلقا، لكنه يستلزم انتفاء التشكيك في الذاتي.

In sum, if gradation by intensity or increase is supposed to occur in what belongs to a thing essentially, three alternatives arise. First, the more intense or greater contains nothing that the weaker or lesser lacks; in that case there is no gradation, whether essential or otherwise. Second, it contains something of this kind included within the concept shared by the gradated cases; then the weaker cannot share that concept, since it lacks part of it. Third, it contains such a difference outside the concept. This does not exclude gradation altogether, but it does exclude gradation in what is essential.
